text:
M. and Others v. Italy and Bulgaria (App. no. 40020/03, ECtHR, 31 July 2012) concerned four Bulgarian nationals of Roma origin: L.M., who was a minor at the time; her parents S.M. and I.I.; and her sister-in-law K.L. They alleged violations of Articles 3, 4, 13 and 14 of the Convention arising from events in Italy in May–June 2003.

The applicants claimed they travelled to Italy after X, a Serbian Roma man, promised work and accommodated them in a villa in Ghislarengo. After several days, X allegedly said his nephew Y wanted to marry L.M. When her parents refused, X threatened them with a gun; they were beaten, threatened with death, and forced to return to Bulgaria on 18 May 2003, leaving L.M. behind. L.M. alleged that she was then kept under constant surveillance, forced to steal, beaten, threatened with death, and repeatedly raped by Y while tied to a bed. During one forced robbery she was injured and taken to hospital, but the family removed her before treatment. On 24 May 2003 the mother returned to Italy and complained to Turin police that she and her husband had been beaten and threatened and that L.M. had been kidnapped and might be forced into prostitution.

On 11 June 2003, eighteen days after the complaint, Italian police raided the villa, found L.M., and made arrests. At the police station, L.M. and her mother alleged they were treated roughly, threatened with perjury and libel charges, denied proper interpretation or legal assistance, and forced to sign documents they did not understand. L.M. was later placed in a shelter and then returned to Bulgaria. The applicants claimed that no effective investigation followed against the alleged kidnappers and that Italian authorities failed to cooperate with Bulgaria to question the father.

The Italian Government disputed this account. It stated that the complaint was promptly transmitted to Vercelli police and prosecutors; police identified and surveilled the villa and raided it on 11 June. After questioning L.M., her mother, and X, Y and Z, and after photographs appeared to show a wedding and payment of a bride price, the prosecutor concluded that the events involved a consensual marriage agreement, not kidnapping. Proceedings were therefore opened against L.M. and her mother for perjury and false accusations. The juvenile case against L.M. was later dropped as socially irrelevant; the mother was acquitted in 2006 because the evidence did not establish guilt. The Bulgarian Government largely relied on the Italian account and said Bulgarian authorities forwarded the father’s complaint to the embassy and helped contact Italian authorities.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants principally alleged that Italy failed to take adequate steps to prevent L.M.’s ill-treatment by the Serbian family, especially by securing her swift release, and failed to conduct an effective investigation into that ill-treatment. They also alleged ill-treatment by Italian police during questioning, lack of lawyer and interpreter safeguards, discriminatory treatment as Roma and Bulgarian nationals, and inadequate assistance from Bulgarian consular authorities. The case thus centred on whether the States complied with positive obligations to protect a minor from serious abuse, investigate credible allegations of ill-treatment, and ensure fair treatment during police questioning.

**Rooney v. Ireland** (Application no. 32614/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case brought by John Rooney, an Irish farmer and barrister, against Ireland. He complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention about the excessive length of two civil actions he began in 1987 and 1995, and about the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay. The Court noted that the issues raised were already addressed in well-established case law, particularly **McFarlane v. Ireland**.

**The 1987 Proceedings.** In November 1987, after some of Rooney’s cattle were destroyed under a Government scheme to eradicate bovine tuberculosis, he began a High Court action challenging the scheme’s constitutionality. The litigation became procedurally complex. There were repeated hearings in 1988 concerning discovery, amendments to pleadings, and motions to join defendants. In February 1990, the High Court refused judgment in default of defence, struck out his case against some defendants, and refused to appoint a shorthand writer. Rooney appealed to the Supreme Court in March 1990. In October 1990, the Supreme Court directed a special case to be heard in the High Court and adjourned the appeal. The High Court rejected the special case in May 1991; appeals were rejected by the Supreme Court in December 1991. Crucially, while the Supreme Court upheld the striking out of claims against certain defendants, it failed to deal with the High Court’s refusal of judgment in default of defence.

Over the following decade, Rooney tried to reopen the appeals because of that omission. In December 2000 and July 2001, the Supreme Court refused to set aside its judgments, and in October 2001 it made a vexatious litigant order against him. Later procedural steps were repeatedly adjourned or blocked by that order. In 2006 the High Court allowed him to re-enter a motion, but in 2007 refused to hear it because of the vexatious litigant order. On appeal, in March 2010, the Supreme Court found that claims outside the special case could still be pursued and that the 2007 High Court decision was incorrect. It also acknowledged a clear “oversight” in failing to determine part of his earlier appeal concerning judgment in default. The Government claimed Rooney had orally agreed not to proceed with that part, but produced no court order confirming this. A later High Court decision in November 2010 rejected his amendment claim; an appeal remained pending.

**The 1995 Proceedings.** From April 1993 to July 1996, Rooney’s cattle herd was restricted under the same TB scheme because of suspected infection. In November 1995, he began a High Court action claiming the restriction was unlawful and that the scheme breached statute, the Constitution, the Convention and EU law. Discovery was ordered in December 1997. A Notice to Admit Facts was refused in 2002, and a Notice of Trial was served in December 2002. The High Court heard the action over ten days in May and June 2004 and dismissed his claims in July 2004. Rooney appealed in August 2004. He filed submissions in July 2006 and a Certificate of Readiness in January 2007. In May 2009, the registrar stated that the waiting time after readiness was 31 months. The appeal was eventually heard with another appeal in October 2009, but the Supreme Court initially omitted to rule on it. After further initiatives, the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal in November 2010.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the exceptional duration of both civil actions, repeated adjournments and procedural omissions by the domestic courts, and the alleged lack of any effective domestic remedy to address that delay.

**Case Summary: Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė v. Lithuania (Application no. 20376/05)**

The applicant, Jolanta Varapnickaitė-Mažylienė, a Lithuanian national born in 1960, was engaged in protracted custody proceedings concerning her son with her former husband. The case before the European Court of Human Rights concerned the alleged violation of her right to respect for private life under Article 8 of the Convention, and her claim that she lacked an effective remedy under Article 13.

The facts centre on a series of media publications in 2001. On 31 March 2001, the daily newspaper *Respublika* published, at the applicant’s own expense, an open letter she had written to the Children’s Rights Ombudsman complaining about the Children’s Welfare Service (CWS). In this letter she disclosed her and her son’s full names, her son’s date of birth, her former husband’s name, and detailed the chronology of the custody litigation, including psychiatric treatment and doctors’ reports. On 3 April 2001, *Lietuvos Aidas* published an interview in which she again divulged names of her son, former husband, and CWS employees, and quoted medical and social-care reports. The Government also submitted that she disclosed similar information on a television programme in May 2001.

The alleged violation, however, arose from an article published by *Lietuvos Aidas* on 15 June 2001, titled “The overworked employees of the CWS are convinced that you cannot buy a child’s love.” In that article, the CWS director and employees commented publicly on the case, describing the mother’s divorce, her new relationship, and her alleged conduct. More significantly, the article cited the child’s medical records obtained from the Vilnius Child Development Centre Psychiatric Unit, revealing psychiatric conclusions that the boy was hostile towards his mother, that conflicts had arisen with her new husband, that the mother had suspected sexual abuse (which was not confirmed), and that on one occasion the mother had pulled the boy’s hair and bitten him. Although the article did not name the applicant or her family or disclose their residence, it contained detailed private and health information.

The applicant complained to the Children’s Rights Ombudsman, who partly criticised the CWS but also admonished the applicant for breaching her son’s privacy by publicising family matters. The director of the Child Development Centre informed her that the CWS had acted unethically in disclosing the medical records. On 11 October 2001, the Inspector of Journalistic Ethics warned the editors that the article breached the applicant’s honour and dignity and that, despite apparent anonymity, she was recognisable and portrayed negatively.

The applicant sued the CWS for damages, claiming 50,000 Lithuanian litai. On 15 December 2003, the Vilnius City Second District Court dismissed her action, finding that the article contained no data permitting her identification and that she had failed to prove deliberate disclosure of private information. This was upheld by the Vilnius Regional Court on 18 June 2004 and by the Supreme Court on 29 November 2004. The Supreme Court held that the Inspector’s and medical institution’s findings were not binding and that the applicant had not been clearly identifiable.

Notably, however, on the same day the Supreme Court issued a separate ruling expressing disapproval of the CWS employees’ conduct. It observed that publicly commenting in detail on a particular child’s circumstances and health was incompatible with the child’s interests, that no legitimate public interest warranted publication, and that such disclosure could only cause distress.

Before the European Court, the applicant alleged that Lithuania had failed to protect her private life and had not provided an effective remedy. The key factual dispute concerned whether the 15 June 2001 article, despite not naming her, allowed her identification and whether the domestic courts adequately protected her privacy against the CWS’s disclosure of confidential medical and family information.

Röman v. Finland (ECtHR, 2013) concerned a Finnish woman’s inability to have her biological father’s paternity legally established because of a transitional time-limit in national paternity legislation. The applicant, Ms Mirja Anneli Röman, was born in 1954 out of wedlock. Her mother and biological father concluded a child support agreement the same year, verified by social services, but under the then-applicable Act on Children Born out of Wedlock, paternity could not be established against a man’s will. In 1956 her mother married another man, and in 1961 the applicant’s name was changed to that of her mother’s husband. The family agreed never to mention the biological father; the applicant had two siblings from her mother’s marriage.

The Paternity Act entered into force on 1 October 1976. Its Implementing Act allowed paternity proceedings for children born before that date, but required them to be initiated within five years—by 1 October 1981—and barred proceedings after the putative father’s death. No such restrictions applied to children born after the Paternity Act entered into force. In 2001 the applicant began investigating her origins. She discovered that the church register listed her mother’s husband as her stepfather, while the State population register, which merged church records in 1993, listed him as her father. She also located the child support agreement, which enabled her to identify her biological father. In 2002 the population register was corrected. In February 2003 she initiated paternity proceedings against her biological father.

The domestic courts dismissed her claim as time-barred. The District Court found that during the five-year period the applicant had been an adult and could have initiated proceedings, questioned her mother, or verified the church register, which had been correct. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision, and the Supreme Court refused leave to appeal. The Parliamentary Ombudsman also found no abuse of the courts’ margin of appreciation. In 2007 a private DNA test showed with 99.99% certainty that the man was her biological father. He died in 2008.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 8 that the five-year transitional time-limit prevented her from having her biological father’s paternity legally established, thereby interfering with her private life and right to know her origins. She also complained under Article 14 that she was discriminated against because children born after the Paternity Act’s entry into force were not subject to the same time-limit. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were that she had not known the relevant facts during the limitation period; the time-limit expired long before she discovered her biological father’s identity; and the rule prevented any judicial confirmation of paternity despite reliable DNA evidence. The Government relied on legal certainty and the protection of putative fathers, but the Court found a violation of Article 8, holding that the applicant’s right to respect for private life, including knowledge of her origins, had been unjustifiably restricted. It found no separate issue under Article 14.

**Hode and Abdi v. the United Kingdom** (Application no. 22341/09), decided by the European Court of Human Rights on 6 November 2012, concerned UK immigration rules governing family reunion for refugees and their post-flight spouses.

The first applicant, Mr Hode, a Somali national, arrived in the UK in February 2004 and was granted asylum in March 2006. Because the UK changed its rules on 30 August 2005, he was not granted indefinite leave to remain (“ILR”) but instead five years’ limited leave to remain, expiring on 16 March 2011, together with a Refugee Convention Travel Document. In 2006 he was introduced to the second applicant, Ms Abdi, a Djibouti national. They married in Djibouti in April 2007 and lived together there until Mr Hode returned to the UK in May 2007.

Ms Abdi applied for a visa to join her husband. She did not qualify for refugee family reunion under paragraph 352A of the Immigration Rules because that route applied only to spouses who were part of the refugee’s family unit before he left his country of habitual residence. She therefore applied under paragraph 281 as the spouse of a person “present and settled” in the UK. In November 2007 the Entry Clearance Officer refused the application because Mr Hode, having only limited leave, was not settled. Her appeal failed: the Immigration Judge accepted that the marriage was genuine and that Mr Hode could maintain and accommodate his family, and that Article 8 was engaged, but found the refusal proportionate. The judge noted that Ms Abdi had never enjoyed family life in the UK and that there was no obstacle to Mr Hode living in Djibouti, other than language and employment difficulties. Further reconsideration was refused.

Mr Hode later obtained ILR in 2011, and in April 2011 the Immigration Rules were amended to allow post-flight spouses of refugees with limited leave to join them under paragraph 319L. Ms Abdi did not reapply. A second child was born in July 2011.

The key alleged violation arose from the difference in treatment created by the rules. At the relevant time, refugees granted asylum after August 2005 received limited leave and were not “present and settled,” so their post-flight spouses could not join them. By contrast, spouses of other persons with limited leave—such as students or workers—could join them without any requirement that the marriage have taken place before the sponsor left his or her country of origin. Domestic cases had recognised that this placed refugees in a disadvantageous position and that there appeared to be no justification for the distinction.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Article 8 alone and Article 14 read with Article 8, alleging unjustified discrimination in the enjoyment of their family life because of Mr Hode’s immigration status as a refugee with limited leave. The Court found a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 8, holding that the differential treatment of post-flight spouses of refugees, compared with spouses of other limited-leave categories, lacked objective and reasonable justification.

text:
In *Wenerski v. Poland (No. 2)*, the European Court of Human Rights considered a Polish national’s Article 3 complaint about inadequate detention conditions, especially overcrowding. Ernest Wenerski, born 1970, had a long criminal record and had been detained since 1997. The application concerned five periods in Łódź Remand Centre: 1 September 2004–10 March 2005; 20 May–30 November 2005; 14 December 2005–19 January 2007; 5 February–22 July 2007; and 8 January 2009–June 2010.

Wenerski suffered from epilepsy with regular seizures and had a personality disorder. Medical experts concluded that his epilepsy did not itself require special detention conditions, but recommended a bottom bunk in a non-overcrowded cell. Psychiatric and psychological experts found his personality disorder developed early and was not caused by overcrowding.

During the first four Łódź periods, Wenerski had numerous epileptic fits, often causing minor injuries such as cut lips, bruises, abrasions, bumps, a bitten tongue, and a head cut. He usually received first aid from cellmates; a doctor was called during the day, and an ambulance at night or on holidays. Yet on at least two occasions he received no medical help after a fit. Once the warden told cellmates to turn him on his side and put something in his mouth; in another cell no assistance was given because the warden thought he was simulating. He also self-mutilated and received adequate treatment after self-injury.

The core complaint concerned conditions. Domestic courts found that from 2002–2006 the statutory minimum space in Łódź Remand Centre was reduced because of nationwide overcrowding and renovations. During Wenerski’s first four terms, he occupied 14 different cells measuring 10.5–12 sq m, shared by four to six prisoners, giving only 2–2.4 sq m per person. The courts found this overcrowding was not temporary, as he spent years with about 2 sq m. Examples included a cell designed for two being used by six, and a 12 sq m cell for four being occupied by six. Overcrowding harmed prisoners’ health and sanitary conditions, increased stress and aggression, and Wenerski had quarrels, fights, and disciplinary punishments. On one occasion, despite medical advice, he was assigned a top bunk without a ladder or safety rail. He alleged cells were dirty, unventilated, infested with bugs and mould; toilet annexes had only partial fabric screening, no privacy, and constant odour.

In his civil action begun 18 February 2005, Wenerski sought PLN 70,000 for overcrowded, unsuitable conditions that allegedly worsened his health and caused distress and pain from epileptic injuries. The Łódź Regional Court on 26 May 2009 found his rights to dignity and humane treatment violated by severe, long-term overcrowding and awarded PLN 2,000. It noted epilepsy was independent of detention conditions, but overcrowding may have affected his personality disorder and increased injury risk. On appeal, the Łódź Court of Appeal increased compensation to PLN 5,000 on 30 October 2009. No cassation appeal was available. His complaints to penitentiary authorities were dismissed as manifestly ill-founded. He lodged the Strasbourg application on 16 June 2009, complaining mainly under Article 3 of inadequate conditions, particularly overcrowding.

In *Rousk v. Sweden*, the applicant, Mr Jim Rousk, owned a close company and was required to file a special income tax return for the 2002 tax assessment year. He failed to do so. After an order and a proposed discretionary assessment, the Tax Authority in November 2002 imposed taxes, tax surcharges and a delay charge totaling SEK 232,572 (approximately EUR 27,000), payable by 26 February 2003. The applicant neither appealed nor requested respite from payment. Because tax debts to the State are immediately enforceable, the claim was transferred to the Enforcement Authority in April 2003.

On 28 May 2003 the Enforcement Authority issued a writ of execution attaching the applicant’s site-leasehold right and the house where he and his wife lived. His total enforceable debts were SEK 255,329; the property’s tax value was SEK 1,372,000, with a mortgage of SEK 960,200. The applicant said he only became aware of the writ in July/August 2003. He appealed on 10 August 2003, arguing that the tax debt was not final, that he had not been properly served, that he would submit his tax return and had requested respite, and that selling his home would have serious economic, social and medical consequences. He submitted a medical certificate showing depression, psychiatric care since February 2003, and antidepressant treatment.

Meanwhile, the Enforcement Authority scheduled a public auction for 3 September 2003. The applicant requested a stay on 28 July 2003, citing illness and payment of another debt. The Enforcement Authority refused on 30 July, and the District Court rejected his appeal on 28 August. An independent valuation on 28 July estimated the property at SEK 1,850,000–2,150,000. On 3 September at 1:45 p.m., the auction proceeded and the highest bid of SEK 1,600,000 was accepted. On the same day, the Tax Authority granted the applicant respite from payment of the taxes and surcharges; the decision was registered at 2:02 p.m. The applicant later argued that the Enforcement Authority could have verified the respite during the pause between bidding rounds, especially since he had informed it of his request. The Enforcement Authority maintained that the respite was not shown before the auction and that other State debts of SEK 23,775 justified the sale. The enforceable tax debt was later reduced to SEK 6,721, and the distribution protocol was corrected.

After the applicant refused to vacate by 1 October 2003, the Enforcement Authority ordered his eviction. He requested respite, citing his and his wife’s poor health, lack of alternative housing, and the pending appeal against the sale. The Enforcement Authority and courts refused to postpone. On 22 October 2003 the eviction was enforced with police and movers present. Some belongings were stored, but other items were discarded or destroyed, including food, flowers and a bed that could not be removed intact. The auction cost SEK 45,660 and the eviction SEK 71,115. In January 2004 the applicant received SEK 524,343 remaining from the sale after debts and costs.

The applicant alleged that the Enforcement Authority’s measures violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (peaceful enjoyment of property) and Article 8 (private and family life and home). The key alleged violations concerned the attachment and sale of his home for a relatively small tax debt, the refusal to stay the sale and eviction despite illness and lack of alternative housing, and the timing of the Tax Authority’s respite order relative to the auction. He exhausted domestic remedies through the District Court, Court of Appeal and Supreme Court.

text:
The case concerns Ms H., a Finnish national born in 1963 who was registered male at birth. Although she had long felt she was female, she married a woman in 1996 and they had a child in 2002. In 2006 she was diagnosed as transgender, began living as a woman, and later underwent gender reassignment surgery in September 2009. She changed her first names, passport, and driver’s licence, but her identity number remained male. According to the applicant, this continued to disclose her transgender status in everyday situations.

In June 2007 the applicant asked the local Register Office to confirm her as female and to change her identity number. The Register Office refused. Under the Finnish Act on Confirmation of the Gender of a Transsexual, confirmation of a new gender required that the person was not married or in a civil partnership, unless the spouse consented to the marriage being transformed into a civil partnership. The applicant’s wife did not consent. The applicant and her wife wished to remain married; divorce would have conflicted with their religious convictions. The applicant also argued that transforming their marriage into a civil partnership would reduce legal security and adversely affect their child, partly because a child could not have two mothers and the applicant could no longer be a legal father or mother.

The Helsinki Administrative Court rejected her appeal in May 2008, relying on the same marital-status requirement. It found that same-sex partners could obtain partial family-law protection through registered partnership and that the law did not violate the applicant’s constitutional rights or those of her child. In February 2009 the Supreme Administrative Court rejected her further appeal. It held that Finnish law allowed marriage only between a man and a woman, that civil partnership was essentially comparable to marriage in juridical and economic terms, and that changing marriage into a gender-neutral institution was a matter for Parliament. The court considered the existing law to fall within the State’s margin of appreciation under the Convention. A later extraordinary appeal, filed after the applicant’s surgery, was refused in August 2010.

Separately, the applicant sought reimbursement for hormonal medicine. In October 2007 the Social Insurance Institution refused reimbursement because she had not yet received a new identity number. The Social Security Appeal Board later allowed her appeal in January 2010. The Ombudsman for Equality also found in 2008 that conditioning reimbursement on the identity number placed transgender persons in a different position from others receiving the same treatment and recommended a change in practice.

The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention that her right to private and family life had been violated, and that she had been discriminated against, because full legal recognition of her new gender was made conditional on transforming her marriage into a civil partnership. The Court also decided ex officio to examine the case under Article 12. The central alleged violation was therefore that Finnish law forced her to choose between legal recognition of her gender identity and preserving her existing marriage and family status, while the male identity number continued to reveal her transgender status.

In **Maksymenko and Gerasymenko v. Ukraine** (Application no. 49317/07), the applicants alleged that Ukraine violated Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention by invalidating the 1995 privatisation of a hostel they had bought in 2004, together with all subsequent transfers of ownership, thereby depriving them of possessions. The first applicant lived in Malyn; the second applicant died in 2009, and his widow pursued the application on his behalf.

In 1995, decision no. 492 transformed State enterprise M. into a joint-stock company, effectively privatising it. An audit showed that M.’s immovable property included several hostels. In 2000, M. was reorganised into four companies, including S., which acquired ownership of the hostels. In 2003, S. was declared insolvent. The liquidator informed local authorities that selling the hostels could create social tensions and suggested the town take them over. In January 2004, the mayor replied that the hostels were not State-owned and that the creditors should decide. In July 2004, the board of creditors agreed to sell one hostel to the applicants. On 21 August 2004, a sale contract was signed; the applicants paid UAH 41,160 (about EUR 6,127) and became equal owners.

After the purchase, the applicants discovered that electricity cables and meters needed replacement and that occupants had not paid rent. In January 2005, they asked the electricity company to cut off supply until a new contract was signed. A cut-off was scheduled, but on 21 January 2005 a prosecutor ordered that electricity not be cut off because he was preparing legal proceedings on behalf of the hostel occupants. The applicants told authorities they had bought the hostel to live there, that occupants had refused to participate in the sale and had not paid rent or communal charges for six months. They asked S. to rehouse the occupants and requested them to vacate by 30 March 2005.

On 26 January 2005, G., a nineteen-year-old occupant with a young child, sought help from the prosecutor after being asked to leave. On 18 February 2005, the prosecutor sued on G.’s behalf in the Malynsky District Court, seeking invalidation of the 16 November 1995 decision and all later ownership transfers. The prosecutor argued that privatisation was unlawful under section 2(2) of the State Housing Stock Privatisation Act, which prohibited privatising rooms in hostels. He also claimed the transfer breached law and “moral principles,” violated occupants’ constitutional housing rights, harmed State interests, and affected G., a vulnerable single mother. He requested that ownership be transferred to Malyn Town Council.

The applicants counterclaimed for compensation, arguing that occupants had refused to participate in the sale, had not paid, and had caused S.’s insolvency. The court returned the counterclaim for lacking logical consistency and causation, and the applicants did not re-lodge it. In January 2006, the first-instance court rejected the prosecutor’s claim. On 8 June 2006, the Zhytomyr Regional Court of Appeal quashed that decision and invalidated the 1995 privatisation and all subsequent transfers. It held that State housing stock, including hostels, could not be privatised under section 3 of the State Property Privatisation Act. It awarded the applicants UAH 41,160 to be paid by S. and transferred ownership to the Council. The applicants appealed, citing a contradictory appellate decision, missed time-limits, and S.’s insolvency. On 21 May 2007, the Vinnytsya Regional Court of Appeal rejected the cassation appeal without explanation. The Council took over ownership in July 2007. S. failed to pay compensation, and by late 2008 occupants had privatised twelve of the fourteen apartments under amended legislation.

The alleged violation therefore arises from the retroactive invalidation of the 1995 privatisation and all later transfers after the applicants had bought the hostel as bona fide purchasers. The key facts include their 2004 purchase, the prosecutor’s action prompted by an occupant’s complaint, the 2006 invalidation based on domestic law prohibiting State housing stock privatisation, the transfer of ownership to the municipality, and the ineffective or unpaid compensation.

**Rooney v. Ireland** (Application no. 32614/10) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section Committee on 31 October 2013. The applicant, John Rooney, an Irish farmer and barrister born in 1956, complained under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention about the excessive length of two civil actions he brought in Ireland—begun in 1987 and 1995—and about the absence of an effective domestic remedy for that delay. The Court noted that these issues had already been addressed in its well-established case law, particularly **McFarlane v. Ireland** (2010).

In the **1987 proceedings**, certain of Rooney’s cattle were destroyed under a Government scheme to eradicate bovine tuberculosis. In November 1987 he commenced a High Court action challenging the scheme’s constitutionality. The litigation became procedurally complex: there were multiple hearings in 1988 concerning discovery and amendments; notices of trial and further pleadings followed in 1988–1990; and his request to join additional defendants led to six hearings. In February 1990 the High Court refused judgment in default of defence, struck out the case against some defendants, and refused to appoint a shorthand writer. Rooney appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 111/1990). The Supreme Court directed a special case in the High Court, adjourning the appeal. The High Court rejected the special case in May 1991; the Supreme Court dismissed the related appeal (no. 224/1991) in December 1991 and also rejected appeal no. 111/1990. However, it failed to deal with the High Court’s refusal of judgment in default of defence. Over the next decade Rooney sought to reopen the appeals. In December 2000 and July 2001 the Supreme Court refused his motions, and in October 2001 it made a vexatious litigant order against him. Subsequent attempts to advance the 1987 action were repeatedly adjourned or blocked by that order. In March 2010 the Supreme Court acknowledged a clear “oversight” in failing to determine the default-judgment aspect of appeal no. 111/1990 and found that certain claims could still proceed. Nevertheless, by late 2010 the 1987 action remained unresolved, with a further appeal (no. 430/2010) pending.

In the **1995 proceedings**, Rooney’s herd was restricted from April 1993 to July 1996 under the same TB scheme. In November 1995 he began a High Court action against State defendants, claiming the restriction was unlawful and that the scheme breached statute, the Constitution, the Convention, and EU law. Discovery was obtained in December 1997; notices were served in 2002; and the action was tried over ten days in May–June 2004. The High Court dismissed his claims in July 2004. Rooney appealed in August 2004 (no. 387/2004), filed submissions in July 2006, and certified readiness in January 2007. A priority-listing request failed in November 2007. In May 2009 the Registrar advised that the waiting time after certification was 31 months and no hearing date had been allocated. The appeal was eventually heard with another appeal in October 2009, but the Supreme Court’s March 2010 judgment dealt only with the other appeal. Although the Supreme Court later claimed the 2004 appeal was covered, the State Solicitor agreed it had been omitted. The appeal was ultimately dismissed in November 2010.

The applicant alleged that both civil actions were excessively long and that Ireland provided no effective remedy for delay. The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13, consistent with **McFarlane**, and awarded just satisfaction.

In *Hode and Abdi v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 22341/09), the applicants were Mr Ilyas Elmi Hode, a Somali refugee in the United Kingdom, and Ms Hawa Aden Abdi, a Djibouti national. The first applicant arrived in the UK in February 2004 and was granted asylum in March 2006. Because his asylum claim was decided after 30 August 2005, he received five years’ limited leave to remain, expiring on 16 March 2011, rather than indefinite leave to remain (“ILR”). He also received a Refugee Convention Travel Document. In June 2006 he was introduced to the second applicant; they married in Djibouti on 5 April 2007, after he had fled Somalia and settled in the UK. He returned to the UK in May 2007.

The second applicant applied to join him as his spouse. Under the Immigration Rules, refugee family reunion was governed by paragraph 352A, which applied only where the marriage took place before the refugee left his country of former habitual residence. Since the marriage was post-flight, she could not rely on that provision. She instead applied under paragraph 281 as the spouse of a person “present and settled” in the UK. On 18 November 2007 the Entry Clearance Officer refused the application because the first applicant, with only limited leave to remain, was not “settled.” Their son was born on 17 February 2008, with the first applicant named as father.

The second applicant appealed. The Immigration Judge accepted that the marriage was genuine and that the first applicant could maintain and accommodate his wife and child. He also accepted that refusing entry engaged Article 8 of the Convention, but dismissed the appeal, finding no disproportionate interference. In particular, the second applicant had never enjoyed family life in the UK, and the first applicant could live in Djibouti, despite language and employment difficulties. Reconsideration was refused in August 2008 and the Administrative Court dismissed further review in October 2008.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights. The central alleged violation was discrimination under Article 14 read together with Article 8. They argued that refugees with limited leave to remain were treated less favourably than other categories of persons with limited leave—such as students or workers—whose spouses could join them without any pre-flight marriage requirement. They were also worse off than refugees granted asylum before 30 August 2005, who received ILR and could use paragraph 281. The rule change meant that, for their first five years, refugees were not “settled” and could not be joined by post-flight spouses even if all other requirements were met. Domestic cases such as *A (Afghanistan)* and *FH (Iran)* had criticised the lack of justification for this distinction.

Later, the first applicant obtained ILR after his leave expired in March 2011. In April 2011 the rules were amended by paragraph 319L to allow post-flight spouses of refugees with limited leave to join them. The second applicant did not reapply and gave birth to a second child in July 2011. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 8, holding that the differential treatment of refugees with limited leave to remain was unjustified.

**Summary of *Klinovská v. Slovakia* (Application no. 61436/09)**

The case of *Klinovská v. Slovakia* originated from an application lodged against the Slovak Republic with the European Court of Human Rights on 10 November 2009. The applicant, Ms. Margita Klinovská, a Slovak national born in 1969, alleged a violation of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time, as guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The core of her complaint concerned the excessive length of civil proceedings she had initiated in Slovakia.

The relevant facts began on 15 November 2004, when the applicant filed an action for damages with the Bratislava I District Court. She sued the Ministry of Finance and three other public authorities, a number that later expanded to eight defendants. Her claim was based on the State Liability Act, arguing that the defendants had failed in their supervisory duties, thereby allowing two private non-banking investment institutions to operate illicitly. These institutions had collapsed in the 1990s after soliciting large-scale public investments with promises of high returns. The applicant sought compensation for the financial loss she suffered due to this failed investment.

The domestic proceedings were protracted and procedurally complex. The applicant repeatedly submitted new evidence, was asked to provide further particulars of her claim, and requested that additional defendants be joined to the case. The District Court had to obtain observations from all defendants and, in 2011, even had to request fresh observations on a procedural point due to an error in its previous summonses. The first hearing on the merits did not take place until 15 March 2012, over seven years after the action was filed. Two more hearings followed, and on 9 November 2012, the District Court discontinued proceedings against three defendants and dismissed the action against the others. The applicant subsequently appealed, and this appeal was still pending at the time of the European Court’s judgment.

Prior to applying to the European Court, the applicant pursued two domestic remedies regarding the delays. First, on 16 March 2009, she complained to the President of the District Court. In a response dated 16 April 2009, the President acknowledged that there had been undue delays caused mainly by objective factors, apologised to the applicant, and informed her that the presiding judge had been instructed to prevent further delays. Second, on 25 May 2009, the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court under Article 127 of the Constitution, alleging a violation of her right to a hearing within a reasonable time. However, on 11 June 2009, the Constitutional Court declared her complaint inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. It reasoned that the complaint to the District Court President had been an effective remedy, as the President had reacted adequately and taken necessary measures. The Constitutional Court concluded that, at that time, the District Court was proceeding with the case properly, and advised the applicant that she could raise a new constitutional complaint if further delays occurred, without needing to first address the District Court President again.

The applicant’s subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights centred on the allegation that the length of the proceedings before the Bratislava I District Court was excessive, violating her right to a timely hearing under the Convention.

text:
Á.F.L. v. Iceland (Application no. 35789/22) concerns the deprivation of the applicant’s custody of his daughter and the alleged discriminatory failure to provide him with reasonable accommodation for his disability. The applicant, an Icelandic national born in 1990, was diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder, ADHD and a mild intellectual disability. He had a history of alcohol and drug abuse but had been sober since 2012 and was employed. His daughter, V.F., was born in February 2019. Child Protection Services (“CPS”) became involved amid parental conflict, the mother’s mental-health problems, the applicant’s diagnoses and reported domestic violence. In September 2019 the applicant assumed care of V.F.

With parental consent, V.F. was placed at Mánaberg, a CPS residential diagnostic and guidance facility. The applicant joined her there in October 2019 after the mother left. Staff knew of his impairment and gave extensive guidance, later moving him to a supported “apartment” within the facility. A December 2019 psychologist’s report found that although the applicant did not test at the level of intellectual disability, his cognitive difficulties and autism affected his parenting. He needed extensive assistance and could not care for V.F. alone. A January 2020 Mánaberg report noted progress but concluded he still required targeted support, guidance, a support family and counselling.

A discharge plan placed the applicant and V.F. with the paternal grandmother, with Mánaberg follow-up visits four times a week, a YLFA counsellor twice a week, a support family and continued counselling. Reports from March to June 2020 found the applicant affectionate but lacking insight into V.F.’s physical, social and emotional needs, stimulation and initiative. Concerns grew about V.F.’s motor skills, emotional control and possible attachment disorder. YLFA recommended more extensive support and eventually foster care. CPS increased support, but COVID-19 disrupted services. In June 2020 reports warned V.F. urgently needed a primary caregiver who could provide security.

In July 2020 the Child Protection Committee ruled that V.F. be removed for two months pending reassessment; she was placed with a foster family. An August 2020 parenting-capacity report found the applicant attached and cooperative but that autism and intellectual challenges restricted his ability to recognise and meet V.F.’s needs. V.F. improved significantly in foster care. The District Court upheld the removal. In September 2020 the CPC decided to seek deprivation of custody after the applicant refused to relinquish it.

A court-appointed expert report in April 2021 considered the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and Icelandic disability-support legislation. It validated earlier findings, concluding the applicant lacked basic parenting skills, was slow to acquire them and could not benefit sufficiently from further support. Returning V.F. to the previous situation was not justified. At trial, the applicant argued he had not received enough support, that his ADHD had improved with medication and that additional services under Act no. 38/2018 on Services for Disabled People with Long-Term Support Needs should have been tried. His witnesses, including disability experts, said earlier measures had not fully accounted for his needs. A YLFA counsellor testified that extra services could not compensate for the lack of bonding and care.

In September 2021 the District Court deprived the applicant of custody under the Child Protection Act, finding extensive measures had been tried, the child’s best interests were paramount and no realistic additional measures existed. The Court of Appeal upheld the decision in February 2022, noting disability alone cannot justify deprivation but that the statutory conditions were met and the support experience had been considered. The Supreme Court refused leave in March 2022. The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Articles 8 and 14 that the authorities failed to provide reasonable accommodation—necessary support measures for his disability—before depriving him of custody, thereby discriminating against him.

**Summary of Drakšas v. Lithuania (Application no. 36662/04)**

The case of *Drakšas v. Lithuania* concerns the interception of the applicant’s telephone conversations and the subsequent public disclosure of their contents, raising issues under Article 8 (right to respect for private life) and Article 13 (right to an effective remedy) of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The applicant, Mr Algirdas Drakšas, was a founding member of the Liberal Democrats political party and a member of the Vilnius City Municipal Council. On 16 March 2003, the State Security Department (SSD) intercepted a telephone conversation between the applicant and Jurij Borisov (J.B.), a major contributor to the electoral campaign of State President Rolandas Paksas. This interception was conducted under a court order authorising the tapping of J.B.’s telephone.

On 17 September 2003, the SSD requested authorisation to tap the applicant’s telephone, based on operational information linking him to J.B. and A.Z., and to a Russian citizen, V.F., who was suspected of spying. The Attorney General submitted a request to the Vilnius Regional Court, which authorised the tapping for three months. The court order was classified as secret and not disclosed to the applicant. The authorisation was based on suspicions that the applicant was involved in smuggling strategic goods, other serious crimes, and attempts to unlawfully take over shares of a road-building company, “Žemaitijos keliai.”

Between 18 September and 11 November 2003, the SSD intercepted the applicant’s conversations, including five calls with the State President and his advisers. Notably, one call was from the President to the applicant. On 1 November 2003, the SSD declassified the recording of the 16 March 2003 conversation between the applicant and J.B. and sent it to the Attorney General’s Office. The following day, this conversation was broadcast on national television (LTV and LNK). The SSD denied leaking the material.

On 11 November 2003, the Attorney General wrote to the SSD, noting that the media had revealed the existence of recordings of the applicant’s conversations with the President. The Attorney General stated that such recordings, if they existed, were unlawful under Article 6 § 3 of the Law on Operational Activities, which prohibits operational activities targeting the head of State. The SSD was ordered to destroy any such recordings and prevent their disclosure. The operational investigation against the applicant was terminated the same day.

The applicant lodged a complaint with the Attorney General on 12 November 2003, alleging unlawful tapping and a breach of privacy. He was informed that his conversations had been monitored lawfully and that his conversations with the President were recorded while tapping his phone, not the President’s. He was advised to seek a civil remedy for the media disclosure.

The applicant attempted to challenge the lawfulness of the court order authorising the tapping before the Vilnius Regional Court and later the Court of Appeal. Both attempts were rejected. The Court of Appeal President stated that granting access to such secret orders would undermine the effectiveness of covert investigations.

On 15 March 2004, the recordings and transcripts of the applicant’s conversations with V.F., J.B., and the State President were deposited with the Constitutional Court for the President’s impeachment proceedings. Prosecutors did not restrict their disclosure. At a public hearing on 19 March 2004, some recordings were played and broadcast on national television. The applicant’s request to open a criminal investigation into this disclosure was refused by prosecutors and upheld by the Vilnius City Second District Court.

The applicant also sought access to the recordings of his conversations held by the SSD but was refused by the Vilnius Regional Administrative Court and the Supreme Administrative Court, which held that the information had wider implications and was protected as evidence in criminal proceedings.

Relying on Article 8, the applicant complained that his telephone conversations had been intercepted and disclosed to the public. He also complained under Article 13 that he lacked an effective domestic remedy for these violations.

**Case: Kristiansen and Tyvik AS v. Norway** (ECtHR, App. No. 25498/08, 2 May 2013)

The applicants were Arne Kristiansen, a Norwegian national born in 1931, and Tyvik A/S, a Norwegian limited liability company. On 30 November 1990, Kristiansen filed patent application no. 19905214 with the Norwegian Industrial Property Office (NIPO) for a method of propulsion for aircraft and sea vessels.

NIPO’s preliminary opinion of 21 March 1991 stated that the application was not patentable because it did not reveal a concrete solution or technical effect. NIPO required the applicant to perform independent practical tests under the patent regulations. Kristiansen disputed the need for tests, citing cost, and said prototypes were being built. Between 1992 and 1994, correspondence continued about confidentiality; the Military Supreme Command advised that the application need not be kept secret on national security grounds.

NIPO reiterated its testing requirement in February 1995. Kristiansen replied with theoretical views and an old research report, arguing tests were unnecessary. In November 1996 he complained about delay; NIPO apologised and prioritised the case. In December 1996 NIPO maintained its position, leading to further exchanges and academic statements. In May 1999 NIPO again required independent tests and set a deadline of 5 November 1999. Kristiansen again complained about delay and NIPO’s technical competence but provided no new arguments. NIPO therefore shelved the application for failure to comply.

After Kristiansen petitioned the Parliamentary Ombudsman in March 2001, NIPO annulled the shelving decision and resumed examination. In October 2001 NIPO refused the application because the applicant had not made the alleged technical effect probable. Kristiansen appealed to NIPO’s Board of Appeals in November 2001. The Board first met in September 2004 and indicated that a patent might be possible for sea vessels only if the claims were reformulated. In February 2005, 50% ownership was transferred to

In *Mežnarič v. Slovenia* (Application no. 41416/06), the European Court of Human Rights considered a Slovenian national’s complaints under Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention. The applicant, Marijan Mežnarič, born in 1950 and living in Šmarje pri Jelšah, lodged his application on 21 September 2006. He alleged that domestic proceedings involving him had lasted excessively and that no effective domestic remedy existed for that delay. The application was communicated to the Government on 14 March 2012.

The underlying proceedings began on 13 June 1995, when the Žiri Municipality brought enforcement proceedings against the company KODA SPAAR d.o.o. before the Kranj Basic Court. A writ of execution was issued on 28 June 1995, but the company objected. On 5 September 1995 the first-instance court annulled the writ. On 6 November 1995 the case was referred to the Kranj District Court to be decided in contentious proceedings.

A lengthy jurisdictional phase followed. On 21 November 1999 the court declared it lacked jurisdiction and referred the case to the Škofja Loka Local Court. That court initiated a jurisdictional dispute on 25 November 1999. Only on 30 August 2000 did the Ljubljana Higher Court assign the case back to the Kranj District Court.

On 17 October 2000 the first-instance court received an extract from the Register of Companies showing that KODA SPAAR d.o.o. had been struck out under Article 580 §§ 5–6 of the Companies Act. On 8 January 2001 the creditor requested continuation of the proceedings against the applicant, since he had been the company’s founder and owner. On 27 August 2001 the first-instance court granted continuation against the applicant. The applicant appealed and requested exemption from court fees on 10 September 2001. The Ljubljana Higher Court rejected the appeal on 24 October 2001, and his subsequent request for protection of legality was also rejected.

On 27 August 2002 the Kranj District Court stayed the proceedings pending a Constitutional Court decision concerning suspension of a chapter of the Financial Operations of Companies Act. Proceedings resumed on 17 January 2003. On 17 December 2003 a settlement hearing was held; the applicant requested legal aid, exemption from fees, and filed a counterclaim for damages. On 11 February 2004 the first-instance court annulled the 1995 writ. The Ljubljana Higher Court remitted the case on 16 February 2005. On 31 August 2005 the first-instance court upheld the writ; the applicant appealed. On 21 June 2006 the Higher Court upheld the appeal and annulled the writ. On 4 September 2006 the applicant sought reimbursement of legal costs, but his request was rejected on 10 October 2006.

The domestic-law background included the 2006 Act on Protection of the Right to a Trial without Undue Delay, which became operational on 1 January 2007, after the applicant’s ECtHR application. Its transitional Section 25 allowed settlement offers and court actions for cases already filed with the international court. The Companies Act and Constitutional Court decision U-I-135/00 § 61 made former shareholders potentially liable as universal successors of struck-off companies, explaining why the applicant was drawn into the proceedings. The key alleged violations were therefore the excessive length of proceedings from 1995 to 2006 and the lack of an effective remedy at the relevant time.

**Budrevich v. the Czech Republic** (Application no. 65303/10) concerned a Belarusian national, Mr Andrei Budrevich, who alleged that he had no effective remedy under Article 13 of the Convention against his expulsion to Belarus. He entered the Czech Republic in October 2006 using an assumed name and applied for asylum, claiming persecution in Belarus for distributing advertisements supporting opposition candidate Aliaxandr Milinkevich. His first asylum request was rejected in 2007 as not credible; the Hradec Králové Regional Court upheld that decision in 2008, and the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed his cassation appeal in 2009 because he failed to provide grounds.

His true identity was revealed in December 2009 after Czech police sent his fingerprints to Belarus. Shortly afterward, Belarus requested his extradition for drug-related offences. In April 2010, the Plzeň Regional Court found the extradition request inadmissible because there were reasonable fears that criminal proceedings in Belarus would violate Articles 3 and 6 of the Convention. It relied on reports describing political persecution, lack of judicial independence, inhuman detention conditions, ill-treatment by police, and unfair trials in Belarus.

Meanwhile, the applicant had been convicted of several thefts in Czech criminal proceedings. In November 2008, the Prague 10 District Court imposed a thirty-month expulsion order. In March 2009, the Prague 8 District Court imposed a one-year prison sentence and a five-year expulsion order. Execution of expulsion was repeatedly stayed because of his asylum proceedings.

The applicant lodged four asylum requests. His second request in January 2010 and third request in September 2010 were rejected as repeated requests containing no new circumstances. A key issue was that, when deciding the second request, the Ministry of the Interior already knew of Belarus’s extradition request but merely asked the applicant whether he knew of any prosecution against him. He said he did not. The Supreme Administrative Court later quashed that decision, holding that the Ministry should have informed him of the extradition request and examined whether the new prosecution and extradition request constituted new circumstances. The third request was also affected by invalid service, as later confirmed by the Supreme Administrative Court. His fourth request in November 2010 eventually led to subsidiary protection in October 2011, later extended, although asylum itself was refused.

Expulsion became imminent after the third asylum request was rejected on 30 September 2010. The District Court cancelled the suspension on 25 October 2010. On 4 October 2010, before boarding a plane, the applicant attempted suicide by cutting his neck. He appealed on 9 November 2010, but the Prague Municipal Court rejected the appeal as belated, finding that service on 5 November 2010 made the deadline 8 November. On 9 November 2010, the European Court of Human Rights applied Rule 39, indicating that the applicant should not be removed to Belarus. The District Court then again stayed the expulsion on 10 November 2010.

Domestic law was central to the alleged Article 13 violation. Under the Asylum Act, judicial review of asylum decisions did not have suspensive effect where a repeated request was inadmissible under Section 10a(e). The Criminal Code made expulsion inadmissible if asylum or subsidiary protection had been granted, or if there was a risk of persecution, torture, or inhuman or degrading treatment. The Code of Criminal Procedure required suspension of expulsion where an asylum request was not manifestly unfounded and barred execution during subsidiary protection. The applicant argued that these mechanisms failed to provide an effective remedy against expulsion, especially given non-suspensive review, the authorities’ failure to inform him about the extradition request, and the risk he faced in Belarus.

Dimitar Ivanov v. Bulgaria (Application no. 19418/07) concerned a Bulgarian national born in 1974, living in Dinkata. The applicant lodged his application with the European Court of Human Rights on 5 April 2007. He alleged that the criminal charges against him had not been determined within a reasonable time, that he lacked effective remedies for that delay, and that the prohibition on his leaving Bulgaria was unlawful and unjustified.

The criminal proceedings began after an incident on 6 October 1994, when the applicant confessed before the police to committing robbery earlier that day together with two other individuals. The stolen goods were confiscated by the police the same day. However, criminal proceedings against him were not formally instituted until 4 October 1995. The case then appears to have remained dormant for approximately nine years, until 5 October 2004, when witnesses were questioned.

During 2001–2004, before being charged, the applicant left Bulgaria on several occasions and returned each time. On 6 October 2004, while he was abroad, an ex officio lawyer was appointed for him and he was charged in absentia with robbery. The first hearing in the case was held on 14 January 2005, with the applicant present. On 12 April 2006, the Pazardzhik District Court found him guilty and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment, suspended for three years. Following an appeal by his co-defendant, the Pazardzhik Regional Court, in a final judgment of 12 October 2006, upheld the lower court’s judgment, including the applicant’s conviction and sentence.

Separately, on 9 March 2007, the Pazardzhik Regional Police Directorate ordered a ban on the applicant leaving Bulgaria. The order was based on his conviction and pending his rehabilitation, relying on section 76(2) of the 1998 Bulgarian Identity Papers Act. The applicant challenged the order, arguing that he was unable to provide for his family in Bulgaria and that he had employment opportunities in Serbia. On 25 May 2007, while attempting to leave Bulgaria, he was refused passage by a border police official because of the prohibition.

By a final judgment of 10 October 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the travel ban. It reasoned that it fell within the administrative authority’s discretion to impose such a ban and that the authority’s assessment was not subject to judicial control. The court also held that domestic law had been complied with, since such a restriction could be imposed where a conviction was in place and before the convicted person’s rehabilitation. It further considered other factors, such as the applicant’s inability to find employment in Bulgaria, irrelevant.

The relevant domestic law and practice concerning travel bans on convicted individuals pending rehabilitation were set out in Nalbantski v. Bulgaria (no. 30943/04, §§ 25–29, 10 February 2011). The provisions concerning rehabilitation of persons convicted with a suspended sentence were also summarised in that judgment at § 30.

The key facts for the alleged violations were therefore the lengthy criminal proceedings—from formal institution in October 1995 to final conviction in October 2006, including a long inactive period—the alleged absence of effective remedies for that delay, and the post-conviction travel ban imposed in March 2007 and upheld in October 2007 without judicial control over the administrative discretion.

**Summary of PETA Deutschland v. Germany (Application no. 43481/09)**

The case of *PETA Deutschland v. Germany* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by PETA Deutschland, the German branch of the animal rights organisation People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. The applicant association complained that German court injunctions prohibiting its planned advertising campaign violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The facts concerned a campaign planned by PETA in March 2004 under the heading "The Holocaust on your plate." The campaign, which had already been conducted in the United States, consisted of a series of posters. Each poster juxtaposed a photograph of Holocaust victims with a photograph of animals kept in mass livestock farming conditions, accompanied by short captions. One poster showed emaciated, naked concentration camp inmates alongside starving cattle under the heading "walking skeletons." Another displayed piled-up human corpses next to a pile of slaughtered pigs under the heading "final humiliation." A further poster showed rows of inmates lying on wooden bunks alongside rows of chickens in laying batteries, with the heading "if animals are concerned, everybody becomes a Nazi." A final poster depicted a starving, naked male inmate alongside starving cattle, bearing the title "The Holocaust on your plate" and the text stating that twelve million humans were killed in the Holocaust between 1938 and 1945, while as many animals are killed every hour in Europe for human consumption.

In March 2004, three individuals—P.S., C.K., and S. Korn—filed a request with the Berlin Regional Court for an injunction to prevent PETA from publishing seven specified posters via the internet, in public exhibitions, or in any other form. The plaintiffs were, at the time, the president and two vice-presidents of the Central Jewish Council in Germany. All had survived the Holocaust as children, and C.K. had lost her family in the Holocaust. They argued that the campaign was offensive, violated their human dignity, and infringed the personality rights of C.K.'s deceased family members.

The Berlin Regional Court granted the injunction on 18 March 2004, a decision confirmed on 22 April 2004. The court held that the plaintiffs had a valid claim under sections 823 and 1004 of the German Civil Code, in conjunction with section 185 of the Criminal Code and Articles 1 and 2 of the German Basic Law. It found that while the posters constituted protected expressions of opinion, they placed the fate of Holocaust victims on the same level as that of animals. Although the campaign's primary aim appeared to be criticism of animal farming conditions rather than debasement of Holocaust victims, this comparison was considered arbitrary given the Basic Law's central emphasis on human dignity. The court concluded that the expression violated the plaintiffs' human dignity as Holocaust victims, particularly by depicting them in a most vulnerable state.

The Berlin Court of Appeal rejected PETA's appeals on 27 August 2004 and 25 November 2005. In the main proceedings on 2 December 2004, the Regional Court confirmed its injunction. On 20 February 2009, the Federal Constitutional Court rejected PETA's constitutional complaint. While expressing doubts about whether the campaign actually violated human dignity, it found the injunction justified without relying on such a violation. The court accepted that the Basic Law distinguishes human life and dignity from animal protection interests, and that the campaign trivialised the fate of Holocaust victims, thereby affecting the plaintiffs' personality rights. It noted that the self-image of Jews in Germany includes belonging to a group singled out by fate, owing a special moral obligation from others, forming part of their dignity.

Consequently, PETA Deutschland brought its case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging a violation of its freedom of expression.

**Case Summary: Tarbuk v. Croatia (Application no. 31360/10)**

The case concerns Mr Dušan Tarbuk, a Croatian national, who was arrested on 23 October 1995 and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of espionage in connection with the Homeland War in Croatia. He was arrested as part of a larger group of eighteen persons suspected of the same offence.

On 24 September 1996, Croatia enacted the General Amnesty Act, granting amnesty for criminal offences committed in connection with the war between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996, except for the gravest breaches of humanitarian law or war crimes, including genocide. Pursuant to that Act, criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 7 October 1996, and he was immediately released from detention.

On 9 June 1998, the applicant lodged a civil action against the State in the Zagreb Municipal Court, seeking compensation for his detention. He relied on Article 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which entitled a person who had been in pre-trial detention but against whom criminal proceedings had not been instituted or had been discontinued by a final decision to compensation.

While his civil claim was pending, the Code of Criminal Procedure was amended. On 2 June 1999, a new Article 484(a) was introduced, providing that no compensation could be granted in connection with the detention of persons whose criminal proceedings had been discontinued pursuant to a pardon or amnesty under special laws or decisions. A further amendment on 27 October 1999 specified that this exclusion applied to criminal offences committed between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996.

The domestic courts applied Article 484(a) retroactively to the applicant’s pending civil action. On 28 May 2004, the Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed his compensation claim for lack of legal basis. On 31 January 2006, the Zagreb County Court dismissed his appeal, holding that Article 484(a) extinguished his claim and that the provision had retroactive effect. On 28 August 2007, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, expressly confirming that Article 484(a) applied retroactively. On 5 November 2009, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning. It held that the constitutional right to compensation concerned unlawful deprivation of liberty; amnesty or pardon did not affect the lawfulness of detention, and the legislature could exclude amnesty beneficiaries from compensation.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) to his civil action—lodged in 1998, before the provision entered into force—had violated his right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He argued that the amendment extinguished an already pending compensation claim and deprived him of legal certainty.

The key issue before the European Court was whether the retroactive legislative interference with the applicant’s pending civil proceedings breached the fair trial guarantee. The Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1, holding that applying Article 484(a) retroactively to the applicant’s civil claim deprived him of a fair hearing and undermined the principle of legal certainty.

The case *Kononova and Others v. Ukraine* (Application no. 11770/03 and 89 other applications) was a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights, Fifth Section, sitting as a Committee, delivered on 6 June 2013. It originated in 90 applications against Ukraine lodged under Article 34 of the Convention. The applicants were Ukrainian nationals, one Russian national, and companies based in Ukraine. The Russian Government declined to intervene in the application by the Russian national. In nine applications, the original applicants died during the proceedings, and their next-of-kin expressed a wish to continue. In two applications, a brother and sister pursued their deceased father’s complaint concerning the same unenforced judgment.

The factual core of the case was the prolonged non-enforcement of final domestic decisions. On various dates, Ukrainian courts and labour disputes commissions issued decisions in the applicants’ favour. These decisions entitled them to specified pecuniary amounts or required certain actions to be taken for them. The decisions became final and enforceable. Despite this, the applicants were unable to obtain timely enforcement. The responsible State authorities—bailiffs, the State Treasury, or other bodies—failed to execute the decisions, sometimes for many years. In several cases, domestic courts themselves acknowledged bailiffs’ misconduct, but enforcement still remained delayed. Some underlying decisions dated back to 1996, 1998, 1999, and 2000. For example, Kononova obtained a judgment from the Suvorovsky District Court of Kherson on 6 June 2003, amended by the Kherson Regional Court of Appeal on 11 February 2004. Other applicants had final awards concerning pensions, labour payments, social benefits, and commercial claims. The applications were communicated to the Ukrainian Government between 2003 and 2011. Some applicants also raised unrelated factual and legal matters, but the central issue remained the failure to enforce final decisions.

The pattern was repetitive. Pikush’s 1996 decision remained unenforced even though the same court acknowledged bailiffs’ misconduct in 2005. Lyovochkina’s 2001 judgment was accompanied by a 2006 finding of bailiffs’ misconduct. Ternovik’s 1999 judgment, Kolosov’s 1998 judgment, and Prudkyy’s 1999 military court judgment also remained unexecuted for lengthy periods. Some domestic decisions were later amended or quashed on appeal, but the non-enforcement complaint concerned the period when they were final and binding. The amounts and required actions varied, yet the common feature was finality and enforceability followed by State inaction.

Relevant to the alleged violations, the applicants complained that the lengthy non-enforcement violated Article 6 §1 of the Convention, because the right to a fair trial includes the right to execution of final judgments. They also alleged a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, arguing that the State’s failure to pay or execute the awards interfered with their peaceful enjoyment of possessions. In addition, they complained under Article 13 that Ukraine lacked an effective domestic remedy for non-enforcement. The Court examined whether the State was responsible for the delays and whether effective remedies existed. The key facts for the alleged violations were therefore the existence of final, enforceable domestic decisions in the applicants’ favour, the State’s failure to enforce them within a reasonable time, and the resulting uncertainty and financial loss.

In *Rooney v. Ireland* (Application no. 32614/10, 31 October 2013), the European Court of Human Rights considered complaints under Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention concerning the excessive length of two Irish civil actions and the lack of an effective domestic remedy. The applicant, an Irish farmer and barrister, challenged measures taken under the State’s bovine tuberculosis (“TB”) eradication scheme.

The first action began in November 1987, after some of the applicant’s cattle were destroyed under the scheme. He brought High Court proceedings challenging the scheme’s constitutionality. The case generated lengthy interlocutory litigation, with numerous hearings in 1988–1990 concerning discovery, amendment of pleadings, joinder of defendants, judgment in default of defence, striking out claims, and the refusal to appoint a shorthand writer. In February 1990 the High Court refused his motions for judgment in default, struck out claims against some defendants, and refused other relief. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Court (appeal no. 111/1990). In October 1990 the Supreme Court directed a special case in the High Court and adjourned the appeal. The High Court rejected the special case in May 1991; the Supreme Court rejected the related appeal (no. 224/1991) and appeal no. 111/1990 in December 1991. However, the Supreme Court failed to deal with the High Court’s refusal of judgment in default of defence—an omission later described by the Supreme Court as a clear oversight.

The applicant made repeated attempts to reopen the appeal and clarify whether the case had been fully determined. In December 2000 and July 2001 the Supreme Court refused motions to set aside earlier judgments. In October 2001 it made a vexatious litigant order against him, which impeded further progress. In July 2007 he appealed against a High Court refusal to hear a motion to amend his statement of claim (appeal no. 217/2007). In March 2010 the Supreme Court found that claims outside the special case could still be pursued and that the default-judgment appeal had not been determined due to oversight. A later High Court refusal in November 2010 was appealed (no. 430/2010) and remained pending.

The second action began in November 1995, after the applicant’s herd was restricted from April 1993 to July 1996 under the same scheme. He claimed the restriction was unlawful and that the scheme breached statute, the Constitution, the Convention, and EU law. Discovery was obtained in December 1997. A Notice to Admit Facts was refused in November 2002, and a Notice of Trial was served in December 2002. The High Court heard the case over ten days in May and June 2004 and dismissed it in July 2004. The applicant appealed in August 2004 (no. 387/2004), filed written submissions in July 2006, and a Certificate of Readiness in January 2007. In November 2007 he failed to have the appeal prioritised. In May 2009 the Registrar stated that the waiting time after certification was 31 months and no hearing date had been allocated. The appeal was eventually heard with appeal no. 217/2007 in October 2009, but the Supreme Court’s March 2010 judgment did not expressly determine the 2004 appeal. The State Solicitor later agreed the appeal had been omitted. After further listings, the Supreme Court dismissed the 2004 appeal in November 2010.

These facts underpinned the applicant’s complaints that the civil proceedings were unreasonably long and that Ireland provided no effective remedy for that delay.
