**Summary of Levin v. Sweden (Application no. 35141/06)**

The case of *Levin v. Sweden* concerns an application brought by Ms. Eleonor Levin, a Swedish national, against the Kingdom of Sweden under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) concerning the severe contact restrictions imposed following the state’s taking of her three children into public care.

The applicant is the mother of three children: T. (born 1999), S. (born 2001), and D. (born 2002). Following her separation from the children's father in 2003, the applicant was granted sole custody. She later married J. in 2004. The family had been known to social services since 2002. In spring 2005, concerns arose from daycare staff regarding the children's hygiene, hunger, and hyperactive behavior, as well as the applicant's apparent stress. The applicant herself sought help from a psychiatric clinic (BUP) in March 2005. On 3 May 2005, in a state of despair, the applicant contacted BUP again. A social emergency unit, accompanied by police and a physician, visited her home and found it destitute—lacking furniture, electricity, and running water. The applicant was in a confused state and blamed the conditions on her son, S. The children were immediately placed in a temporary family home, and the applicant was committed to compulsory psychiatric care the following day.

After her release, the applicant had frequent but contentious contact with social services. She withdrew consent for the voluntary placement of her daughters, T. and D., leading the Social Council to take them into public care on a provisional basis in summer 2005. On 19 September 2005, the Council applied for a permanent care order for all three children. A comprehensive investigation cited the applicant’s serious lack of parenting ability, noting the children were dirty, had endless appetites, and exhibited developmental delays and trauma. The applicant initially believed her son caused the home’s destruction but later realized her husband, J., was responsible; they subsequently divorced. Despite this, the County Administrative Court granted a permanent care order on 19 October 2005, finding the applicant lacked the ability to care for the children and that there was a serious risk of harm to their health and development. This decision was upheld on appeal in January 2006, and leave to appeal to the Supreme Administrative Court was refused in February 2006.

The central issue arose from the contact restrictions. Following the care order, the applicant had limited, supervised visits with each child. In December 2006, the Social Council, based on an investigation in consultation with BUP, drastically restricted her contact to once every six months (balancing the father's contact rights). The investigation found the children—particularly T. and S.—suffered severe negative reactions (anxiety, bedwetting, stomach pains, fear) before and after contact with the applicant, jeopardizing their positive development in their foster homes. The applicant appealed, arguing for more frequent contact, but the restrictions were upheld by the County Administrative Court in April 2007 and the Administrative Court of Appeal in October 2007.

The restrictions were reviewed every three months. In November 2008, a court slightly increased contact to four times per year, four hours each time. However, upon the Administrative Court of Appeal's request, the children were consulted in early 2009. T. stated she did not want to meet her mother more than twice a year and found meetings exhausting, causing headaches and concentration issues. S. did not want to talk about his mother, showed signs of fear, and wanted to see her only once a year. D. was more positive but did not want to meet alone. A neuropsychological exam in February 2009 revealed the applicant met the criteria for ADHD (mainly inattentive type), though it noted this "could hardly be sufficient to 'disqualify her as a parent'." In May 2009, the Administrative Court of Appeal upheld the lower court's decision, finding increased contact was not in the children's best interests due to the negative reactions of T. and S. The applicant's complaint to the European Court of Human Rights focused on these contact restrictions as a breach of her right to family life under Article 8.

The case concerns Pavel and Vitalie Levinţa, Moldovan nationals arrested in Russia in October 2000 and extradited to Moldova. They alleged ill-treatment to force self-incriminating statements and were convicted partly on those confessions. In the earlier *Levinţa v. Moldova* judgment of 16 December 2008, the European Court found violations of Articles 3 and 6. Relying on that judgment, on 3 April 2009 they lodged an extraordinary appeal seeking annulment of their convictions. Before the Court, they alleged that they had been detained without legal basis and without reasons, that they lacked an opportunity to present their case, and that the courts failed to decide on their detention pending trial within a reasonable time.

On 8 February 2010 the Plenary Supreme Court of Justice accepted the request, quashed all convictions, ordered a re-hearing, and stated that the applicants “shall continue to be detained; the trial court shall decide on the preventive measure.” The applicants’ lawyer complained to the Minister of Justice and Prosecutor General, seeking immediate release because no valid detention order by an investigating judge or trial court existed. The Prosecutor General’s Office referred to the 8 February judgment; the Ministry said it had no information about any judgment concerning the applicants after 16 April 2002.

On 15 March 2010 the Supreme Court sent the case to the Chişinău Court of Appeal. On 13 April 2010 the lawyer asked that court to release the applicants, while the prosecutor requested 30 days’ detention pending trial. After hearings on 14 and 16 April were postponed, on 19 April the Court of Appeal noted that the Plenary Supreme Court had not decided preventive measures. It found continued detention necessary for the proper conduct of proceedings, citing reasonable grounds to believe the applicants had committed exceptionally serious crimes and risks that they would abscond or obstruct proceedings. It rejected the release request and ordered detention for 30 days from 2 p.m. on 14 April 2010.

The lawyer appealed, arguing that no lawful detention order or arrest warrant existed; that the “reasonable grounds” finding breached the presumption of innocence; that detention pending trial exceeded the maximum 12 months; that the prosecution submitted no evidence of risk; that no detention request had been made before 8 February 2010; and that hearings had been postponed. On 13 May 2010, at 10:30 a.m., the lawyer was telephoned that a Supreme Court hearing was set for noon. The Supreme Court rejected the appeal as unfounded, finding the lower court competent and no procedural violations.

Later that day, around 2 p.m., a Court of Appeal clerk allegedly told the lawyer of a 4 p.m. hearing on the prosecution’s request to extend detention. The lawyer was in Anenii Noi on another case and did not attend. At 5 p.m. the Court of Appeal examined the prosecution’s request, submitted 7 May, for 60 days’ detention. The applicants were absent (one refused, one claimed unfit), their chosen lawyer was absent, and a State-appointed lawyer represented them and objected. The court granted the extension for similar reasons. A dissenting judge noted that the request reached the Supreme Court only on 11 May; the prosecution merely repeated legal provisions without showing specific danger or precise grounds; and the defence was not informed, despite the parties having attended the Supreme Court that morning. The lawyer appealed, also claiming a two-hour period without legal basis after the previous order expired, short notice, and appointment of a State lawyer without the applicants’ consent.

On 3 June 2010 the Supreme Court rejected the appeal. It found no breach of defence rights because the applicants refused to appear, the lawyer was informed but unavailable, and substitute counsel was properly appointed. It held the earlier 30-day order did not expire until 14 May, so there was no two-hour unlawful detention. It also found that after the convictions were quashed, detention pending trial was exceptional and required a prosecution request; deadlines were observed; and grounds existed based on serious charges, prior

**Harroudj v. France (Application no. 43631/09)**

The applicant, Ms Katya Harroudj, is a French national born in 1962 who lives in Villeurbanne, France. The case concerns her inability to adopt a child placed in her legal care under the Algerian institution of *kafala*.

Zina Hind was born in Algeria on 3 November 2003 and was abandoned at birth by her anonymous mother. As her father was also unknown, she became a ward of the Algerian State, with the director of social services in Boumerdès appointed as her guardian.

On 13 January 2004, the President of the court of Boumerdès granted the applicant—then aged 42 and unmarried—the right to take the child into her legal care (*kafala*), and authorised the child to leave Algeria and settle in France. A subsequent Algerian court decision authorised the child's name change to Hind Harroudj. The child arrived in France on 1 February 2004 and has since lived with the applicant and the applicant's mother.

On 8 November 2006, the applicant applied for full adoption of Hind. She argued that adoption was the solution most consistent with the child's best interests under Article 3 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child and Article 1 of the Hague Convention on Intercountry Adoption.

On 21 March 2007, the Lyons *tribunal de grande instance* dismissed her application. It noted that *kafala* already gave her parental authority and that, under Article 370-3 of the French Civil Code, a child could not be adopted where the law of his or her country prohibited adoption—which Algerian law did, as Article 46 of the Algerian Family Code states that "adoption is prohibited by the Sharia and by legislation."

The Lyons Court of Appeal upheld this judgment on 23 October 2007. It reasoned that the choice-of-law rule referring to the child's personal law was non-discriminatory and compliant with Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and with international law. It noted that Article 4(a) of the Hague Convention requires the State of origin to establish that the child is adoptable, which was not the case since Algeria prohibits adoption. The court distinguished *kafala* from adoption, observing that *kafala* preserves the child's interests by conferring legal status on the care provided by guardians and is expressly recognised by Article 20 § 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. It also noted that Islamic law makes other provision for inheritance.

The applicant appealed on points of law, relying on Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. She submitted that it was in the child's interest for a legal parent-child relationship to be established between them, and that her inability to adopt entailed a disproportionate interference with her family life. She further argued that denying her the right to adopt established a difference in treatment regarding the child's family life on account of the child's nationality and country of origin, as children born in countries that do not prohibit adoption could be adopted in France.

On 25 February 2009, the Court of Cassation dismissed her appeal. It found that the Court of Appeal had not established any difference in treatment or disregarded the right to respect for family life, holding that *kafala*—expressly recognised by Article 20 § 3 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child—preserves the child's best interests on a par with adoption.

**Summary of Vikulov and Others v. Latvia**

The case of *Vikulov and Others v. Latvia* (Application no. 16870/03) originated from an application lodged by three Russian nationals—Mr Sergey Vikulov, his wife Mrs Galina Vikulova, and their son Mr Anton Vikulov—against the Republic of Latvia on 9 May 2003. The applicants alleged violations of Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), Article 5 § 1(f) (right to liberty regarding expulsion), and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights, concerning their detention and deportation.

The first applicant was a Soviet army officer stationed in the Latvian SSR from 1985, supervising a radar station in Skrunda. Following Latvia's independence in 1991 and the Russian Federation's assumption of jurisdiction over former Soviet armed forces, the applicants acquired Russian citizenship. Bilateral treaties in 1994 required the complete withdrawal of Russian armed forces and the radar station's dismantling by 2000. The first applicant was demobilised effective 11 November 1998, and the family's service visas expired on 30 November 1998.

In October 1998, the applicants sought residence permits, citing family ties (the second applicant's parents and daughter in Latvia) and the third applicant's enrolment in a State school. This request was dismissed on 8 April 1999, as they had entered Latvia due to military service and lacked a legal basis for permanent residence. Appeals were unsuccessful. Subsequent requests for temporary permits in March 2000 led to an order on 23 May 2000 requiring them to leave by 12 June 2000, with a five-year re-entry ban. Appeals through three court levels were dismissed, with the Supreme Court's final decision on 19 February 2003.

On 3 September 2003, during the execution of these orders, the applicants were arrested by the State Border Guard Service and placed in the Rīga detention unit for illegal immigrants. On 8 September 2003, a non-appealable deportation decision was issued. Their detention was extended by a court on 12 September 2003, which noted they lacked lawful residence and identity documents. They were transferred to the Olaine accommodation centre from 12 to 15 September 2003, then returned to Rīga, and deported to Russia on 17 September 2003.

The applicants described harsh detention conditions. In Rīga, they were held together in a small (3m x 3m), dirty cell with two steel bunk beds, a lavatory pan, and a washbasin. They alleged foul air, constant light, ants in food, and poor-quality meals. They were allowed only two 15-minute outdoor walks in fourteen days. They had limited family visits (twice) and were denied return to their home for belongings before deportation. On 9 September 2003, following an incident with an aggressive detainee, a woman was placed in their cell for up to two days despite protests. On 16 September 2003, a man was placed in their cell, forcing the first applicant to sleep on the floor. At Olaine, conditions were similarly poor: a dirty cell with dilapidated walls, a high fence with barbed wire, and a watchtower. They had to cook their own food in a shared kitchen.

The second applicant suffered heart problems during detention, including a heart attack on the deportation day, and received some medical treatment. The Government contested many claims, providing documentation on cell sizes, pest control, food regulations, and authorised visits. The case involved third-party intervention by the Russian Government and referenced CPT reports. The core alleged violations concerned the conditions of detention and the lawfulness and necessity of the measures leading to deportation.

In *Standard Verlags GmbH v. Austria (No. 3)* (Application no. 34702/07, judgment 10 January 2012), the applicant company, owner of the Vienna daily *Der Standard*, published on 4 April 2006 an economics article concerning an investigation into huge speculative losses at Hypo Alpe-Adria Bank. The article reported that, after a Financial Market Authority audit, the Klagenfurt public prosecutor’s office had opened an investigation into suspected embezzlement by senior bank managers. It mentioned Jörg Haider’s criticism of the prosecution and stated that losses of about EUR 328 million had arisen from swap transactions. Crucially, it named Christian Rauscher, head of the bank’s treasury department in 2004 and son of a former SPÖ regional government member responsible for finance, as someone whom Hypo’s executive board and Haider had previously blamed for the losses. It added that Rauscher had been demoted rather than dismissed and was relieved only after the losses became known, and described the treasury department’s supervisory and auditing context.

Rauscher sued the publisher under section 7a of the Austrian Media Act, seeking damages for disclosure of his identity. He argued that he was not a public figure, that he had acted under instructions and supervision, and that naming him harmed his professional advancement without any public interest. The applicant company countered that the article portrayed Rauscher as a scapegoat, not as the person responsible, and that the public interest in identifying a senior bank official outweighed his privacy interests, especially given his father’s political background. The reporting, it said, was neutral.

The Vienna Regional Criminal Court dismissed the claim. It found that Rauscher had headed the treasury, that the losses fell under his responsibility, and that although he was not a public figure, there was a sufficient connection with public life: the Land of Carinthia owned 45% of the bank, so taxpayers bore much of the loss. The public therefore had an overriding interest in knowing who was responsible. The Vienna Court of Appeal reversed on

The case *Yavuzdoğan v. Turkey* originated in application no. 8472/07, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 February 2007 by Mr Duran Yavuzdoğan, a Turkish national born in 1943 and living in Eskişehir. He invoked Article 34 of the Convention. The applicant died on 20 May 2009. On 25 May 2010 the Court was informed that his successors—Döndü Yavuzdoğan, Ayşe Yavuzdoğan, Tülay Arslan (Yavuzdoğan), Erkan Yavuzdoğan, Şenay Yavuzdoğan, and Seyit Yavuzdoğan—wished to pursue the application. For practical reasons, the Court continued to refer to Mr Duran Yavuzdoğan as “the applicant,” although his successors were now to be regarded as such. The Turkish Government was represented by its Agent. On 4 September 2009, the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government.

The underlying facts concern a property dispute between the applicant and the Turkish State Railways. On 13 October 2000, the Turkish State Railways brought compensation proceedings against the applicant before the Eskişehir Civil Court of First Instance. The administration alleged that the applicant was unlawfully occupying its property. In the same proceedings, it also requested that the unlawful occupation of the building on the property be stopped and that the building be demolished. The domestic proceedings therefore concerned both financial compensation and the applicant’s continued occupation and use of the property.

On 21 June 2005, the Eskişehir Civil Court of First Instance partially granted the administration’s request. It ordered the applicant to pay the plaintiff the principal amount of TRL 1,374,000,000, plus TRL 787,205,000 as interest. It also decided that the building on the property should be demolished. The applicant challenged the judgment. On 22 February 2006, the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance judgment of 21 June 2005. The applicant then sought rectification of the Court of Cassation’s judgment. On 5 October 2006, the Court of Cassation dismissed that request.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation(s) center on the domestic civil proceedings and the resulting interference with the applicant’s occupancy of the property. The proceedings began on 13 October 2000 and ended at the latest on 5 October 2006, when the rectification request was dismissed—a period of approximately six years. The first-instance judgment was delivered only on 21 June 2005, and the Court of Cassation upheld it on 22 February 2006. The applicant lodged his Convention application on 12 February 2007. He died in May 2009, and his successors pursued the case. The Government was notified in September 2009. However, the supplied excerpt does not expressly set out the applicant’s specific complaints or the Court’s findings on violations. The key facts presented are therefore the chronology of the State Railways’ compensation and demolition action, the domestic courts’ orders requiring payment and demolition, the appellate stages, and the procedural continuation by the applicant’s successors. These facts would be relevant to any complaint concerning the length or fairness of the civil proceedings and any alleged interference with property rights.

In *Zeynalov v. Azerbaijan* (Application no. 31848/07, judgment of 30 May 2013), the applicant, Ahmadshah Mammadshah oglu Zeynalov, an Azerbaijani farmer born in 1935, lodged an application with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 April 2007. He alleged in particular that the Supreme Court’s examination of the criminal case against him had not complied with the guarantees of Article 6 of the Convention.

The case arose from a dispute over ownership rights to a plot of land between the applicant and the Sadan Municipality in the former Davachi district. On 29 December 2004, the Davachi District Court convicted the applicant under Article 188 of the Criminal Code for violating a lawful owner’s right to a plot of land by unauthorised occupation or cultivation. He was fined 100 conventional financial units—550,000 old Azerbaijani manats, equivalent to 110 new Azerbaijani manats (AZN), or approximately EUR 84 at the time. The court found that he had unlawfully occupied and cultivated 0.8 hectares of land owned by the Municipality, relying on witness statements and information from the State Committee of Land and Cartography (“the SCLC”).

The applicant appealed, arguing that the disputed plot formed part of a larger 50-hectare parcel belonging to his family farming business. On 18 March 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant then lodged an appeal on points of law, alleging that the lower courts had erred in assessing the facts. On 9 August 2005, the Supreme Court, sitting as a panel of three judges including judge N.H., quashed the Court of Appeal’s judgment and remitted the case for fresh examination. It noted that the conviction had been based on insufficient evidence.

On remittal, the Court of Appeal sought detailed information from the SCLC and the Municipality about the exact location, measurements and ownership of the plot. The Municipality stated that official records showed the land belonged to it, and the SCLC conducted an on-site inspection and concluded that the plot was part of the Municipality’s estate. On 12 July 2006, the Court of Appeal again upheld the applicant’s conviction. The applicant appealed once more. On 10 October 2006, the Supreme Court, again composed of a panel of three judges including judge N.H., dismissed his appeal and upheld the Court of Appeal’s judgment. It found that all relevant evidence had been examined and that there had been no substantive or procedural breaches.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Article 6 violation concern judge N.H.’s repeated participation in the Supreme Court’s examination of the same criminal case. Under Article 109.1.6 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a judge cannot participate if he has already participated as a judge in the examination of the same criminal case in a court of first instance, appeal or Supreme Court. Article 109.2 requires such a judge to disqualify himself or herself. Furthermore, in decision no. 3 of 24 November 2005, the Plenum of the Supreme Court stated that a judge must withdraw when legal grounds for disqualification exist, even if the parties have not raised an objection, and that a judge who has already heard a criminal case at first instance, appeal or cassation cannot take part in its re-examination. The applicant’s complaint therefore focused on the alleged lack of an impartial tribunal because the same Supreme Court judge first quashed and remitted the case and later sat on the final cassation panel, contrary to domestic disqualification rules. The application was communicated to the Government on 10 November 2010, and the Court decided to rule on admissibility and merits together.

**Tarbuk v. Croatia** (Application no. 31360/10) concerned the applicant, Mr Dušan Tarbuk, a Croatian national who was arrested on 23 October 1995 and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of espionage connected with the Croatian Homeland War. He was detained as part of a larger group of eighteen suspects.

On 24 September 1996 Croatia enacted the General Amnesty Act, granting amnesty for criminal offences committed in connection with the war between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996, except for grave breaches of humanitarian law, war crimes, and genocide. Pursuant to that Act, the criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued on 7 October 1996, and he was immediately released.

On 9 June 1998 the applicant brought a civil action against the State in the Zagreb Municipal Court, seeking damages for his detention. He relied on Article 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which entitled a person who had been in pre-trial detention but against whom proceedings were not instituted or were discontinued by a final decision to compensation. His claim was therefore based on the law in force at the time it was lodged.

While the civil proceedings were pending, the legal basis for such compensation was removed. A June 1999 amendment introduced Article 484(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, providing that no compensation under Articles 476–484 could be granted where a person had been pardoned or amnestied under special laws or decisions. An October 1999 amendment specified that this exclusion applied to offences committed between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996—the period covering the applicant’s case.

The domestic courts applied Article 484(a) retroactively to the applicant’s pending claim. On 28 May 2004 the Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed the compensation claim for lack of legal basis. On 31 January 2006 the Zagreb County Court dismissed his appeal, holding that Article 484(a) excluded the application of Article 480 and had retroactive effect. On 28 August 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, expressly confirming that Article 484(a) applied retroactively and left no doubt that it covered the applicant’s situation. On 5 November 2009 the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional complaint, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning. It held that the Constitution did not guarantee compensation in such circumstances because the detention had been lawful and amnesty did not imply unlawful deprivation of liberty; the legislature could exclude amnestied persons from compensation.

The alleged Convention violation concerned Article 6 §1, the right to a fair trial. The applicant argued that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) to his civil action—lodged a year before that provision entered into force—extinguished his compensation claim and interfered with the judicial determination of his pending case. The key issue was whether the legislature’s retrospective intervention in pending civil proceedings, effectively predetermining their outcome, violated the fair-trial guarantee and the rule of law. The European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 6 §1, because the legislative change had been applied so as to influence the outcome of the applicant’s pending case, depriving him of a fair hearing.

In *Sýkora v. the Czech Republic*, Milan Sýkora, a Czech national with a psycho-social disability, alleged that his rights to liberty and private life were violated by the removal of his legal capacity and his subsequent involuntary detention in a psychiatric hospital. He had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia and had received psychiatric treatment in the past, but had not taken medication for years because he believed it damaged his eyesight.

The legal-capacity proceedings began in 2000, when the Brno Municipal Court deprived him of legal capacity at the request of the City of Brno. The court relied on a 1998 expert report by Dr H., which stated that the applicant suffered from paranoid schizophrenia. Although the applicant was aware of the proceedings, he was not summoned to appear, the judgment was not served on him, and he was formally represented by a court employee who had never met him and did not participate substantively. That decision became final in December 2000. After the applicant appealed, the Regional Court quashed it in August 2001 and remitted the case. In 2004, the Municipal Court again deprived him of legal capacity, relying on a new report by Dr H. prepared without examining him because he refused medical examinations. The court again did not hear him, did not serve the judgment on him, and appointed the City of Brno as guardian. The judgment became final in January 2005. The applicant learned of it only in June 2006 and appealed. The Regional Court quashed the decision in October 2006. In 2007, the Municipal Court finally decided not to deprive him of legal capacity. In total, he was deprived of legal capacity for about two and a half years.

In separate proceedings, the applicant sought damages from the State for procedural violations. The Ministry of Justice awarded him compensation for the unreasonable length of proceedings and accepted that the judgments had not been served on him, but said that a finding of violation was sufficient satisfaction. His damages action was rejected by the ordinary courts and, in 2012, the Constitutional Court dismissed his constitutional appeal.

The involuntary detention occurred in November 2005. Following a verbal argument with his partner, the police and an ambulance were called. Although the police found no violence and his partner said he had not been aggressive, an ambulance doctor took him to the Brno-Černovice Psychiatric Hospital. The applicant disagreed but did not resist. On admission, two examinations concluded that he suffered from schizophrenia. He insisted there was no reason for detention. Despite warning that neuroleptic medication harmed his eyesight, he was ordered to take it and, when he refused, it was administered by injection; his eyesight allegedly deteriorated.

The hospital notified the Municipal Court of his involuntary admission, but also contacted his guardian, the City of Brno, which consented to the detention on 14 November 2005. The employee who signed the consent had never met the applicant and did not inform him. A lawyer from the Mental Disability Advocacy Center challenged the detention and requested release. The applicant was released on 29 November 2005. However, no court ever reviewed the lawfulness of his detention. After release, he was told that no review proceedings had been instituted because his guardian had consented. Later complaints and constitutional appeals were dismissed, partly because he was no longer detained and partly because the guardian’s consent was considered sufficient.

The alleged violations therefore concerned Article 5 (unlawful detention and lack of judicial review), Article 8 (private life and autonomy, including forced medication and incapacitation), and related fair-hearing and effective-remedy issues.

In *Austin and Others v. the United Kingdom*, four applicants complained that their containment within a police cordon—known as “kettling”—at Oxford Circus, London, on 1 May 2001 amounted to a deprivation of liberty in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicants were held inside the cordon for periods of up to approximately seven hours during a large May Day anti-globalisation demonstration.

The first applicant, Lois Austin, was a Socialist Party member and experienced demonstrator. She attended the protest and needed to leave around 3:45 p.m. to collect her 11-month-old daughter from a crèche. She explained this to police officers at the cordon but was told she could not leave and that it was unclear when she would be released. A friend had to collect the child, and Ms Austin was not allowed out until about 9:30 p.m.

The second applicant, George Black, was a passer-by attempting to cross Oxford Circus to reach a bookshop. Police first told him he could not walk down Oxford Street and directed him along Margaret Street. There he encountered riot police advancing south, was forced into Oxford Circus at about 2:30 p.m., and was then unable to leave. He was told there was an exit at Bond Street, but when he went there, no exit existed. He was released at about 9:20 p.m.

The third applicant, Bronwyn Lowenthal, had no connection with the demonstration. She worked in the Oxford Circus area and was on her lunch break when police lines prevented her from returning to work. She tried another direction, but that exit was also blocked by police who advanced toward her. She was held until about 9:35 p.m. despite repeatedly asking to leave. The fourth applicant, Peter O’Shea, also worked locally and was caught in the cordon during his lunch break; he was released at about 8 p.m. All applicants said they were refused permission to leave, with police stating they had orders to let no one pass.

The domestic courts found that the police imposed the cordon at about 2 p.m. using common-law powers to prevent a breach of the peace. This decision followed serious disorder at previous May Day and globalisation protests, intelligence that 500–1,000 hard-core demonstrators sought confrontation, and concerns about serious injury, death, and property damage. Nearly 6,000 officers were deployed. The crowd at Oxford Circus grew faster than expected, and police decided to contain it. Conditions inside were uncomfortable: cold, wet, no food, water, toilets, or shelter. The first public announcement came at 4 p.m.

Controlled release was repeatedly planned but delayed by missile throwing, attempts to break the cordon, and disorderly crowds outside. Around 392 individual releases occurred, mostly before 4 p.m., including vulnerable persons. Full dispersal was almost complete by 9:45 p.m. In the domestic test case, Tugendhat J found the containment was a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 but was necessary and proportionate. The Court of Appeal held it was not a deprivation of liberty within Article 5 and was not arbitrary. The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation of Article 5 § 1, holding that the measure did not cross the threshold into deprivation of liberty in the particular circumstances. The key issue was whether a police cordon imposed for crowd control and public safety, detaining protesters and uninvolved passers-by for hours, constituted arbitrary detention under Article 5.

**F.N. and Others v. Sweden (Application no. 28774/09)**

**Summary of Key Facts**

The applicants are a family of four Uzbek nationals—a husband (F.N.), his wife, and their two minor children—who arrived in Sweden in December 2005 and applied for asylum. They alleged that deportation to Uzbekistan would expose them to a real risk of treatment contrary to Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment).

The first applicant claimed a history of persecution dating back to 1995, when he was allegedly arrested during a mosque raid, held in solitary confinement, and later convicted in 1998 as a "Muslim separatist" before receiving clemency. He asserted that he was placed on an authorities' blacklist of suspected Islamists.

The central event concerns his alleged participation in the Andijan demonstrations of 13 May 2005, during which Uzbek security forces opened fire on protesters. The first applicant claimed he fled the scene, but police subsequently arrested him at home, detained him for four days, and tortured him to extract a confession. He alleged release was secured through bribery, after which he went into hiding for six months before the family fled Uzbekistan illegally.

The second applicant claimed she was interrogated and subjected to degrading treatment regarding her husband's activities. The third applicant, a minor with pre-existing health issues, reportedly developed anxiety and learning difficulties. The family submitted documentary evidence including a medical certificate, a summons naming the first applicant as a witness, and posters of wanted persons purportedly listing him among Andijan suspects.

Swedish authorities rejected the asylum claims. The Migration Board and Migration Court found the applicants' accounts lacking credibility, citing vague testimony, inconsistent statements, and an "escalation" of their story over time. The courts noted that the first applicant traveled freely after the demonstration despite claimed road closures, questioned whether police would arrest someone not identified as a demonstrator, and found the wanted posters had "very low evidentiary value" due to formatting inconsistencies. The summons appeared to call him as a witness, not a suspect.

The applicants later introduced additional claims, including the first applicant's membership in the opposition party Birdamlik while in Sweden (sur place activities) and his alleged criminal charges related to the Andijan events. They argued that failed asylum seekers face particular risk upon return, referencing international reports documenting endemic torture in Uzbekistan and the vulnerability of those connected to Andijan.

Swedish courts rejected these claims, finding the Birdamlik activities limited and unproven to be known by Uzbek authorities. The authorities suggested the family could return without detection, possibly via neighboring countries. The applicants alleged that Migration Board contact with the Uzbek Embassy regarding travel documents would identify them as failed asylum seekers, increasing their risk. The courts found this speculative, noting other legitimate reasons for such contact existed.

The applicants lodged their case with the European Court of Human Rights in May 2009, which applied Rule 39 (interim measure) preventing deportation pending consideration.

text:
**Summary of the Case of Genderdoc-M v. Moldova**

The case of *Genderdoc-M v. Moldova* (Application no. 9106/06) originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 7 March 2006 by Genderdoc-M, a Moldovan non-governmental organisation advocating for the LGBT community. The applicant alleged a violation of their rights under the European Convention on Human Rights, specifically concerning the freedom of peaceful assembly.

The key facts revolve around the applicant’s attempt to hold a peaceful demonstration. On 7 April 2005, Genderdoc-M applied to the Chişinău Municipal Council for authorisation to hold a demonstration in front of the Parliament on 27 May 2005. The stated purpose was to encourage the adoption of laws protecting sexual minorities from discrimination.

The application was rejected. On 27 April 2005, the Municipal Council refused it, claiming the demonstration was baseless since a law on the protection of national minorities was already in place. On 6 May 2005, the Mayor’s Office also refused permission, reiterating the previous reason and adding that legal provisions dictated who had the power of legislative initiative.

Genderdoc-M contested the Mayor’s Office decision, arguing it was illegal and discriminatory. On 2 June 2005, the Chişinău Court of Appeal ruled in favour of the applicant, declaring the Mayor’s Office decision void. The court found the refusal’s justification legally ungrounded, stating that the law did not permit such reasons for banning an assembly. The court held that authorisation should not be conditional on the nature of the problems the assembly intended to address. The Mayor’s Office subsequently appealed this decision.

On 7 September 2005, the Supreme Court of Justice allowed the appeal, quashed the Court of Appeal’s decision, and remitted the case for re-examination. In the new proceedings, the Mayor’s Office shifted its justification, arguing that the assembly for promoting sexual minority rights would endanger public order and social morality. They also claimed the organisers had not assumed responsibility for the demonstration's management. Genderdoc-M again argued the ban was illegal and discriminatory.

On 14 June 2006, the Court of Appeal found against the applicant. This decision was upheld by the Supreme Court of Justice on 18 October 2006. The Supreme Court justified its ruling on two main grounds. First, it found that Genderdoc-M had failed to provide undertakings for various obligations required by domestic law on assemblies, such as designating responsible persons, creating a group with police to maintain order, and establishing a route. Second, the court considered there was a risk that the demonstration would breach public order.

The applicant alleged before the European Court that the refusal to authorise the demonstration violated Article 11 (freedom of assembly and association) and Article 14 (prohibition of discrimination) of the Convention. The central issue was whether the domestic authorities' interference with the right to peaceful assembly was justified. The case file highlights the shifting official justifications for the ban—from legally flawed reasoning about existing legislation to concerns over public order and alleged procedural shortcomings by the organisers—which formed the basis of the alleged violation of the right to peaceful protest.

text:
**Summary of the Case of G v. Germany (Application no. 65210/09)**

The case of *G v. Germany* concerns an application lodged against the Federal Republic of Germany with the European Court of Human Rights on 9 December 2009. The applicant, a German national born in 1968, alleged that the order for his retrospective preventive detention and its execution violated Article 7 § 1 of the Convention, which prohibits punishment without law. The applicant's identity was granted anonymity by the Court.

The key facts revolve around the applicant's criminal history. In February 1992, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court convicted the applicant, a first-time offender, of three counts of murder and one count of attempted murder, committed between 1988 and 1990. The victims were four young women he did not know, and the crimes were committed treacherously to satisfy his sexual desires. Psychiatric and psychological experts diagnosed him with a sadistic sexual deviation, lack of empathy, and brain damage, concluding he suffered from a serious mental abnormality and acted with diminished criminal responsibility. He was deemed liable to reoffend and dangerous to the public. Consequently, he was sentenced to fifteen years' imprisonment and ordered to be placed in a psychiatric hospital under Article 63 of the Criminal Code, as this was considered a more suitable measure than preventive detention at the time.

In March 1994, after therapy failed, the court ordered him to serve his prison sentence first. He served his full sentence by March 2005 and was transferred back to a psychiatric hospital in April 2006. However, in April 2007, the Kassel Regional Court terminated his psychiatric placement under Article 67d § 6, finding that he had never actually suffered from the condition that diminished his criminal responsibility. On the same day, the court ordered his provisional detention pending a decision on retrospective preventive detention. The applicant had been detained since August 2007.

In March 2008, the Frankfurt am Main Regional Court ordered his retrospective preventive detention under Article 66b § 3 of the Criminal Code. The court found that the requirements were met: he had been placed in a psychiatric hospital after committing several murders, and a comprehensive assessment showed it was very likely he would again commit serious offences, causing considerable harm. Experts considered him highly dangerous due to his lack of empathy and refusal to undergo treatment. The applicant appealed, but the Federal Court of Justice dismissed his appeal in September 2008. He then lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing that the retrospective preventive detention breached the prohibition on retrospective punishment and the protection of legitimate expectations.

In August 2009, the Federal Constitutional Court declined to consider his complaint as ill-founded. It held that preventive detention was not a penalty but a purely preventive measure for public protection, and thus Article 66b § 3 did not violate the ban on retrospective criminal laws or double punishment. It further found that the public interest in protecting society from dangerous offenders outweighed the applicant's legitimate expectations, even though the sentencing court in 1992 had deliberately declined to order preventive detention. The Constitutional Court deemed the measure compatible with the right to liberty, emphasizing the limited disadvantages compared to his prior psychiatric detention.

The applicant remained in preventive detention, with reviews in 2009 and 2011 refusing suspension or termination, as he was still considered dangerous. He also unsuccessfully sought reopening of his proceedings based on the European Court's judgment in *M. v. Germany*. The case before the Court centered on whether this retrospective preventive detention, ordered after his original sentence and psychiatric placement had ended, constituted a violation of Article 7 § 1 of the Convention.

**Summary of *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* (Application no. 43918/08)**

The case of *Hatice Duman v. Turkey* originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 September 2008 by Ms Hatice Duman, a Turkish national born in 1974. She was represented by lawyer F. Ertekin. The Turkish Government was represented by its Agent. The application was communicated to the Government on 8 February 2010. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s arrest, pre-trial detention, and the judicial review of that detention. On 9 April 2003, the applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership in the MLKP (Marxist-Leninist Communist Party), an illegal organisation. On 13 April 2003, she was brought before the public prosecutor and an investigating judge, who ordered her pre-trial detention.

On 23 July 2003, the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant and eight other persons. The charges included attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State, membership of an illegal organisation, and aiding and abetting such an organisation. Following the abolition of the State Security Courts by Law no. 5190, the criminal proceedings were resumed by the Istanbul Assize Court.

During the proceedings before the Istanbul Assize Court, the court repeatedly extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention and rejected her requests for release pending trial. It relied on reasonable grounds to suspect that she had committed the offence, the severity of the criminal charge against her, and the state of the evidence in the case file. At a hearing on 1 April 2009, the Istanbul Assize Court again rejected the applicant’s claim that her detention had been unreasonably lengthy and her request to be released pending trial.

The applicant challenged that decision by lodging an objection with the higher division of the Assize Court. In the course of the proceedings for review of her detention, the applicant alleged that neither she nor her lawyer was given an opportunity to make oral submissions against the lawfulness of her continued detention in a hearing. She also alleged that they were not notified of the observations submitted by the public prosecutor. On 17 April 2009, the 13th Chamber of the Istanbul Assize Court rejected the applicant’s objection against the prolongation of her detention, taking into account the nature of the criminal charge and the establishment of reasonable suspicion that she had committed the alleged crime.

On 4 May 2011, based on the evidence before it, the Istanbul Assize Court convicted the applicant of attempting to undermine the constitutional order, pursuant to Article 146 § 1 of the former Criminal Code, and sentenced her to life imprisonment. According to the latest information in the case file, the applicant lodged an appeal against the judgment with the Court of Cassation, and those proceedings were still pending. The applicant was serving her sentence in Gebze Prison.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are therefore the lengthy period of pre-trial detention from April 2003 until conviction in May 2011, the repeated judicial extensions of detention and rejections of release requests, and the alleged procedural shortcomings in the detention-review proceedings. In particular, the applicant complained that the review of her continued detention was not adversarial: she and her lawyer were allegedly denied an oral hearing and were not informed of the public prosecutor’s observations. These circumstances formed the basis of her complaints before the European Court of Human Rights, principally concerning the length of pre-trial detention and the effectiveness of judicial review of detention under Article 5 of the Convention.

text:
**Summary: Keskinen and Veljekset Keskinen Oy v. Finland**

This case originated in application no. 34721/09 against Finland, lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 30 June 2009 by Mr Vesa Petteri Keskinen, a Finnish national, and Veljekset Keskinen Oy, a Finnish limited liability company. The applicants alleged in particular that their right to a fair trial had been violated because the Vaasa Appeal Court convicted the first applicant and ordered forfeiture of the profit gained by the applicant company without holding an oral hearing.

The facts concerned an ice fishing competition organised by the applicants in February 2005. It was the seventh such event they had organised. The entrance fee was 20 euros. The applicants rented a lake and stocked it with 5,551 marked salmon: one weighing five kilos, 50 weighing about three kilos, 500 weighing about two kilos, and 5,000 weighing about one kilo. Winners were those who caught the most fish, and anyone catching a marked salmon won a prize according to its weight. The fisherman of the five-kilo salmon would win one million euros; the three-kilo fish carried a 20,000-euro gift certificate; the two-kilo fish a 2,000-euro certificate; and the one-kilo fish a 200-euro certificate. Each participant could buy only one entrance ticket and use only one rod and hook. The event attracted 27,731 participants. Of the 5,551 marked salmon, 2,188 were caught. Prizes awarded included three 20,000-euro certificates, 48 2,000-euro certificates and 2,137 200-euro certificates.

Regulatory authorities had previously examined the competition. When the 2003 event was organised, the Ministry of the Interior asked the applicant company to clarify its nature and concluded in March 2003 that it was partly a lottery under the Lotteries Act because fishers of marked salmon received separate prizes. This interpretation was sent to the county administrative board and local police, but the 2003 competition had no legal consequences. Preparations for the 2005 event began in 2004 and involved many local persons, including police. The Ministry again asked the applicant company to clarify the event. On 17 and 21 January 2005 it concluded that the event might constitute a lottery. This view was communicated to local police and leading county police officials. The applicants informed the police well in advance, and the police did not prohibit the event, although they had the right to do so if organising it was illegal.

Criminal proceedings were brought in 2006. The public prosecutor charged the first applicant, inter alia, with organising a lottery without a permit in connection with the ice fishing competition, because the outcome was partly based on luck. The prosecutor also asked that the profit gained from the offence by the applicant company be forfeited to the State.

On 5 June 2006 the Seinäjoki District Court, after an oral hearing, dismissed all charges against the first applicant and the forfeiture request against the applicant company. The court found that the lottery had been illegal, but that the first applicant’s misinterpretation of the law was excusable because the provisions were unclear, similar events had been organised before, and the authorities had not prevented the event.

The public prosecutor appealed to the Vaasa Appeal Court, reiterating the charges and requesting an oral hearing. He wanted two Ministry of the Interior civil servants heard about the Ministry’s role, the question of intent, and the applicants’ reactions to the Ministry’s queries and guidelines. As to forfeiture, he argued that an oral hearing was needed to assess evidence and the amount of profit. The applicants also appealed regarding costs and expenses and requested an oral hearing. They wanted two witnesses heard about the nature, content and organisation of the competition, and the company’s financial manager heard about the financial outcome. If no oral hearing was held, they asked to be allowed to submit further comments. Both parties had an opportunity to comment on the other’s appeal.

On 8 August 2007 the Vaasa Appeal Court rejected the request for an oral hearing. It sentenced the first applicant to 50 day-fines, amounting to 13,300 euros, for breach of the lottery provisions. It found that the facts and background were undisputed, that the written correspondence between the Ministry and the applicants had already been included in the District Court’s judgment, and that the Ministry’s role as supervisory and expert organ was apparent from the Lotteries Act. It therefore considered an oral hearing clearly unnecessary. It also found that the forfeiture did not require an oral hearing and that no further comments were needed. The alleged violation thus concerned the Appeal Court’s decision to convict the first applicant and order forfeiture of the applicant company’s profit without an oral hearing.

In *Gas and Dubois v. France* (Application no. 25951/07, ECtHR, 15 March 2012), the applicants were two French women, Valérie Gas and Nathalie Dubois, who had cohabited since 1989 and entered a civil partnership (PACS) in 2002. In 2000, Dubois gave birth in France to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. Because the donor was anonymous under Belgian law, A. had no legal father. She lived continuously with both women, and Dubois was her sole legal parent.

In 2006, Gas applied to the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance for a simple adoption of A., with Dubois’s consent. The public prosecutor objected. The domestic courts accepted that the statutory conditions for simple adoption were satisfied and that Gas was actively involved in A.’s upbringing, providing care and affection. Nonetheless, they refused the adoption. Under Article 365 of the French Civil Code, a simple adoption of a minor normally vests all parental responsibility in the adoptive parent alone. An exception exists where the adoptive parent is married to the child’s mother or father: then the adoptive parent and spouse may share parental responsibility. Gas and Dubois were not married—same-sex marriage was not available in France—and their PACS did not make them spouses for this adoption rule. Thus, granting the adoption would have transferred parental responsibility to Gas and deprived Dubois, the birth mother, of her parental rights. The courts found this contrary to A.’s interests. The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld the refusal in December 2006. The Court of Cassation’s case-law had also rejected similar applications on the same basis.

The applicants complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 14 taken together with Article 8 of the Convention. They alleged discriminatory treatment based on sexual orientation. They argued that French law provided no legal means for same-sex couples to obtain second-parent adoption, whereas married heterosexual couples could use adoption of a spouse’s child to create a legal parent-child tie while preserving the birth parent’s parental responsibility. They contended that this denied their family life legal recognition and discriminated against them as a same-sex couple.

Relevant background: French law distinguished full adoption from simple adoption. Simple adoption does not sever original family ties but creates an additional legal parent-child relationship. For a minor, however, it usually removes parental responsibility from the biological parents. The exception for adoption of a spouse’s child enabled married couples to share parental responsibility. Marriage was restricted to opposite-sex couples; PACS was open to same-sex couples but did not confer equivalent adoption or parental-responsibility rights. Assisted reproduction in France was available only to opposite-sex couples, so A. was conceived in Belgium. Delegation or sharing of parental responsibility was possible, but it did not create legal parentage and was temporary.

The alleged violation therefore concerned whether the refusal of simple adoption, based on Article 365 and the applicants’ inability to marry, amounted to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in violation of Article 14 read with Article 8. The Court declared the application admissible. Ultimately, it held that there had been no violation of Article 14 taken together with Article 8.

In *Balogun v. the United Kingdom* (Application no. 60286/09), the applicant, Mr Moshood Abiola Balogun, a Nigerian national born in 1986, alleged that his deportation to Nigeria would breach Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Article 3 was engaged by his claimed risk of suicide and mental health deterioration upon removal; Article 8 concerned his alleged family and private life in the United Kingdom.

The applicant claimed to have arrived in the UK aged three, but official records began in 1994, when he was eight, after a family court sought clarification of his immigration status in his aunt’s residence-order application. In 2003 his aunt applied for indefinite leave to remain, listing him as a dependant. Southwark Social Services also applied, stating that the aunt had thrown him out in January 2002 and that he had entered foster care; he alleged beatings by his aunt and her boyfriend from age three. Indefinite leave was granted in December 2003 outside the immigration rules. He lived in foster care from 2002 until age eighteen, then in council accommodation alone.

In February 2007, aged twenty, he was convicted of two counts of possessing Class A drugs with intent to supply and sentenced to three years’ imprisonment. He pleaded guilty on the basis that he had been coerced by a group he feared after being shot in 2005. In October 2007 the Secretary of State notified him of the intention to deport him. The Secretary of State found no evidence he had been in the UK since age three; his aunt said he was left with her at age five; the first official record was at age eight. Even accepting a long stay, only four years had been with valid leave. It was believed he remained in contact with his mother in Nigeria and, having lived alone after majority, was independent and adaptable. No family life was accepted.

His appeal was dismissed by the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal in March 2008. The Tribunal noted earlier convictions for drug and stolen-goods offences. It rejected his claimed serious relationship as inconsistent and late-disclosed. It found no protected family life: he had no contact with his former aunt; another aunt alleged to be a surrogate mother had not taken him in and was unaware of his conviction; his half-brother relationship was exaggerated. His private-life ties—long residence, education, and some work experience—were not strong enough to make deportation disproportionate. His mother lived in Nigeria and contact could be re-established. A deportation order was signed in October 2008; revocation and judicial review were refused in 2009.

Relevant to Article 3, the applicant was detained in November 2009, with removal set for 19 November. On 13 November he sought interim measures. A psychiatric report dated 14 September 2009 stated he had attempted suicide on 13 August 2009 after refusal of his human rights claim, was an inpatient until 7 September, expressed despair, and suffered moderate depression. The Court applied Rule 39 on 18 November, later extending it. The Government said it had not known of the suicide attempt but that detention staff provided constant supervision, trained staff, and possible medical escort; Nigeria had mental health facilities. The applicant took a paracetamol overdose in December 2009, assessed as a few tablets, and was released in January 2010 without further attempts.

Domestic law allowed deportation conducive to the public good, with Convention-based appeals. UK case law in *J v. Secretary of State for the Home Department* set a high threshold for suicide-based Article 3 claims, requiring strong grounds of a real risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, a causal link to removal, and consideration of protective mechanisms in the UK, transit, and the receiving State.
