text:
In *Sarkizov and Others v. Bulgaria* (ECtHR, 17 April 2012), four Bulgarian nationals complained principally that their criminal conviction was based to a decisive extent on anonymous witness testimony and that their defence rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) were unacceptably restricted. The second and fourth applicants also alleged that post-release travel bans were unjustified and lacked effective domestic remedies, contrary to Articles 8 and 13 and Article 2 §§ 2–3 of Protocol No. 4.

The criminal proceedings began on 12 October 2004 for sexual procurement. The prosecution alleged that the applicants induced, procured or transported women into prostitution. Several witnesses, including Mr Zh.M., Mr N.P., Ms R.M. and Ms D.M., were questioned before a judge at the pre-trial stage, but neither the applicants nor their lawyers attended those interviews. Three other witnesses were granted anonymity. Anonymous witnesses nos. 15 and 16 were questioned before a judge in October 2004. The applicants and their lawyers were then given the records and invited to put questions, but they stated in writing that they had none. Witness no. 17 was questioned before a judge on 27 October 2004; some applicants and lawyers attended, while others were absent. Those present also stated that they had no questions. The anonymous witnesses described prostitution arrangements, travel abroad, recruitment and money transfers.

At trial, the anonymous witnesses repeatedly failed to appear. The prosecution said that some were abroad or could not be found. The applicants’ lawyers repeatedly asked that they be found and questioned and challenged the need for anonymity. The District Court ordered efforts to secure their attendance but eventually, on 28 March 2006, read out and admitted their pre-trial statements when they were absent. It convicted the applicants of inducing or attempting to induce women into prostitution, procuring or transporting the anonymous witnesses and other women. Sentences ranged from three years’ imprisonment plus fines to five years’ imprisonment plus a fine. The court found that the victims’ statements, including the anonymous ones, were corroborated by other evidence: other witness statements, international money-transfer reports, border-control reports and secret surveillance material. On appeal, the Regional Court upheld the conviction on 17 July 2006 and refused to question the anonymous witnesses again. The Supreme Court of Cassation later dismissed a reopening request, holding that there had been no procedural breach, that the anonymous testimony had not been the sole or decisive evidence, and that the applicants had had the opportunity to question those witnesses but had declined.

As to the travel bans, the second applicant was conditionally released in April 2007. In June 2007 the police prohibited him from leaving Bulgaria pending rehabilitation. His appeal was dismissed in January 2008; the Supreme Administrative Court said the ban complied with law and aimed to prevent criminally active persons from travelling until reformed. The fourth applicant was released and in April 2008 received a similar ban pending rehabilitation. His appeal was dismissed in December 2008; the court held that the administrative assessment was not subject to judicial control and that police need not state reasons. The bans were tied to judicial rehabilitation and would have lasted until at least October 2010 or 2011, but after a 2009 amendment they ceased in July 2010.

Domestic law required protected-witness decisions to state reasons, judicial verification of identity, immediate access by the accused and lawyer to records, and a right to put questions. Conviction could not be based exclusively on anonymous testimony. The key fair-trial issue was therefore whether reliance on anonymous pre-trial statements, coupled with the later inability to question those witnesses at trial, breached Article 6. The travel-ban complaints concerned whether the restrictions and limited judicial review breached private life, liberty of movement and the right to an effective remedy.

**Summary**

*Dadiani and Machabeli v. Georgia* (Application no. 8252/08) was decided by the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section) on 12 June 2012 and became final on 12 September 2012. The applicants, Elene Dadiani and David Machabeli, are Georgian nationals living in Tbilisi; the second applicant is the first applicant’s nephew. The first applicant’s mother had been deprived of her land and other assets by the Soviet authorities in the 1920s. In 2004, the applicants brought an action against the relevant local authority seeking restitution of their ancestral lands. They relied on archival documents confirming their ancestor’s title and on general rules of property protection and inheritance under Georgian and international law.

On 31 January 2005, the Gurjaani District Court established the applicants’ joint ownership of land in the village of Bakurtsikhe, identified as “plot no. 604.” The defendant local authority did not appeal, and the judgment became binding. On 15 February 2005, the applicants’ lawyer obtained an enforcement writ stating that Dadiani and Machabeli were recognised as co-owners of plot no. 604.

On 26 October 2005, the applicants submitted the final judgment and enforcement writ to the Gurjaani Public Registry for enforcement. By letter of 2 November 2005, the registrar refused to register the land in their names, saying the documentation was incomplete. The registrar noted that the final judgment neither indicated the size of plot no. 604 nor specified whether it was agricultural or non-agricultural. The lawyer was asked to submit his identity document, proof of authority to represent the applicants, the original enforcement writ, and a cadastral plan. The applicants claimed that their lawyers visited the registry several times and raised concerns about non-enforcement, but that they could not produce an amended final court decision. The registry continued to refuse registration for various reasons. The judgment of 31 January 2005 remains unenforced.

In a separate set of proceedings, on 25 May 2005 the applicants lodged another action claiming ownership of plot no. 646, adjacent to plot no. 604, on the same legal basis. The action was registered by the Gurjaani District Court on the same day. According to the applicants, examination of this second action had not yet started.

Before the European Court, the applicants complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the authorities’ failure to enforce the domestic judgment in their favour. They also alleged violations of Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 on account of the inexplicable delay in the second set of proceedings. Finally, they complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the expropriation of their ancestral lands by the Soviet authorities.

Relevant domestic law included the National Public Registry Agency’s registration functions; the Land Registration Act, which allowed the registrar to request any document necessary for registration and required immediate compliance; Article 1005 of the Civil Code, providing for State liability for damage caused by a public servant; Article 381 of the Criminal Code, criminalising non-execution or obstruction of binding judicial decisions by officials; and the General Administrative Code, which excluded enforcement of final court judgments from its scope. The Court gave notice of the application to the Government on 28 April 2008 and decided to rule on admissibility and merits simultaneously. The central factual issues concerned the refusal to register plot no. 604, the continued non-enforcement of the final judgment, and the prolonged inactivity in the second restitution proceedings.

Tarbuk v. Croatia (Application no. 31360/10) concerned the retroactive removal of a compensation claim for pre-trial detention following a general amnesty. The applicant, Dušan Tarbuk, a Croatian national born in 1956 and living in Zagreb, was arrested on 23 October 1995 and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of espionage connected to Croatia’s Homeland War. He was arrested as part of a group of eighteen persons suspected of the same offence.

On 24 September 1996, Croatia enacted the General Amnesty Act, granting amnesty for criminal offences committed in connection with the war between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996, except for the gravest breaches of humanitarian law, including war crimes and genocide. Pursuant to that Act, criminal proceedings against Tarbuk were discontinued on 7 October 1996, and he was immediately released.

On 9 June 1998, Tarbuk brought a civil action against the State in the Zagreb Municipal Court, seeking damages for his detention. He relied on Article 480 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which provided that anyone who had been in pre-trial detention but against whom criminal proceedings had not been instituted or had been discontinued by a final decision was entitled to compensation.

However, after Tarbuk had lodged his civil claim, the Code of Criminal Procedure was amended. On 2 June 1999, a new Article 484(a) was introduced, providing that no compensation was to be granted in connection with detention where proceedings had been discontinued pursuant to a pardon or amnesty under special laws or decisions. On 27 October 1999, another amendment specified that Article 484(a) applied to criminal offences committed between 17 August 1990 and 23 August 1996. That amendment therefore directly covered Tarbuk’s situation.

The domestic courts rejected Tarbuk’s compensation claim. On 28 May 2004, the Zagreb Municipal Court dismissed the claim on the ground that it had no legal basis. On 31 January 2006, the Zagreb County Court dismissed his appeal, holding that Article 484(a) had extinguished his compensation claim and that the provision had retroactive effect. On 28 August 2007, the Supreme Court dismissed his appeal on points of law, expressly confirming that Article 484(a) applied retroactively and excluded the application of Article 480.

On 19 November 2007, Tarbuk lodged a constitutional complaint, arguing that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) to his civil action—filed about a year before the provision came into force—had extinguished his right to compensation. On 5 November 2009, the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint, endorsing the lower courts’ reasoning.

The alleged violation concerned the applicant’s right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Tarbuk complained that the retroactive application of Article 484(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure to his pending civil claim deprived him of a fair hearing and effectively extinguished a claim he had already brought under the law in force at the time. The European Court of Human Rights communicated this fair-trial complaint to the Croatian Government on 5 September 2011 and decided to examine admissibility and merits simultaneously.

Relevant domestic law included Article 25 of the Croatian Constitution, providing a right to compensation for unlawful deprivation of liberty, and Article 29, guaranteeing a fair hearing. The Code of Criminal Procedure contained Article 480, which originally founded Tarbuk’s claim, and Article 484(a), which later barred it. The General Amnesty Act provided the underlying amnesty. In Constitutional Court decision no. U-I-2023/2002 of 7 December 2005, the Constitutional Court had upheld Article 484(a), reasoning that compensation depended on the unlawfulness of detention; amnesty or pardon did not affect the lawfulness of detention, and the legislature could exclude compensation for persons amnestied. The case thus centred on whether the retroactive application of Article 484(a) violated Tarbuk’s fair-trial rights by removing his compensation claim after he had already initiated civil proceedings.

In *Zarochentsev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 39327/06), the European Court of Human Rights considered a Ukrainian criminal case that lasted nearly a decade. The applicant, Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Zarochentsev, a Ukrainian national born in 1974 and living in Bakhchysaray, lodged his application on 8 December 2006. The application was communicated to the Government on 5 May 2009. He was represented by A. V. Lesovoy; the Government were represented by Y. Zaytsev, later V. Lutkovska.

The facts relevant to the alleged violation centre on the length and conduct of the criminal proceedings. On 7 March 2001 the Kyivskyy District Prosecutor of Simferopol opened a criminal case against the applicant on suspicion of embezzlement while he was a shop manager. Similar proceedings were brought against the shop director, Mr Z. From 30 May to 9 August 2001 the investigation was stayed because the authorities could not establish the applicant’s whereabouts, and he was placed on a wanted list. He was apprehended on 13 August 2001. On 23 August 2001 the Kyivskyy District Court of Sevastopol remanded him in custody pending trial, but on 29 August 2001 the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea quashed that ruling and released him under an obligation not to leave the town.

On 13 November 2001 the applicant and Mr Z. were indicted and the case was referred to the Kyivskyy Court for trial. The trial began on 3 December 2001 and involved nine hearings. Five adjournments, totalling about five months, were caused by the applicant’s requests or absence. Another adjournment of about five months resulted from the judge’s absence. The examination was further delayed by about a year after the court, at the prosecutor’s request, ordered a repeated forensic accounting evaluation.

On 14 February 2005 the Kyivskyy Court, again at the prosecutor’s request, remitted the case for additional investigation. The Court of Appeal upheld that ruling on 5 April 2005. After April 2005, the investigation was stayed on three occasions: for eight months, for one year and three months, and for about a year, respectively, because the whereabouts of the applicant and Mr Z. were unknown. However, all those rulings by the investigator were quashed by the Prosecutor’s Office of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea as unfounded, and new investigators were assigned.

The applicant stated that he enquired repeatedly about the investigation’s progress and requested disciplinary action against the prosecutors and investigators concerned. By letter of 18 February 2011, the Crimea Prosecutor’s Office informed him that the criminal proceedings against him and Mr Z. had been terminated on 27 December 2010 for lack of corpus delicti.

The key issue was therefore whether this lengthy criminal process violated the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, and possibly whether there was an effective remedy under Article 13. The facts show a total duration of almost ten years, with significant periods of delay or repeated suspensions attributable to the authorities, alongside some delays linked to the applicant. The repeated remittals, stays, and changes of investigators were central to the alleged unreasonable length and procedural inefficiency.

The applicant, a Danish national born 30 November 1991, was arrested on 13 September 2007 in Qaqortoq, Greenland, at the age of fifteen. He was charged with rape and homicide under sections 216(2) and 237 of the Danish Penal Code for offences committed on 26 May 2007 against an eighty-five-year-old woman in Aalborg, Denmark, where he attended a youth school institution. The case attracted massive media coverage. The applicant pleaded guilty to both charges and was ordered held in pre-trial detention for four weeks.

After one week, he was transferred to Denmark and brought before Aalborg City Court, which on 20 September 2007 extended his detention on remand until 11 October 2007, and until placement in an appropriate home or institution could be secured under section 765 of the Administration of Justice Act. The court also ordered a forensic psychiatric examination, which commenced on 21 November 2007. The applicant was initially placed in a closed young offender institution and then, from 10 October 2007, at "Grenen," a secure residential institution for young people aged 12 to 17.

His detention was extended by four weeks on numerous occasions throughout late 2007 and 2008. The first forensic psychiatric report, submitted on 22 January 2008, concluded that the applicant fell within Article 16(2) of the Penal Code concerning mentally ill persons and recommended placement in an institution for patients with a far-reaching mental handicap. The Medico-Legal Council subsequently recommended placement in an institution for persons with extensive mental disabilities under section 68 of the Penal Code. However, on 21 April 2008, the Joint Council for the Mentally Disabled found the documentation inadequate and urged further examination, prompting a second forensic psychiatric report.

On 11 September 2008, for the first time, the applicant objected to an extension of his pre-trial detention, invoking section 768a of the Administration of Justice Act, which had entered into force on 1 July 2008 and specifically limited pre-trial detention of persons under eighteen to a maximum of eight months unless "very special circumstances" applied. By that date, his detention had exceeded eight months. The City Court extended detention until 9 October 2008, finding that very particular circumstances justified deviating from the maximum period. The High Court upheld this decision on 19 September 2008, and the applicant did not seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court.

A second forensic psychiatric report was submitted on 3 November 2008. On 6 November 2008, the City Court again extended detention, noting that hearing the Medico-Legal Council was of significant importance and that very particular circumstances applied. The High Court upheld this on 14 November 2008, and leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 19 December 2008. On 10 December 2008, the second Medico-Legal Council report concluded that the applicant's case fell under section 69 of the Penal Code rather than section 16(2), recommending structured, supervised socio-pedagogical measures or, alternatively, ordinary punishment.

Detention was extended again on 4 and 17 December 2008, and 13 January 2009. The trial commenced on 27 January 2009, and the applicant was convicted and sentenced to eight years' imprisonment. He had been in pre-trial detention for approximately sixteen and a half months. The domestic courts found that the length of proceedings was justified by the need for two mental status examinations and submissions to the Medico-Legal Council, which were of vital significance for determining the sanction, and that the prosecution had acted with due diligence. The applicant alleged that the length of his detention on remand breached Article 5 § 3 of the Convention.

In *Aleksejeva v. Latvia* (Application no. 21780/07), the applicant, Jeļena Aleksejeva, a Latvian national born in 1984, lodged an application on 13 April 2007. She alleged violations of Articles 3 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, claiming that the national authorities failed to protect her from potential attacks by other prisoners and that they violated her right to respect for private and family life by restricting visits from her partner and mother.

On 18 October 2006 the applicant was detained in Iļģuciema Prison, the only prison in Latvia for female detainees. Her mother had worked at the same prison for approximately 25 years and, in 2006, was assistant to the prison governor; she retired on 22 October 2006. According to the applicant, prison security advised her to conceal this family connection because relatives of prison staff could be in danger from other inmates. A guard removed her mother’s photograph from her cell, saying it could reveal their relationship and endanger her. The applicant allegedly lived in constant fear that her mother’s former employment would become known. One inmate reportedly knew of the connection. A former inmate, V.M., claimed to have witnessed another prisoner, L.A., using derogatory language and veiled threats toward the applicant, implying that she had learned about the relationship from a prison staff member, T.J.

On 5 February 2007 the applicant complained to the Ombudsman’s Office and requested a transfer to an open prison or separation from other prisoners. The deputy governor of Iļģuciema Prison told her that separation could not be ensured unless she was kept in complete isolation, but both agreed that isolation would be comparable to additional punishment. In April 2007, before an administrative commission considered her transfer to the medium imprisonment regime, she signed a form waiving her right to a lawyer but added in her own hand that she did not object to sharing a cell if transferred. In May 2007 she was transferred to the medium regime and placed with other prisoners, specifically first-time prisoners according to the Government. In August 2007 the Ombudsman found sufficient safeguards and considered that her life and health were not under threat. In January 2008 she was transferred to Vecumnieki Open Prison under the highest regime and later released.

As to visits, on 26 February 2007 the prison governor refused the applicant’s request for a long-term visit from a man she described as her partner. She was told that non-close relatives could receive long-term visits only if her close relatives did not visit her, and she was asked to prove her divorce. On 28 February 2007 a prison official repeated this refusal despite a court statement that her divorce case was pending. The applicant also stated that prison staff told her visits from her mother would be “problematic” because other prisoners would discover their relationship. Her mother therefore did not visit, though the applicant used her four monthly phone calls to speak with her. After her divorce on 16 April 2007, she was allowed five long-term and six short-term visits from her partner between 26 April and 22 September 2007. From 29 August to 5 September 2007 she was granted leave to visit her mother.

Domestic law required certain former law-enforcement employees and their close relatives to be detained separately in some circumstances, and long-term prison visits were normally reserved for close relatives unless close relatives did not visit. The applicant alleged that Latvia breached Article 3 by failing to protect her from prisoner violence and Article 8 by restricting visits from her partner and mother.

Austin and Others v. the United Kingdom concerned the police containment tactic known as “kettling” during the May Day 2001 anti-globalisation protests in central London. Four applicants were caught inside a police cordon at Oxford Circus for periods of roughly six to seven hours. They alleged that this restriction amounted to a deprivation of liberty in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The police imposed the cordon around 2 p.m. after intelligence suggested that 500 to 1,000 hard-core demonstrators planned violence, and after serious disorder at similar protests in 1999 and 2000. The cordon was intended to prevent a breach of the peace and to protect people and property. It took between five and twenty-five minutes to establish. No announcement was made until 4 p.m. Conditions became uncomfortable: the weather was cold and wet, and there was no food, water, shelter or toilet access. The police planned controlled release, but dispersal was repeatedly delayed by missile-throwing, attempts to break the cordon, violent crowds outside, and insufficient resources. About 400 individual releases were recorded. Collective release began around 7 p.m., was halted, resumed, halted again, and finally resumed at 8 p.m.; dispersal was almost complete by 9:45 p.m.

The applicants’ individual circumstances varied. Ms Austin was a demonstrator. At about 3:45 p.m. she needed to leave to collect her 11-month-old daughter from a crèche, but police refused permission; she arranged for a friend to collect the child and was released at about 9:30 p.m. Mr Black was a passer-by trying to cross Oxford Circus to a bookshop. Police directed him into the area, and when he asked to leave he was told there was an exit at Bond Street, but on reaching it he was told there was no exit. He was held until about 9:20 p.m. Ms Lowenthal had no connection with the demonstration. She worked in the area and was on her lunch break when police blocked her return to work; she was held until about 9:35 p.m. Mr O’Shea, also working locally, was caught during his lunch break and released at about 8 p.m. Several applicants repeatedly asked to leave but were told police had orders to let no one pass.

Domestically, the High Court (Tugendhat J) found that the containment did amount to a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 § 1, but that it was lawful: the police acted out of necessity to prevent a breach of the peace, and the purpose included preventing offences and enabling arrest. The Court of Appeal disagreed on Article 5, holding that the containment did not amount to a deprivation of liberty. It compared the situation to crowds held at football matches or motorists delayed on a motorway, and found the police had no alternative but to impose the cordon to avoid violence.

The case reached the European Court of Human Rights Grand Chamber. The key factual issue was whether the containment, in the context of serious threatened public disorder, crossed the threshold from a restriction on movement into a deprivation of liberty under Article 5 § 1. The Grand Chamber ultimately found no violation, holding that in the exceptional circumstances the containment did not amount to a deprivation of liberty.

In *Boukrourou and Others v. France*, six French nationals—the family of M.B.—complained under Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention about M.B.’s death and treatment during a police arrest. M.B., aged 41, had long-standing psychiatric disorders and regularly collected neuroleptic medication from a pharmacy in Valentigney. On 12 November 2009, he asked to exchange medicine, became angry, spoke incoherently, accused pharmacy staff of “night visits,” and refused to leave. Staff called the police. At 4:53 p.m., four officers arrived and were told the incident involved a person with psychiatric disorders. They repeatedly asked M.B. to leave; he refused. Officers then seized him by the arms and leg. A struggle followed, and M.B. fell at the pharmacy entrance. While officers tried to handcuff him, Constable M. punched him twice in the solar plexus using “diversionary blows.” M.B. was handcuffed in front with interlinked handcuffs and forced into a police van.

Inside the van, M.B. continued struggling and shouting. Officers restrained him: one positioned himself over M.B.’s shoulders, while two others placed themselves on his legs and buttocks; he was attached to the fixed back seat. Five minutes after arriving, at 4:58 p.m., the officers called the fire brigade and SAMU. Firefighters arrived, but police refused to transfer M.B. to them, citing his agitation. Firemen monitored him; his breathing stopped and circulation was absent. He was moved back into the pharmacy and resuscitated, but death was recorded at 6:02 p.m.

Autopsy findings showed facial and wrist injuries and marks consistent with two violent abdominal blows, but no internal bleeding or fractures; M.B. also had severe heart artery stenosis. The first forensic report concluded death was likely due to heart failure, with stress and agitation possibly contributing, but mechanical asphyxia was not confirmed. Later experts found death resulted from natural causes/myocardial failure, and then more specifically from cardiac rhythm disorders caused by a coronary spasm triggered by intense, prolonged emotional and physical stress and agitation from the pharmacy through the arrest. Mechanical asphyxia was ruled out. A psychiatric expert confirmed serious delusional psychosis and said superficial injuries were compatible with immobilisation and the punches.

Witness evidence was conflicting. Pharmacists saw the struggle but not what happened inside the van. A firefighter described M.B. face down and restrained. A shopkeeper and her son alleged police punched, kicked, or trampled M.B., including in the van, but the forensic doctor found no injuries matching such violence except the stomach punches. The Ombudsman criticised the police: they quickly sought emergency help, but the incident room misdescribed the situation; there was no imminent danger requiring immediate removal; and the immobilisation/compression in the van was dangerous and disproportionate, amounting to a serious infringement of dignity and inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 3. He also noted conflicting police statements and recommended discipline and better training.

A manslaughter investigation opened. In 2012 four officers were charged with manslaughter for a manifestly wilful violation of a duty of caution and security. The investigating judges found no case to answer: force was necessary and proportionate; pinning was not the direct medical cause; police did not know of M.B.’s heart disease; and he was already stressed. The Court of Appeal upheld this in 2013, and the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicants’ appeal in 2014. The applicants then brought the ECtHR complaint alleging violations of Articles 2 and 3 arising from M.B.’s death and restraint.

text:
**Summary of *Traustason and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 44081/13)**

The case originated from an application lodged against Iceland with the European Court of Human Rights by three Icelandic nationals: Reynir Traustason, Jón Trausti Reynisson, and Ingi Freyr Vilhjálmsson. The first two applicants were editors, and the third was a journalist for the newspaper *DV*. They alleged that domestic court judgments against them for defamation violated their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

The facts concern a private company declared bankrupt on 30 September 2010, owing approximately 7.15 million euros to a major Icelandic bank, a debt that had increased significantly after the 2008 financial crisis. In October 2010, the bankruptcy estate’s liquidator hired an accountancy firm to investigate the company’s accounts. On 31 January 2011, the firm finalised a report indicating a suspicion of criminal misconduct by the board members, including its chairman and co-owner, identified as "A," who was also an assistant professor at the University of Iceland. The liquidator reported the suspected misconduct to the police, as did a holding company and a bank.

On 14 March 2011, *DV* published an article and front-page headline stating, "Black report on [the company]: Police investigate Assistant Professor." The article, authored by the third applicant, was based on the accountant's report and detailed allegations that the company had paid for A's personal expenditures, that A and a co-owner knew of the company's grave financial situation long before bankruptcy, and that assets had been transferred while insolvent. Crucially, the article stated that police were investigating A.

On 16 March 2011, A's lawyer received an email from a police prosecutor confirming that the liquidator's complaint was being "examined" along with two other complaints, but that no formal decision had been taken to instigate a police investigation. A's lawyer requested a correction, which the first applicant refused.

A subsequently lodged defamation proceedings. On 5 March 2012, the Reykjavík District Court found the statements "Police investigate Assistant Professor" and "Assistant Professor entangled in police investigation" defamatory. The court reasoned that while the police had received complaints, no formal investigation had been opened. It found the statements were factually wrong, as it was "not unreasonably difficult" for the media to verify whether an investigation had been initiated. The statements were declared null and void, and the applicants were ordered to pay compensation and costs.

The applicants appealed, but on 6 December 2012, the Supreme Court upheld the lower court's judgment. It found that the prosecutor's email could only be understood as meaning no investigation had been instigated and that the statements were "wrong and defamatory," damaging A's reputation without grounds. The applicants' subsequent application to the European Court of Human Rights, complaining that these judgments violated their Article 10 rights, forms the basis of this case.

**Summary of Brennan v. Ireland (Application no. 44360/15)**

The case of *Brennan v. Ireland* concerns an application lodged by Ms. Margaret Brennan, an Irish-British national born in 1947, against Ireland. The applicant alleged a violation of the Convention, specifically concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings she initiated regarding structural defects in her home. The core of the case relevant to the alleged violation lies in the protracted timeline and procedural history of the domestic litigation.

In November 1999, Ms. Brennan purchased a newly built house, her residence since March 2000. The transaction involved two agreements: one for the land purchase from Mr. and Mrs. F and another building agreement with their company, T and C Developments Ltd. Critically, the house was covered by a structural guarantee from Homebond. Upon moving in, the applicant discovered major structural defects. After reporting these to Homebond in September 2001, the company inspected the property and, in September 2002, offered repairs under the guarantee. However, a dispute arose, with the applicant claiming Homebond refused to issue a necessary engineer’s certificate upon completion.

In February 2003, the applicant initiated High Court proceedings against multiple parties, including the landowners, the building company, Homebond, and the engineer who certified compliance. The procedural history that followed is marked by significant delays. Key factual elements contributing to the length of proceedings include:

- **Delays in Pleadings:** The first three defendants failed to deliver their defence for an extended period, despite requests and court orders. Their defence was eventually filed in September 2004. The claim was not served on Homebond until December 2003, with its defence filed in May 2004.
- **Default Judgment Issues:** A default judgment obtained against the engineer and his company in December 2004 was never enforced, with the applicant later receiving conflicting legal advice about its validity. A separate motion for default judgment against the initial defendants was struck out in July 2009.
- **Periods of Dormancy:** The case experienced periods of inactivity. Notably, the applicant’s solicitors focused on engaging with Homebond from 2005 to 2008. After her solicitor ceased representing her in April 2009, Ms. Brennan proceeded as a lay litigant.
- **Resumption and Scheduling:** From late 2009 onwards, the applicant periodically issued notices of intention to proceed to prevent the case from being struck out for dormancy. A hearing date was eventually secured for early 2013.

The High Court delivered its rulings in 2013. On 20 March 2013, it found Homebond liable under the guarantee, awarding approximately €51,000, and dismissed the case against the engineer. On 15 May 2013, it held the first three defendants jointly and severally liable for €94,082. Appeals followed. Homebond’s appeal was ultimately successful in the Court of Appeal on 23 February 2015. The first and second defendants’ appeal was also allowed on 9 March 2015, with the Court of Appeal ruling they were not liable as they were not party to the building agreement. The applicant’s request for leave to appeal to the Supreme Court was refused on 29 July 2015.

Overall, the civil proceedings, from initiation in February 2003 to the final refusal of leave to appeal in July 2015, spanned approximately twelve and a half years. This extensive duration, involving multiple defendants, procedural delays, periods of inactivity, and a complex appeal process, forms the factual basis for the applicant’s complaint regarding the length of proceedings which was communicated to the Government.

Gas and Dubois v. France (Application no. 25951/07) concerned access to second-parent adoption for a same-sex couple in France. The applicants, Ms Valérie Gas and Ms Nathalie Dubois, are French nationals who had lived together since 1989 and entered a civil partnership (PACS) in 2002. In 2000, Ms Dubois gave birth in France to a daughter, A., conceived in Belgium through anonymous donor insemination. Because the donor was anonymous under Belgian law, A. had no established legal tie to her father and was legally recognised only by her mother. The child lived continuously in the applicants’ shared home, and both women jointly raised her.

In March 2006, Ms Gas applied to the Nanterre tribunal de grande instance for a simple-adoption order in respect of A., after Ms Dubois gave her express consent before a notary. The public prosecutor objected under Article 365 of the French Civil Code. On 4 July 2006, the first-instance court found that the statutory conditions for adoption were satisfied and that the applicants were actively and jointly involved in A.’s upbringing, providing her with care and affection. Nevertheless, it refused the application. It reasoned that the requested adoption would transfer parental responsibility to the adoptive parent and thereby deprive the birth mother, Ms Dubois, of her parental rights, which would run counter to the child’s interests and to the applicants’ own intentions.

The Versailles Court of Appeal upheld that refusal on 21 December 2006. It also accepted that Ms Gas ensured A.’s emotional and material well-being and that the formal adoption conditions were met. However, it held that the legal consequences of adoption would not be in the child’s interests. Under Article 365, the only exception allowing parental responsibility to be shared is where a person adopts the child of his or her spouse. Since the applicants were not married—and could not marry under French law—Ms Dubois would lose all parental responsibility, and a later delegation of parental responsibility would not sufficiently eliminate the risks to the child. The Court of Appeal regarded the application as seeking legal recognition and legitimisation of the couple’s joint parenting. The applicants appealed on points of law but did not pursue the proceedings; in September 2007 the Court of Cassation declared the appeal forfeited.

The case therefore concerned the absence of any legal means in France for a same-sex couple to obtain second-parent adoption. Under French law, marriage was not available to same-sex couples. A civil partnership did not create kinship, inheritance, or adoptive ties and had no effect on parental responsibility. Simple adoption preserved the child’s original family ties but vested parental responsibility solely in the adoptive parent, unless the adoptive parent was married to the child’s mother or father. Same-sex couples could not benefit from that exception. Full adoption would sever the legal tie with the birth mother and was therefore not a realistic option. Assisted reproduction was also reserved for opposite-sex couples.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants alleged that they had been discriminated against compared with heterosexual couples. Relying on Article 14 of the Convention taken together with Article 8, they claimed discriminatory treatment based on sexual orientation and a breach of their right to respect for private and family life, because French law provided no legal route for same-sex couples to access second-parent adoption. The Court declared the application admissible on 31 August 2010.

In *Kuc v. Slovakia*, the applicant, Ladislav Kuc, a Slovak national born in 1979, complained under Article 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4 ECHR that his detention was too long, lacked relevant and sufficient grounds, and that domestic courts failed to account for his mental (schizotypal) disorder when reviewing his continued detention. He was arrested on 1 January 2012 and charged the next day with endangering public safety. He was suspected of making homemade explosive devices, sending some with threats to veterinarians and a supermarket chain, and planting one near a fast-food outlet, allowing it to explode to promote animal rights.

On 4 January 2012 the Košice I District Court remanded him to prevent further criminal activity, noting the charge and his long-term psychiatric treatment. Courts later dismissed release applications, relying on risk of reoffending, new charges, witness and victim evidence, and evidence of long, systematic planning. They later added risk of absconding based on an alleged statement that he would flee and computer evidence suggesting he had considered counterfeiting an ID. On 11 June 2012 his detention was prolonged until 1 January 2013 because the investigation was unfinished, further charges had been brought, and the charges were reclassified as terrorism and firearms offences; the grounds remained reoffending and absconding. He was twice hospitalised pre-trial for anxiety, suicide threats, and mental examination. After indictment on 1 October 2012, further release attempts failed; courts cited terrorism charges and a witness statement about a will and suicide attack, and rejected parental bail/guarantees because his parents had not prevented the crimes.

The District Court convicted him on 19 June 2013 and imposed 25 years. The Regional Court quashed that judgment on 30 October 2013 because expert reports conflicted: the first pre-trial report found no mental illness but a personality disorder; the second, submitted on 24 October 2013, found schizotypal disorder preventing him from understanding or controlling the illegality of his conduct. A third expert opinion was ordered. The Regional Court kept him detained on the earlier grounds on 4 September 2013.

After remittal, on 23 December 2013 he sought release, relying on his schizotypal disorder, daily medication, suicidal thoughts, dependence on his parents, no realistic flight risk, and no danger if medicated or institutionalised. His parents offered guarantees and parole supervision. On 10 January 2014 the District Court heard him and asked the detention centre about his treatment; the director confirmed medication was available. On 13 January 2014 release was refused; the Regional Court upheld that decision on 29 January 2014. The courts found strong suspicion, systematic bomb-making, a severe potential penalty, the flight statement, the fake-ID idea, family inability to prevent the conduct, expeditious proceedings, and unsuitable alternatives. They did not separately assess his mental condition, and the treatment correspondence was not mentioned.

On 2 April 2014 the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint as manifestly ill-founded, endorsing the ordinary courts and not answering his mental-disorder argument. Later, after the third expert report, he was again convicted on 10 July 2014 and sentenced to 25 years, but the Supreme Court quashed that due to a wrong interpretation of terrorism. On 29 September 2016 he was convicted again and sentenced to 23 years and 6 months; appeal proceedings remained pending. He remained detained as of 14 April 2016 and was transferred to Trenčín hospital on 29 November 2016 after collapsing. These facts underpin his complaints about prolonged detention and inadequate review in light of his mental disorder.

**Summary of *Braga v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* (Application no. 76957/01)**

The case of *Braga v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia* originated from an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 14 November 2001 by Mr. Andrian Braga, a Moldovan national residing in Râbniţa. The applicant alleged violations of the Convention by the authorities of the self-proclaimed "Moldavian Republic of Transdniestria" ("MRT"), a separatist region not recognized internationally, and by both respondent States.

The key facts concern the applicant's arrest, conviction, and detention. On 28 July 1999, the applicant was arrested in Râbniţa by order of an "MRT" prosecutor and charged with fraud and incitement to bribery. On 17 May 2000, the Camenca District Court, operating under the "MRT" jurisdiction, convicted him and sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. His subsequent appeal to the "MRT" Supreme Court was rejected. These judicial proceedings were conducted by authorities of an unrecognized entity, which formed the basis of his complaint of unlawful arrest and conviction.

A crucial series of events occurred in late 2001. After initially serving his sentence in Tiraspol Prison no. 2, the applicant was transferred on 25 October 2001 to Pruncul Prison Hospital, a facility under the control of the Moldovan authorities. On 30 October 2001, he signed a form authorizing the Chişinău-based NGO "Lawyers for Human Rights" (LHR) to represent him before the European Court. His application reached the Court in November 2001.

On 20 November 2001, an LHR lawyer informed the Moldovan Prosecutor General’s Office that the applicant and seven others were being held in the Moldovan-controlled hospital based on convictions from unlawful "MRT" courts. The lawyer demanded their immediate release, warning that transferring them back to the "MRT" would incur Moldova's responsibility. The following day, 21 November 2001, members of LHR held a press conference publicizing these circumstances. Later that same day, all eight detainees, including the applicant, were allegedly transferred back to "MRT" prisons. This transfer, occurring immediately after Moldovan authorities were formally notified and the case was publicized, is a central fact relevant to the alleged violation of the applicant's right to communicate effectively with the Court and to Moldova's positive obligations.

The applicant also described severe conditions of detention in the "MRT," alleging he was held in a cell with tuberculosis-infected detainees, subject to parasitic insects, and denied medication for his disability. He claimed food was inadequate. These facts underpin his allegation of ill-treatment.

The applicant was ultimately released on 22 January 2002 under an amnesty act. The case was communicated to the Moldovan Government on 23 June 2010. The core facts relevant to the alleged violations center on the applicant's subjection to the judicial and detention systems of an unrecognized regime, and the actions of Moldovan authorities who, having custody of him, transferred him back to that regime despite being alerted to his pending application and the unlawful nature of his convictions, thereby allegedly preventing his effective communication with the Court and failing to protect him from ill-treatment.

**Case: Đuković v. Montenegro (Application no. 38419/08)**  
**Court:** European Court of Human Rights, Second Section  
**Judgment date:** 13 June 2017

The applicant, Mr Batrić Đuković, born in 1939, was a Montenegrin and Serbian national then serving a sentence in Spuž Penitentiary. The Montenegrin Government were represented by Agent V. Pavličić. The application was communicated to the Government on 13 November 2013. Judge Nebojša Vučinić, the judge elected in respect of Montenegro, withdrew from sitting in the Committee, and Judge Georges Ravarani was appointed to sit in his place.

The case concerned two sets of civil proceedings, but the first set is central to the alleged violations. On 25 March 1996, the applicant brought a compensation claim before the Court of First Instance in Bar against the Municipality of Bar and one of the local primary schools. He sought damages for losses suffered as a consequence of the expropriation of his property. On 11 April 1996, the applicant’s representative informed the Court of First Instance that he had initiated a separate set of proceedings to determine the value of those damages. The Court of First Instance then suspended the compensation proceedings pending the final resolution of that separate valuation matter.

Critically, no documents were submitted by the parties to show whether the compensation proceedings had ended in the meantime. It therefore appeared that both sets of proceedings—the original compensation claim and the separate proceedings to determine the value of damages—were still pending before the Court of First Instance. This means that, as of the time of the European Court’s judgment, the applicant’s expropriation-related compensation claim had remained unresolved for over two decades, having been suspended since 1996. The prolonged suspension and continuing uncertainty formed the factual basis for the applicant’s complaint that his civil claim had not been determined within a reasonable time. These facts engage primarily Article 6 §1 of the Convention, which guarantees a fair hearing within a reasonable time, and may also engage Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 concerning protection of property, since the applicant was seeking compensation for expropriated property.

The second set of civil proceedings is less directly relevant to the alleged violation. On 2 February 2004, the applicant instituted proceedings before the same Court of First Instance in Bar against his neighbour, seeking a demarcation between their two plots of land. On 25 March 2004, he amended his proposal. On 14 September 2004, the applicant and the respondent reached a friendly settlement, which the Court of First Instance approved the same day. That dispute was therefore resolved relatively quickly and did not raise the same lengthy-delay concerns.

In essence, the key facts relevant to the alleged violation are: the applicant’s 1996 compensation claim for expropriation damages; the court’s suspension of that claim in April 1996 pending separate valuation proceedings; the separate proceedings to determine the value of damages; the absence of any evidence that either set of proceedings had concluded; and the resulting delay of more than twenty years in resolving the compensation claim. The second demarcation case ended by friendly settlement in 2004 and serves mainly as background. The case therefore focuses on the protracted failure of the domestic courts to determine the applicant’s compensation claim, contrary to the reasonable-time requirement under Article 6 §1 and, potentially, his property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

In *Zarochentsev v. Ukraine* (Application no. 39327/06), the European Court of Human Rights examined an application by Mr Aleksey Gennadyevich Zarochentsev, a Ukrainian national born in 1974, living in Bakhchysaray. The application was lodged on 8 December 2006 and concerned the alleged excessive length of criminal proceedings brought against him, primarily under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicant was represented by Mr A. V. Lesovoy, and the Ukrainian Government was represented initially by Mr Y. Zaytsev and later by Ms V. Lutkovska.

The relevant facts began on 7 March 2001, when the Kyivskyy District Prosecutor of Simferopol opened a criminal case against the applicant on suspicion of embezzlement while he was employed as a shop manager. Similar criminal proceedings were also instituted against the shop director, Mr Z. Between 30 May and 9 August 2001, the investigation was stayed because the authorities could not establish the applicant’s whereabouts, and he was placed on a wanted list. He was apprehended on 13 August 2001.

On 23 August 2001, the Kyivskyy District Court of Sevastopol remanded the applicant in custody pending trial. However, on 29 August 2001, the Court of Appeal of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea quashed that ruling and released him under an obligation not to leave the town. On 13 November 2001, the applicant and Mr Z were indicted, and the case was referred to the Kyivskyy Court for trial.

The trial began on 3 December 2001. The court held nine hearings in total. Five adjournments, amounting to about five months, occurred at the applicant’s request or because of his absence. A further adjournment of about five months was caused by the judge’s absence. The examination of the case was also delayed by about a year after the court ordered a repeated forensic accounting evaluation at the prosecutor’s request.

On 14 February 2005, the Kyivskyy Court, again at the prosecutor’s request, remitted the case for additional investigation. On 5 April 2005, the Court of Appeal upheld that ruling. After April 2005, the investigation was stayed on three occasions: for eight months, for one year and three months, and for about one year, respectively. Each stay was based on the authorities’ inability to establish the whereabouts of the applicant and Mr Z. However, all those rulings by the investigator were later quashed by the Prosecutor’s Office of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea as unfounded, and new investigators were assigned to the case.

Meanwhile, according to the applicant, he repeatedly enquired about the progress of the investigation and requested disciplinary action against the prosecutors and investigators involved. By a letter dated 18 February 2011, the Crimea Prosecutor’s Office informed the applicant, in reply to his enquiry of 18 January 2011, that the criminal proceedings against him and Mr Z had been terminated on 27 December 2010 for lack of corpus delicti in their actions.

Overall, the criminal proceedings against the applicant lasted from 7 March 2001 until 27 December 2010, nearly ten years. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation include the prolonged investigation, repeated stays due to unestablished whereabouts, the remittal for additional investigation, the forensic accounting delay, multiple adjournments, and the eventual termination of the case without conviction. The central complaint was that the domestic authorities failed to conduct the proceedings within a reasonable time.

**Case: Babak Hasanov v. Azerbaijan (Applications nos. 43137/13 and 43153/13), ECtHR, 16 February 2017.**

The applicant, Babak Hasanov, was an Azerbaijani national and a member of the opposition Popular Front Party of Azerbaijan. The case concerned two administrative arrests and convictions following opposition demonstrations in Baku on 17 November 2012 and 10 March 2013.

For the first demonstration, organisers gave notice to the Baku City Executive Authority (BCEA), which refused authorisation in general terms, saying the assembly would not comply with the Law on Freedom of Assembly and that the proposed square was a public leisure area. Organisers nevertheless proceeded. The applicant attended; he claimed the demonstration was intended to be and remained peaceful. Participants demanded democratic reforms and protested against restrictions on freedom of assembly. Police dispersed the demonstration shortly after it began. The applicant was arrested, allegedly by plain-clothes officers, taken to a police station, and charged under Article 310.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences (CAO) for deliberately failing to comply with a lawful police order. He refused to sign the administrative-offence report and claimed he was never served copies of case documents and had no access to a lawyer after arrest or in custody.

For the second demonstration, no proper prior notice was given to the BCEA; information was spread through Facebook and the press. The protest concerned the deaths of soldiers. The applicant attended and was again arrested when police dispersed the assembly. He was charged under Article 298.2 of the CAO for participating in a public assembly not organised in accordance with the law. A State-funded lawyer was instructed to assist him.

In both cases, the applicant was brought before the Sabail District Court soon after arrest—on 17 November 2012 in the first case and on 11 March 2013 in the second, after an overnight police custody. He alleged the hearings were very brief, that the public was excluded without a formal closure decision, and that he was not allowed to hire a lawyer of his choice. State-funded lawyers were appointed. In the first case, no submissions by that lawyer were recorded; in the second, the lawyer merely said in general terms that the applicant was not guilty. The first court heard no witnesses. The second questioned three police officers, who said the applicant was arrested for staging an unauthorised demonstration, and a defence witness, who said he and the applicant were arrested before entering the assembly area.

On 17 November 2012, the applicant was convicted under Article 310.1 and sentenced to seven days’ administrative detention. On 11 March 2013, he was convicted under Article 298.2 and sentenced to six days’ administrative detention. His appeals argued that the demonstrations were peaceful, his arrests unlawful, and the hearings unfair. He also complained that the courts ignored his second-degree disability, which under domestic law should have prevented administrative detention. In the first appeal he had a lawyer of choice; in the second he was unrepresented. The Baku Court of Appeal dismissed both appeals on 26 November 2012 and 27 March 2013.

At the relevant time, Article 5 IV of the Law on Freedom of Assembly did not require prior written notification for spontaneous assemblies. Article 298 of the CAO originally punished assembly-rule breaches by reprimand or a small fine, while Article 310.1 allowed a fine or administrative detention up to fifteen days if a fine was inadequate. Law no. 462-IVQD, effective 1 January 2013, amended Article 298 to expressly punish participation in assemblies organised in breach of the rules and introduced detention up to fifteen days. Law no. 457-IVQD increased the Article 310.1 fine. International documents, including PACE Resolution 1917 (2013) and a Council of Europe Commissioner report, criticised the restrictive climate for assembly in Azerbaijan, the blanket ban on protests in central Baku, and the chilling effect of increased penalties.

These facts formed the basis of the applicant’s communicated complaints under Articles 3, 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11 of the Convention, particularly concerning freedom of assembly, liberty, fair trial, and legality of penalties.

**Ustyantsev v. Ukraine** (Application no. 3299/05) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Sergey Vladimirovich Ustyantsev, who complained under the Convention about the conditions of his detention, the length of his pre-trial detention and trial, and the lack of compensation for his lengthy detention.

In September 2001, the applicant was implicated in two criminal matters. On 7 September 2001, a group allegedly including him burgled a house. On 12 September 2001, he stole a car and was involved in a collision; he was caught the same day. He was charged with car theft on 13 September 2001, and on 14 September the Leninskyy District Court of Odessa authorised his detention on remand. By 7 November 2001, the car theft investigation was completed and the case sent to court.

On 11 January 2002, the court learned that burglary proceedings were also pending against the applicant. It remitted the car theft case for further investigation and joinder with the burglary case, while confirming his detention. On 17 January 2002, after the cases were joined, the applicant attempted suicide in protest. He made further suicide attempts and went on hunger strikes later. On 2 February 2002, he was formally charged with burglary. The joined case was transferred to the District Court by 14 March 2002.

The trial was delayed repeatedly because victims and witnesses failed to appear. The court complained to the prosecutor and police about failures to secure attendance, noting that delays lengthened detention in the overcrowded SIZO with poor sanitary conditions. On 3 March 2003, the District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to nine years’ imprisonment, continuing his detention pending appeal. The applicant alleged the judgment was given in his and his lawyer’s absence and that he learned of it only on 11 March 2003. On 31 July 2003, the Odessa Regional Court of Appeal quashed the burglary conviction and remitted it for retrial, reducing the car theft sentence to five years and six months. The Supreme Court dismissed his cassation appeal on 22 March 2005.

On retrial of the burglary charge, hearings were delayed by defence lawyers’ and witnesses’ non-appearance. In April 2005, a handwriting examination found that the applicant’s signatures had been forged on crucial procedural documents. On 1 June 2005, the court remitted the case for additional investigation and issued a special ruling against the investigator. On 4 October 2005, the proceedings were discontinued for lack of proof.

As to detention, the Government stated the applicant was held in the SIZO during several periods from 15 September 2001 to 10 February 2006, and in various correctional colonies. He was released on parole on 22 January 2007, then rearrested in August 2007 on suspicion of a new crime. The applicant alleged that in the temporary detention centre detainees were fed once daily and lights remained on at night. In the SIZO, he alleged overcrowding—about one square metre per person, with a cell of 7.5–10 square metres holding four detainees, including a toilet and washstand—constant lighting, a concrete floor, no facilities to prepare his defence, and lack of basic necessities, medical assistance, press, gym access, and private correspondence. He also complained of overcrowded prison vans and lack of food in court holding rooms. His health allegedly deteriorated, including chronic prostatitis, thrombophlebitis, and a venereal disease.

The Government disputed these claims, stating cells provided at least 2.5 square metres per person, basic furniture, separated toilets, sufficient light and ventilation, adequate food, daily walks, eight hours’ sleep, weekly baths, a library, and medical care. Medical records showed pre-existing conditions and later treatment.

The applicant unsuccessfully sought civil compensation for detention conditions; his claim was dismissed in April 2006 and his appeal in September 2006. He lodged his Convention application on 1 November 2004, alleging violations of Article 3 regarding conditions in the Odessa Remand Centre, excessively long pre-trial detention and trial, and inability to obtain compensation. On 16 March 2009, the Court communicated the complaints to the Government.
