text:
Alković v. Montenegro (Application no. 66895/10) concerned a Montenegrin Roma Muslim, Rizo Alković, who alleged that Montenegro failed to effectively investigate a series of ethnically and religiously motivated attacks and threats against him and his family between 26 May and 22 September 2009. At the material time, he lived in Podgorica in an apartment building intended for socially disadvantaged families. He alleged violations concerning private life, an effective remedy, and discrimination.

The key incidents began on 26 May 2009. While neighbours Y and X were watching a televised kickboxing match involving a Bosnian Muslim contestant, Alković overheard anti-Muslim remarks. X allegedly retrieved a gun, Y said “turn it to the left”—towards Alković’s terrace—and nine or ten shots were fired. Y then insulted Alković’s “Turkish mother,” and X, Y and Y’s family picked up the spent cartridges. On 9 September 2009, Alković overheard neighbours V, S and B discussing “dirty gipsies” and referring to weapons including a hammer, pruning knife, axe, sword and a sledgehammer “like the one used on pigs.” On 15 September 2009, during an argument, X allegedly said that if he “saw red” he would kill the other man and his brother “like a dog,” pointed towards Alković’s flat, and called him a “dirty gypsy” and “trash.” This was witnessed by another neighbour.

The most direct incident occurred on 22 September 2009, Ramadan Bayram. A large cross was drawn on Alković’s apartment door and a message was written beside it: “move out or you’ll bitterly regret it.” Alković called the police, who photographed the scene, and he filed a criminal complaint against several neighbours.

The subsequent investigation was central to the alleged violations. In October 2009 police interviewed the suspects and other neighbours. The suspects denied the allegations, claimed remarks were directed at others, and suggested the cartridges had been picked up by children. In November 2009 the State prosecution service concluded that the May and September remarks did not target Alković and that the 15 September incident was not a threat. It found only the 22 September incident could amount to jeopardising security, asked police to find the perpetrator, and kept the complaint until it became time-barred in September 2012. A hate-crime complaint was rejected by the higher State prosecutor.

Alković then sought a court investigation. In March 2010 the High Court dismissed it for lack of evidence, treating his video recordings as inadmissible because they had been obtained without a court order, and noting that the neighbours denied targeting him. It also criticised him for not calling the police or collecting evidence, although he maintained he had called them. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in May 2010, and the Constitutional Court dismissed his appeal in March 2014.

Other relevant facts included earlier neighbour conflicts, Alković’s own conviction for firing a starting pistol during Bayram 2007, and later reported incidents such as a brick through his window, an attempted car collision, threats, gunshots, firecrackers damaging his car, and a threat to his daughter. His family moved out in July 2010. Domestic law criminalised jeopardising security, incitement to ethnic, racial and religious hatred, and discrimination. The applicant’s core complaint was that the authorities failed to properly investigate and prosecute these hate-motivated acts.

In *Antović and Mirković v. Montenegro*, the applicants were two professors at the School of Mathematics, University of Montenegro. They complained under Article 8 that video surveillance installed in the university auditoriums where they taught violated their right to respect for private life.

On 1 February 2011, the Dean informed professors at a School Council session that video surveillance had been introduced in classrooms. On 24 February 2011, the Dean issued a formal decision introducing cameras in seven amphitheatres and in front of the Dean’s Office. The stated aims were safety of property and people, including students, and monitoring teaching activities. Access to the data was protected by codes known only to the Dean. The decision provided for storage for one year, but the servers actually retained data for thirty days before automatic erasure.

On 14 March 2011, the applicants complained to the Personal Data Protection Agency that data about them were collected without consent. They argued that the amphitheatre was locked before and after classes, contained only fixed desks, chairs and a blackboard, and that other methods could protect people and property and monitor classes. They sought removal of the cameras and erasure of the data. On 21 March 2011, Agency inspectors reported that the surveillance complied with the Personal Data Protection Act. They noted past incidents such as destruction of property, bringing animals, drink and tobacco, and the presence of non-students. They found the cameras produced distant, unclear images, could not zoom, and recorded no audio. The applicants objected, saying they knew of no such incidents and that employees had not received written notice before surveillance began. The formal decision came on 24 February, but surveillance had started weeks earlier.

On 28 April 2011, the Agency Council ordered the School to remove the cameras within fifteen days. It held that the statutory grounds were not met: there was no evidence of danger to safety of people, property or confidential data in the auditoriums, and monitoring teaching was not a legitimate basis for video surveillance. No administrative dispute was brought against that decision. The decision was served on 25 January 2012; cameras were removed by 27 January 2012 and the data were apparently erased later.

In January 2012, the applicants sued the University, the Agency and the State for compensation, alleging unauthorised collection and processing of personal data violated their private life under Article 8. They claimed the interference lacked a legal basis, legitimate aim, and necessity. The Court of First Instance ruled against them on 27 December 2012. It accepted that private life can include professional activities, but found that university auditoriums were public work areas, like courtrooms or parliament, where professors were not alone and could not invoke privacy; the collected data were therefore not personal data. It said the failure to remove the cameras immediately was unauthorised but not an Article 8 interference, and that monitoring public actions was not private-life interference unless footage became public. A witness mentioned theft and damage, including stolen laptops, and that police had suggested cameras. The High Court upheld this on 17 July 2013. The applicants did not file a constitutional appeal. Before the European Court, they alleged that the unlawful installation and use of video surveillance in their teaching auditoriums violated Article 8. The key issues were whether the surveillance interfered with private life, whether it was lawful and necessary, and whether domestic remedies provided adequate protection.

**CASE OF TONOV AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA** (Application no. 48704/07) is a judgment of the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), delivered on 30 October 2012. The applicants were three Bulgarian nationals: Mr Iliya Atanasov Tonov (b. 1975), Ms Vatka Markova Udvareva (b. 1930), and Ms Pena Marinova Karalakova (b. 1927). Tonov and Udvareva lived in Sofia; Karalakova lived in Tryavna. The case concerned the annulment of their title to a flat and their subsequent inability to obtain compensation bonds.

In 1968, the second applicant, Ms Udvareva, and her husband purchased a 97-square-metre flat from the Sofia municipality. The flat had become State property through the nationalisations carried out by the communist regime in Bulgaria after 1947. In 1998, after the time-limit to bring an action under section 7 of the Restitution Law was renewed, the pre-nationalisation owner of the flat sued Ms Udvareva and her husband. The former owner sought a declaration that their title was null and void. During the pendency of the proceedings, Ms Udvareva’s husband died. His grandson, Mr Tonov, inherited his share of the flat. As a result, Mr Tonov and Ms Udvareva each owned one half of the flat, and Mr Tonov joined the civil proceedings.

The domestic proceedings ended with a final judgment of the Supreme Court of Cassation on 23 April 2007. The domestic courts found that Ms Udvareva’s and Mr Tonov’s title was null and void ab initio. The reason was that the 1968 sale had been flawed: a document related to the sale had not been signed by the municipality official who had the relevant power. On an unspecified date, Ms Udvareva, who had been living alone in the flat, vacated it.

On 20 September 2007, Ms Udvareva and Mr Tonov requested compensation bonds. Under domestic law, such a request had to be made within two months following the final judgment of the Supreme Court of Cassation. Their request was dismissed because it had not been submitted within that two-month period, which had begun on 23 April 2007. Consequently, they did not receive compensation bonds for the loss of their property.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 12 October 2007, invoking Article 34 of the Convention. They were represented by Mr N. Runevski, a lawyer practising in Sofia. The Bulgarian Government were represented by Ms R. Nikolova of the Ministry of Justice. On 6 December 2010, the application was communicated to the Government. The relevant background facts, domestic law, and practice had been summarised in the Court’s earlier judgments in *Velikovi and Others v. Bulgaria* and *Tsonkovi v. Bulgaria*.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation(s) are that the applicants lost their property by a final domestic judgment that annulled their title due to a formal defect in the original municipal sale, a defect not attributable to them. They were then refused compensation bonds solely because they missed a strict two-month deadline following that final judgment. The applicants complained before the Court that this annulment and the refusal of compensation amounted to a violation of their property rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention. The Court was therefore called upon to assess whether the deprivation of property and the denial of compensation imposed a disproportionate burden on the applicants.

In *Kemal Coşkun v. Turkey* (Application no. 45028/07, judgment 28 March 2017), the applicant was a Turkish police officer. On 3 July 2004, the gendarmerie received a call about a woman crying for help in a white civilian car. They located the car, driven by the applicant, in an isolated area outside Samsun. The woman, Ç.V., was crying with blood around her mouth and said the applicant had kidnapped and beaten her. The applicant was seen trying to discard a knife, hatchet and mobile phone; a later search found a gun, duct tape, rope, a bloodstained towel, handcuffs and a truncheon in his car.

Ç.V. told the prosecutor that she had had an extramarital affair with the applicant but wanted to end it. She alleged that he drove her out of the city without consent, hit her stomach with a truncheon, tied her hands with rope, and threatened sexual assault. The applicant denied kidnapping, claiming Ç.V. had demanded money and behaved erratically, and that he had hit her during a quarrel. A medical report recorded a cut on her tongue, neck bruising, chest lesion and thumb pain, rendering her unfit for work for seven days. Ç.V. later submitted a written retraction, but then claimed she had done so under duress and maintained her initial accusations.

Criminal proceedings were brought for attempted rape, false imprisonment and robbery. In March 2006, the Samsun Assize Court acquitted the applicant of false imprisonment and robbery. It found no attempted rape but convicted him of assault and battery based on the same underlying conduct. In September 2012, the Court of Cassation quashed the assault conviction because the five-year limitation period had expired, discontinued those proceedings, and upheld the acquittals.

In parallel, disciplinary proceedings were initiated. The Samsun Police Disciplinary Council found that the applicant had committed false imprisonment, attempted rape and threatening violence with a weapon, and referred the case to the Supreme Disciplinary Council for dismissal under section 8 § 6 of the Disciplinary Regulations. In February 2005, the Supreme Disciplinary Council found attempted rape, assault and threatening violence with a weapon established, largely relying on the criminal investigation file, and dismissed him from the police force.

The applicant challenged the dismissal. In September 2005, the Samsun Administrative Court upheld it, relying on Ç.V.’s initial statements, the medical report, the seized items and the applicant’s attempt to conceal evidence, despite the absence of corroborating witnesses. It concluded that he had committed attempted rape, false imprisonment and threatening with a weapon. In April 2007, the Supreme Administrative Court rejected his appeal, holding that under section 131 of Law no. 657, an acquittal in criminal proceedings did not preclude disciplinary sanctions on the same facts.

After the 2012 criminal acquittal and discontinuation, the applicant sought reopening and rectification of his civil servant record, arguing that his dismissal violated the presumption of innocence because it was based on allegations that had not resulted in a final criminal conviction. The administrative courts declared these applications inadmissible; the Supreme Administrative Court upheld that outcome in February 2014.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2, complaining that his dismissal from the police force followed unfair proceedings and occurred despite the absence of a criminal conviction against him. He later also complained under Articles 3 and 7. The key issue concerned the disciplinary authorities’ use of criminal-law labels and findings—attempted rape, false imprisonment and threatening violence—after the criminal courts had acquitted him of the main charges and the remaining conviction was discontinued due to limitation.

The case *Svorcan v. Montenegro* (Application no. 1253/08) originated in an application lodged with the European Court of Human Rights on 24 December 2007 by Olga Svorcan, a Serbian national born in 1950 and living in Belgrade. The Montenegrin Government was represented by V. Pavličić. On 3 December 2014, the Court communicated to the Government only the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the proceedings in question; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The underlying facts concerned civil property litigation. In the first set of proceedings, on 18 September 1995, the applicant and her family members instituted proceedings before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi, seeking division of their joint property. On 5 May 1997, that court discontinued the proceedings and instructed the parties to initiate a separate civil case because a number of contentious issues remained.

The second set of proceedings began on 8 September 1997, when the applicant’s cousins brought a claim against the applicant and her parents before the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi. On 30 December 1997, the cousins lodged an additional claim concerning the same matter. The two claims were joined and examined in the same civil proceedings. On 1 October 2002, the Court of First Instance in Herceg Novi ruled against the applicant and her parents. On 25 June 2004, the High Court in Podgorica upheld that judgment on appeal. The judgment thereby became final and was served on the applicant on 15 July 2004.

On 17 August 2004, the applicant lodged an appeal on points of law (*revizija*) with the Supreme Court of Montenegro. This appeal was misplaced until 20 January 2006, when the applicant’s lawyers intervened and urged the authorities to find it. On 12 January 2007, the applicant amended her appeal on points of law. On 14 February 2008, the Supreme Court of Montenegro rejected the appeal as unfounded. That decision was served on the applicant on 6 March 2008.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violation are therefore the prolonged duration of the civil proceedings. The second set of proceedings ran from September 1997 until the Supreme Court’s decision was served in March 2008—approximately ten years and six months. The first-instance phase lasted from 1997 until October 2002, about five years; the High Court appeal phase lasted from 2002 until June 2004, about two years; and the Supreme Court phase lasted from August 2004 until March 2008, about three years and seven months. A notable delay was the period during which the appeal on points of law was misplaced: from 17 August 2004 until 20 January 2006, roughly seventeen months, before it was located following the applicant’s lawyers’ intervention. After it was found, the applicant amended it in January 2007, and the Supreme Court decided it in February 2008.

The only complaint that survived for examination was that the length of these civil proceedings violated the applicant’s rights. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The case of *Mives DOO v. Serbia* (Application no. 48966/09) originated in an application lodged against Serbia under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights on 31 August 2009. The applicant, Mives DOO, is a limited liability company based in Serbia. It was represented by Mr D. Simić, a lawyer practising in Novi Sad. The Serbian Government were initially represented by Ms V. Rodić and later by Ms N. Plavšić. On 23 October 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The Government objected to the case being examined by a Committee of the Third Section, but the Court rejected that objection.

The facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the applicant’s inability to enforce final domestic judgments against a socially-owned company. On 24 April 1997 and 3 September 1998, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered DD Lola Utva Vazduhoplovna industrija, a socially-owned company based in Pančevo (“the debtor”), to pay the applicant specified amounts. These amounts represented damages relating to an airplane that the applicant had bought from the debtor but which had never been delivered, together with the costs of the civil proceedings. The judgments became final by 4 June 1998 and 25 September 1998 respectively.

On 5 June 2002, at the applicant’s request, the Pančevo Commercial Court ordered enforcement of those judgments. It also ordered the debtor to pay the applicant the costs of the enforcement proceedings. However, enforcement was not completed. On 11 February 2008, the Commercial Court noted that on 29 January 2008 the Privatisation Agency had ordered the restructuring of the debtor. As a result, the enforcement proceedings were stayed until the conclusion of that restructuring process.

At the time of the proceedings before the European Court, information obtained from the Serbian Business Registers Agency indicated that the debtor was still an active company and that it was predominantly comprised of State-owned capital. This fact is significant because the case concerns the State’s responsibility for the debts of a socially-owned company and the prolonged non-enforcement of final judgments.

The relevant domestic law concerns the status of socially-owned companies, as well as enforcement and insolvency proceedings. The Court referred to its previous case-law in *R. Kačapor and Others v. Serbia*, *Jovičić and Others v. Serbia*, *Marinković v. Serbia*, and *Ferizović v. Serbia*. These authorities outline how Serbian law treats socially-owned companies, enforcement proceedings, insolvency, and constitutional redress. They are relevant to the applicant’s complaints, which essentially concern the failure of the Serbian authorities to enforce final domestic judgments given in its favour. The key facts for the alleged violation are therefore: the existence of final and enforceable domestic judgments in the applicant’s favour; the 2002 enforcement order; the 2008 stay of enforcement following the Privatisation Agency’s restructuring order; the debtor’s ongoing active status; and its predominantly State-owned capital, which engages the question of State responsibility under the Convention.

In *Centre for the Development of Analytical Psychology v. the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia* (Applications nos. 29545/10 and 32961/10), the applicant company complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that it lacked access to a court in claims against the State Health Insurance Fund (“the Fund”). The company was incorporated in Skopje and owned by Dr Marija Arsovska, a psychiatrist. It descended from a private psychiatric practice established in 1995 under her former name, Dr Marija Karanfilova’s Independent Psychiatric Practice (“the original Practice”), which used an individual tax number beginning with 503. In 2004, the original Practice signed a contract with the Fund for funding treatment provided to health insurance beneficiaries.

In February 2006, following amendments to the Health Protection Act, the Ministry of Health’s Inspectorate ordered the Practice to re-register as a private health institution. The psychiatrist applied accordingly. On 28 February 2006, the Ministry issued a decision registering the new Practice at the same address, stating that the 1995 registration would cease to be in force once the new decision was entered in the register. The decision was sent to several institutions, including the Fund. A March 2006 inspection confirmed full compliance. On 29 March 2006, the Central Registry recorded the new Practice and assigned it a new tax number beginning with 403. In June 2006, the new Practice notified the Fund of the changes. In November 2006, the Fund said it would not sign a new contract after the previous one expired. In August 2007, the Central Registry allowed the new Practice to transform into a single-member limited liability company—the applicant company—keeping the new Practice’s tax number.

Two sets of civil proceedings were relevant. First, in January 2006, the original Practice sued the Fund for compensation for non-adherence to the 2004 contract. The new Practice and later the applicant company continued the case as claimant. In June 2008, the first-instance court partly granted the claim. On appeal, the Fund objected for the first time that the applicant lacked standing, arguing it was a different legal entity from the 2004 contracting party because the tax numbers differed. The applicant replied that the re-registration had complied with the Inspectorate’s orders, the Fund knew of the changes, accepted reports from the new Practice, and terminated the contract by notice to the new Practice, thereby implicitly recognising legal continuity. In April 2009, the first-instance court dismissed the claim for lack of standing, relying on the different tax numbers. The Court of Appeal upheld that decision in December 2009.

Second, in July 2006, the new Practice lodged a civil debt claim against the Fund. After transformation, the applicant company continued the proceedings. The Fund again objected to standing in June 2008. In February 2009, the first-instance court dismissed the claim for lack of standing, again citing the different tax numbers. In December 2009, the Court of Appeal upheld the dismissal, stressing that a tax number is a unique attribute that remains unchanged regardless of structural changes.

Thus, the domestic courts refused to examine the merits of the applicant’s contractual claims solely because of the formal difference in tax numbers, despite evidence of continuity and the Fund’s dealings with the successor entity. The applicant alleged that this formalistic approach denied it access to a court under Article 6 § 1. In separate proceedings concerning the same contract, the Supreme Court later found that the lower courts had incorrectly denied standing, noting that the Fund had terminated the contract by notice to the new Practice, which had the same tax number as the applicant.

In *Jóhannesson and Others v. Iceland* (Application no. 22007/11), the applicants were two Icelandic nationals, Jón Ásgeir Jóhannesson and Tryggvi Jónsson, and Fjárfestingafélagið Gaumur, an Icelandic private limited company. They alleged that Iceland violated Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights—the right not to be tried or punished twice—because they were first subjected to tax surcharges and later criminally prosecuted for aggravated tax offences based on the same facts.

The tax proceedings began on 17 November 2003, when the Directorate of Tax Investigations audited the applicants’ tax returns and bookkeeping. Its reports concluded in 2004–2005. The Directorate of Internal Revenue found that the first applicant had failed to declare significant payments received in 1998–2002, car allowances for 2000–2002, life-insurance payments, and profits from the sale of shares in the Baugur Group. It re-assessed his taxes for 1999–2002 and imposed a 25% tax surcharge. The second applicant was found to have failed to declare significant payments from 1999–2002 and life-insurance payments made by Baugur Group; his taxes were re-assessed and a 25% surcharge was imposed. The third applicant, the company, had failed to account for and declare allowances enjoyed by the first applicant and other employees, failed to withhold public levies, misdeclared share-sale profits and losses, and overdeclared expenditure. Its taxes were re-assessed for 1998–2002, with a 25% surcharge and an additional 10% surcharge for failure to withhold levies.

On appeal, the Internal Revenue Board upheld most of the surcharges in decisions of 29 August and 26 September 2007. The applicants did not seek judicial review of those decisions, which became final in February and March 2008 when the appeal time-limit expired.

Meanwhile, on 12 November 2004, the Director of Tax Investigations reported the matter to the National Police Commissioner and forwarded the tax investigation reports. In August 2006, the applicants were interviewed by the police for the first time and, according to the Government, were informed that they were suspects. On 18 December 2008, the National Police Commissioner indicted them for aggravated tax offences. The indictment largely mirrored the earlier tax findings: underdeclared income for 1999–2003, failure to declare payments, car allowances, life-insurance payments, share-sale profits, failure to withhold public levies, and overdeclared expenditure.

In June 2010, the Reykjavik District Court dismissed parts of the indictment. It found that the criminal charges were based on the same facts as the tax-surcharge decisions and that those surcharge proceedings had involved a “criminal charge” under Article 4 of Protocol No. 7. Relying mainly on *Sergey Zolotukhin v. Russia*, it held that the later criminal prosecution was barred by *ne bis in idem*. The Supreme Court overturned that ruling in September 2010. It held that, under Iceland’s dualist legal system, domestic courts could not invalidate the existing system of tax surcharges followed by criminal proceedings; legislative amendment would be required. It considered the European Court’s case-law unclear and ordered the District Court to examine the merits.

In December 2011, the District Court convicted the applicants on some charges, finding gross negligence, but suspended penalty determination for one year because of the excessive length of proceedings and the earlier 25% surcharge. On appeal, the Supreme Court in February 2013 upheld most convictions, convicted the first applicant on two additional charges, revoked earlier suspended sentences, and imposed suspended prison terms of twelve months for the first applicant and eighteen months for the second, plus large fines. It took into account the excessive length of proceedings and the tax surcharges already imposed. The European Court of Human Rights later found a violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7, holding that the tax surcharges were criminal penalties and that the subsequent criminal trial concerned the same facts.

The applicant, Mr Ulrich Sommer, is a German criminal defence lawyer practising in Cologne. In 2009 he represented a client in criminal proceedings. After those proceedings ended and the client was imprisoned, the client’s fiancée transferred €1,500 from her private bank account to the applicant’s professional bank account. The transfer reference stated “Prof Dr Sommer fees” followed by the client’s surname.

In 2010–2011, the Bochum public prosecution office investigated several individuals suspected of commercial gang fraud. One suspect was the applicant’s former client, who again retained him as defence counsel. During the investigation, authorities inspected bank accounts of several persons, including the client and his fiancée. They found that the fiancée had received €7,400 suspected to come from illegal activities and had transferred €1,500 to the applicant’s account as legal fees.

On that basis, the prosecution contacted the applicant’s bank. On 1 March 2011, the prosecutor requested a list of all transactions concerning the applicant’s bank account from 1 January 2009 onward and asked the bank not to inform him. The request relied on Articles 161a, 51, 70 and 95 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 1 April 2011, the prosecutor sent further questions, asking for information on other accounts, rights of disposal, balances, closed accounts, addresses, foreign transfers, all transactions since January 2009, and connected credit cards. The bank complied with both requests. The prosecutor did not formally order the bank to produce the information but pointed to witness obligations and possible coercive consequences for non-compliance.

The information was analysed by police and prosecutors, and a list of 53 transactions considered relevant was placed in the investigation file as evidence. Consequently, anyone with access to the case file—including lawyers for co-accused—could see the applicant’s banking information and the names of clients who had transferred fees.

The applicant only learned of the measures on 31 January 2012, when he was granted access to the investigation file as defence counsel. On 24 April 2012, he asked the Chief Public Prosecutor to return all bank data and destroy related records. He stressed that his role as a criminal defence lawyer was known to the prosecutor and that disclosure of the banking information affected his clients’ interests. He argued that the investigative measures lacked a legal basis.

On 2 May 2012, the Chief Public Prosecutor refused. He said there was suspicion that the money transferred by the fiancée came from illegal activity, so it was legitimate to investigate whether further transfers had occurred between the applicant and his client or the client’s fiancée. He added that the information had to remain in the investigation file and that there was no legal basis for returning or removing it. He cited Article 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the bank was a public-law bank and therefore considered an authority.

The file was later transferred to the Bochum Regional Court for trial against the client. The applicant asked the court to return the data. On 19 July 2012, the Regional Court refused. It found the investigation lawful, that the bank had provided information voluntarily, and that the documents could only be returned to the bank, not to the applicant. It also held that the seizure prohibition under Article 97 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not apply because the information had not been in the applicant’s possession. However, to protect lawyer-client privilege, it separated the documents from the general file and restricted access.

The Hamm Court of Appeal confirmed that decision on 13 September 2012, finding the measure proportionate and the safeguards inapplicable, particularly because the bank was not a person assisting the applicant or involved in his professional activities under Article 53a of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 19 September 2013, the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit the applicant’s constitutional complaint without reasons.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged under Article 8 that the public prosecution office had collected and stored information about his professional bank account in a disproportionate manner, circumventing safeguards protecting lawyer-client confidentiality.

Case *Erol v. Germany* (Application no. 68250/11) concerned a Turkish national, Ramazan Erol, born in 1974 and living in Aachen. On 20 April 2010, his café was searched. He was found in a back room weighing and packaging about 400 grams of cocaine and had €2,325 in his pocket. He was arrested. The next day, the Aachen District Court issued a remand detention warrant, finding a strong suspicion of commercial trafficking in a substantial amount of drugs and a risk of absconding. It relied on the possibility of a considerable prison sentence, his weak ties to Germany, unemployment and social-security dependence, and the ease of fleeing to Turkey.

At a 5 May 2010 detention review, counsel sought release on bail, saying family could provide bail. The next day counsel withdrew after the court indicated bail would not be granted. On 6 July 2010 the Public Prosecutor indicted him on three counts of commercial trafficking. On 29 September 2010 the District Court convicted him on one count, acquitted him on two, sentenced him to two years and six months, and ordered continued detention. Both sides appealed. The applicant also challenged continued detention, arguing there was no flight risk: he had lived in Germany for 20 years, was married for 13 years, had two young children, and his parents and brother lived in Germany. His only Turkish tie was a parents’ holiday home.

The District and Regional Courts rejected his appeals. They accepted a flight risk, noting the family lived on social security since 2001, his German was insufficient, he had no employment prospects, his wife was Turkish, the children were young, and his parents owned a holiday home in Turkey; he might flee there with family. On 26 October 2010 he lodged a further appeal and offered €10,000 security from family. The Cologne Court of Appeal indicated it was considering staying detention, but asked that the money be placed at the applicant’s free disposal and its lawful origin shown. On 23 November 2010 counsel replied that the family would furnish €10,000 and prove lawful origin, but would not put the money at the applicant’s disposal because they feared the repayment claim would be attached for other claims by authorities. If the security would be forfeited regardless of absconding, it could not remove the flight incentive.

On 3 December 2010 the Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the further appeal. It endorsed the flight-risk findings and noted the possible sentence was not limited to two years and six months because the prosecution had appealed the acquittals. It would consider a stay if security were provided, but since the family would not place the funds at the applicant’s disposal, it inferred they lacked confidence in him and that family ties were not strong enough to prevent absconding. It also found a risk of reoffending and based the detention order subsidiarily on that risk. The applicant was released on 3 January 2011 after the conviction became final and another person furnished €5,000 security.

The alleged violation was under Article 5 § 4 ECHR: the applicant complained that the Cologne Court of Appeal’s 3 December 2010 decision not to stay execution of the detention order breached his right to judicial review of the lawfulness of his detention. The Court communicated this complaint to the German Government; the remainder was declared inadmissible. Domestic law permitted a stay where the sole ground was flight risk and adequate security was furnished, but courts could refuse third-party security and security could not be offset against other claims.

**Case Summary: Ļutova v. Latvia (Application no. 37105/09)**

The case of *Ļutova v. Latvia* originated from an application lodged against the Republic of Latvia with the European Court of Human Rights on 26 June 2009. The applicant, Ms Tatjana Seļezņova (later Ļutova), a Latvian national born in 1964 and residing in Riga, alleged a violation of her right to a fair trial under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, specifically concerning the excessive length of civil proceedings. On 2 April 2014, the Court communicated this complaint to the Latvian Government, declaring the remainder of the application inadmissible.

The facts center on a protracted civil dispute initiated on 24 November 2005. A residential building maintenance services provider, Kurzemes Namu Apsaimniekotājs, filed a claim against the applicant to recover an alleged debt of 320 Latvian lati (approximately EUR 455) for services. The applicant contested the claim, arguing that no service agreement existed and that she was free to choose another provider. She was represented by Mr S. Seļezņovs, who was not a lawyer.

The proceedings, which began in the Riga City Kurzeme District Court ("City Court"), were marked by numerous delays. The first hearing was scheduled for 21 April 2006, over four months after the claim was filed. During this hearing, the applicant’s representative requested additional time to examine legal norms and obtain documents, leading to a postponement to 9 August 2006. Subsequent hearings were repeatedly postponed, often at the request of the plaintiff to increase the claim amount and submit further documents (e.g., on 9 August, 17 October 2006, 31 January, 23 March 2007, and 4 June 2008). The applicant’s representative also sought postponements to review new submissions (e.g., on 17 October 2006, 13 November 2007, and 17 April 2008).

Other delays included a change of judge in September 2007 and a monetary fine imposed on the applicant’s representative for disobeying a judge’s order on 4 June 2008. The City Court held its final hearing on 28 October 2008 and dismissed the plaintiff’s claim on 6 November 2008, finding the expenses unsubstantiated. The plaintiff appealed on 27 November 2008.

The appeal proceedings before the Riga Regional Court ("Regional Court") faced further significant delay. The first hearing was not held until 13 September 2010—nearly two years after the appeal was lodged. At this hearing, the plaintiff increased the claim to LVL 3,173 (approximately EUR 4,515). The final hearing occurred on 8 December 2010, and on 22 December 2010, the Regional Court partly allowed the claim, ordering the applicant to pay LVL 2,854 (approximately EUR 4,059). It found that although no service agreement existed, domestic law obliged her to pay for maintenance services, and she had failed to contest the bills.

The applicant then appealed on points of law to the Senate of the Supreme Court on 18 January 2011. However, procedural deficiencies (failure to pay a security deposit) led to the appeal being remitted on 3 February 2012. After rectifying these issues, the Senate refused to institute proceedings on points of law on 3 April 2012.

The total duration of the civil proceedings, from 24 November 2005 to 3 April 2012, was approximately six years and four months across three court levels. The key facts relevant to the alleged violation include the frequent postponements, largely driven by the plaintiff’s incremental claim increases and the resulting need for the applicant to examine new documents, as well as the substantial gap of nearly two years between the City Court’s judgment and the first Regional Court hearing, and the additional time lost due to procedural issues with the cassation appeal. These factors collectively formed the basis of the applicant’s complaint regarding the unreasonable length of the proceedings.

In *Sacharuk v. Lithuania*, Aleksandr Sacharuk, a Lithuanian national and former member of the Seimas (Parliament) from 2008 to 2012, complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 that the Supreme Court panel which upheld his conviction was not impartial, and under Article 7 that his conviction was not foreseeable.

The key facts concern his conduct as an MP in January 2010. Between 14 and 19 January 2010, he used another Seimas member L.K.’s parliamentary identity card to register and vote electronically in L.K.’s place during L.K.’s absence. L.K. was abroad in Southeast Asia without parliamentary authorisation. The Seimas Ethics and Procedures Commission concluded that Sacharuk had deliberately voted for another member, breached Article 111 § 4 of the Seimas Statute—which required MPs to vote in person—and breached the Code of Conduct for State Politicians. It proposed a warning as a disciplinary sanction.

The Seimas Special Investigation Commission later found the accusation well-founded and referred the matter to the Prosecutor General’s Office, suggesting possible criminal offences under Articles 300 and 302 of the Criminal Code. Because Sacharuk had parliamentary immunity, the prosecutor sought the Seimas’ consent to prosecute. On 17 June 2010, the Seimas did not lift his immunity: 46 voted in favour, 12 against, and 28 abstained. The prosecutor therefore refused to start a pre-trial investigation, but noted possible elements of offences under Articles 228, 300 and 302.

Impeachment proceedings followed. On 27 October 2010, the Constitutional Court concluded that Sacharuk had breached his parliamentary oath and grossly violated the Constitution by deliberately voting for L.K. eight times. However, on 11 November 2010, the Seimas failed to annul Sacharuk’s mandate: 80 votes were in favour, short of the required 85. He therefore remained an MP; L.K.’s mandate was annulled.

In June 2011, the Code of Criminal Procedure was amended to allow prosecution of persons who had lost immunity. Sacharuk’s term ended in November 2012. On 20 November 2012, the prosecutor annulled the earlier refusal and opened a pre-trial investigation because immunity no longer barred prosecution. Sacharuk was charged under Article 228 § 1 (abuse of office), Article 300 § 3 (forgery), and Article 302 § 2 (unlawful use of a document).

The Vilnius Regional Court acquitted him in July 2015, and the Court of Appeal upheld the acquittal in May 2016. Those courts relied on an established practice in the Seimas of MPs voting for absent colleagues from the same political group, the availability of disciplinary warning under the Seimas Statute, the absence of major damage, and the applicant’s alleged lack of awareness of criminal liability. The Supreme Court quashed the acquittal in December 2016 and remitted the case, holding that such practice did not eliminate criminality and that the lower courts had assessed the evidence one-sidedly.

On retrial, the Court of Appeal convicted Sacharuk in June 2017 under Article 228 § 1 and Article 302 § 1, imposing a fine of €1,882; the Article 300 charge was discontinued as time-barred. The court found direct intent, major non-pecuniary damage to the State, and noted his legal education and parliamentary experience. The Supreme Court dismissed his final appeal on 13 February 2018.

Regarding Article 6 impartiality, Judge D.B. had participated in the earlier Supreme Court panel that quashed the acquittal and made adverse comments on the merits. She later sat as reporting judge on the final panel. Sacharuk requested her removal, but the court refused, finding prior participation insufficient to raise doubts about impartiality.

Regarding Article 7 foreseeability, Sacharuk argued that only disciplinary liability—a warning—was foreseeable, that similar conduct by other MPs had not been prosecuted, and that criminal prosecution became possible only after the 2011 procedural amendment. The domestic courts ultimately held that criminal liability was foreseeable and that unlawful practice did not excuse him.

The case *Nikolić and Others v. Serbia* (Application no. 9235/11) is a European Court of Human Rights judgment delivered on 24 January 2017 by the Third Section. It concerned fourteen applicants who complained about Serbia’s failure to enforce a final domestic judgment awarding them compensation for land.

The factual background began in 1961, when the applicants’ predecessors were deprived of certain land in favour of the State. The land was later used by PIK Niš, a company predominantly composed of socially-owned capital. On 26 January 2006, the Niš Municipal Court ordered PIK Niš, as the end user of the land, to pay the applicants specified amounts as compensation. That judgment became final and enforceable by 16 August 2006.

After the judgment, the applicants sought enforcement. On 25 October 2006 and 1 February 2007, the Niš Municipal Court ordered enforcement and required the debtor to pay enforcement costs. All applicants except Tomislav Đorđević lodged enforcement requests. Despite these orders, the judgment was not enforced.

In June 2009, the Niš Commercial Court opened insolvency proceedings against PIK Niš. Only one applicant, Milica Nikolić Jajčević, duly submitted her claim in those proceedings. The insolvency proceedings were still ongoing at the time of the Strasbourg case. This insolvency context is significant because the debtor’s socially-owned status and the ongoing insolvency affected the prospects for enforcing the final judgment.

The applicants also pursued constitutional redress. In March 2009, August 2009, and June 2010, all applicants lodged constitutional appeals. In decisions issued between March 2011 and May 2012, the Serbian Constitutional Court found a violation of the right to a hearing within a reasonable time for all applicants except Mr Đorđević. However, it awarded no damages, stating that the applicants had not claimed non-pecuniary damages. The Constitutional Court dismissed Mr Đorđević’s appeal because he had failed to request enforcement of the judgment. Thus, while the domestic court recognised excessive delay, the applicants received no compensation and the underlying judgment remained unenforced.

The applicants lodged their application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 December 2010. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection. The applicants’ central allegations were that the Serbian authorities failed to enforce the final and enforceable domestic judgment in their favour, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The key facts relevant to those alleged violations include the finality of the 2006 judgment, the issuance of enforcement orders, the debtor’s socially-owned status, the lengthy non-enforcement, the opening of insolvency proceedings, the limited participation of applicants in those proceedings, and the Constitutional Court’s findings of unreasonable delay without compensation. These facts were central to assessing whether Serbia was responsible for the non-enforcement and whether the applicants had effective domestic redress.

Van Colle v the United Kingdom (ECtHR, 13 November 2012) concerned the 2000 murder of Giles Van Colle. His parents, Mr and Mrs Van Colle, complained under Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention that the UK police failed to protect their son’s life from Daniel Brougham, the accused in a theft prosecution in which Giles was a prosecution witness.

Giles, an optometrist, had employed Brougham under the alias Lee Jordan. After Brougham left, a dispute arose over equipment. Police later found optical equipment and charged Brougham with thefts from Giles, Southern Counties and Alpha Optical. He was bailed. During 2000, Brougham attempted to bribe several witnesses not to testify. Some approaches were not reported to police. On 13 October 2000, Brougham telephoned Giles and threatened that he knew where Giles lived, where his businesses and parents lived, and that if he did not drop the charges he would be “in danger.” Giles reported this to Detective Constable Ridley and gave a statement on 19 October. Ridley did not arrest Brougham, partly because he doubted Giles’s identification, though he later accepted this was a serious threat and that he should have done more.

Other incidents included a fire to Giles’s car on 24 September, not reported because it was initially thought accidental, and fires to Mr P’s car and business premises on 28–29 October. These were initially considered possibly accidental and not linked to Brougham, though later experts found they were deliberate. On 9 November Brougham telephoned Giles again, saying: “Give Alpha Optical a call and get them to drop the charges, you motherfucker.” Giles reported it and sent a written account. **Moreira Ferreira v. Portugal (No. 2)** (Application no. 19867/12, Grand Chamber, 11 July 2017) concerned a Portuguese woman convicted of threatening and insulting conduct after an altercation. A psychiatric expert report found she had limited intellectual and cognitive capacities but considered her criminally responsible. In March 2007, the Matosinhos District Court rejected her defence of diminished responsibility, convicted her, and imposed 320 day-fines (€640), plus damages to victims.

On appeal, the applicant argued she lacked criminal responsibility due to psychiatric disorders, requested a fresh assessment of the facts, and asked to be heard. The Oporto Court of Appeal held a hearing in December 2007, attended by the prosecutor and her lawyer, but did not examine the applicant personally. It upheld the conviction, reduced the sentence to 265 day-fines (€530), and found no need for a fresh factual assessment. The applicant paid the fine; her criminal record was later cleared in 2016.

The applicant first complained to the European Court of Human Rights that the Court of Appeal’s failure to hear her personally violated Article 6 § 1. In its 2011 judgment, the Court found a violation. It reasoned that the appellate court had to decide issues concerning her criminal responsibility and personal circumstances, and that this required direct assessment of her testimony. It awarded €2,400 in non-pecuniary damages. It rejected pecuniary damage, stating it could not speculate what the appeal court would have decided had she been examined. It also observed that a retrial or reopening would in principle be an appropriate remedy, but that specific remedial measures depended on the circumstances.

In October 2011, the applicant applied to the Portuguese Supreme Court for review under Article 449 § 1 (g) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, arguing that the Court of Appeal’s judgment was irreconcilable with the European Court’s 2011 judgment. The prosecution supported review, citing serious doubts, particularly regarding sentencing. In March 2012, the Supreme Court refused. It held that the conviction was not incompatible with the European Court’s judgment; the lack of a personal hearing was a procedural irregularity not amenable to review; and no serious doubt about the conviction arose because the European Court had not declared the conviction itself unfair and had awarded compensation for the procedural defect. It further noted that even an irremediable nullity under domestic law could not ground an extraordinary review in these circumstances.

The applicant then lodged the present application, relying on Articles 6 and 46 of the Convention. She complained that the dismissal of her application for review violated her fair-trial rights and failed to redress the earlier Article 6 violation. The key issue was whether the refusal to reopen/review the criminal proceedings was compatible with the Convention, especially given the prior finding that she had not been heard personally on appeal. The Grand Chamber ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1 concerning the refusal to grant review, and found no separate issue under Article 46.

**Tsartsidze and Others v. Georgia** (Application no. 18766/04) concerned thirteen Georgian nationals, all Jehovah’s Witnesses, who alleged that they had been subjected to religiously motivated violence and that the Georgian authorities and courts failed to protect them or provide redress. They invoked Articles 6, 8, 9, 11, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application covered five separate incidents.

In **Case no. 1**, on 16 September 2000, Jehovah’s Witnesses travelling to a convention in Marneuli were stopped by police checkpoints and prevented from reaching the site. At the same time, police allowed a coach carrying Orthodox extremists led by Father Basil Mkalavishvili to proceed. The attackers destroyed religious objects and seized property at Mr Tsartsidze’s premises, including 1.5 tonnes of religious literature, which was burned. Police present refused to intervene. The applicants’ administrative complaint was dismissed; the domestic courts accepted that the police had not known about the convention and had been engaged in an anti-drug operation, and found no intentional or negligent breach by officers.

In **Case no. 2**, on 26 October 2000, plainclothes police entered Mr Aliev’s home in Marneuli as about thirty Jehovah’s Witnesses prepared to meet. They ordered the meeting stopped, insulted participants and confiscated religious books and Bibles. Mr Aliev and Mr Mikirtumov were taken to a police station, where they were threatened: Mikirtumov was told to leave Marneuli, and Aliev was told not to host further religious gatherings. Their complaint was dismissed. The court rejected eyewitness statements because the witnesses were Jehovah’s Witnesses and therefore allegedly interested, while accepting police denials.

In **Case no. 3**, on 2 September 2000 in Kutaisi, Mr Dzamukov was stopped by police while carrying religious tracts. His literature was confiscated, he was taken to a police station, struck by officers and briefly strangled with his tie. The next day, Mr Gabunia was punched by a police officer, had his bag seized, and his religious literature was torn up; two Bibles were kept by officers. He was threatened with being dumped in the Rioni River. The domestic courts dismissed the complaint, emphasising that there was no medical evidence, questioning the credibility of Jehovah’s Witness witnesses, and stating that criminal proceedings, not administrative proceedings, were required to establish police guilt.

In **Case no. 4**, on 1 April 2001, Jehovah’s Witnesses returning from a meeting in Dviri, Borjomi region, were attacked by local residents. Mr Gogoladze was wounded and his bag torn away; Ms Tvaradze and Ms Kapanadze were struck. The deputy governor and local governor allegedly watched, insulted the victims and left with the assailant. The courts dismissed the claim because the governors had no legal duty to maintain public order and had not personally organised or carried out the attack.

In **Case no. 5**, on 27 March 2001, Orthodox extremists led by Mr Bluashvili burst into Mr Gogelashvili’s flat in Rustavi during a Jehovah’s Witness meeting. They insulted the participants, confiscated religious literature, threw benches and literature from windows, and Mr Kurua was briefly strangled by his tie. A video allegedly showed a plainclothes police officer observing without intervening. The next day the literature was burned at Rustavi market, again without police reaction. The domestic courts found that an attack had occurred but held that police passivity or breach of duty had not been proven, and the Supreme Court ultimately found no intentional or negligent breach.

Overall, the facts centred on alleged police passivity or complicity, failure to prevent or investigate religiously motivated attacks, dismissive treatment of Jehovah’s Witness evidence by domestic courts, and the absence of effective compensation or redress under Georgian law.

**Case summary: Melandri v. San Marino (Application no. 25189/21)**

The applicant, Vincenzo Secondo Melandri, an Italian national, complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(a) and (b) of the Convention—fair trial, prompt information of the nature and cause of the accusation, and adequate time and facilities to prepare a defence—and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1—protection of property. The case arose from criminal proceedings in San Marino for money laundering and the subsequent confiscation of his assets.

In November 2012, San Marino’s Financial Intelligence Agency reported to the Investigating Judge several banking transactions by the applicant and L.C. at a San Marino bank as possible money laundering. Between September 2009 and March 2010, the applicant deposited large sums into an account in his name—approximately EUR 4,865,830 in cash and about EUR 500,000 in cheques. L.C., introduced by the applicant, opened an account for company O., and EUR 310,000 was later credited to company O. by company A.G., which was traceable to the applicant.

The FIA learned from press reports that the applicant and L.C. had been involved in Italy’s “Operation Baccus,” promoted by the Bari Anti-Mafia District Directorate. Italian proceedings concerned money laundering, extortion, usury, fraud against the State and fictitious wine-sector operations intended to defraud Italian tax authorities and the EU. Italian courts found the applicant guilty of issuing false invoices and criminal association. San Marino authorities obtained Italian documentation by letters rogatory, which allegedly showed that the deposited funds were not compatible with the applicant’s lawful savings but were proceeds of criminal activity.

San Marino opened criminal proceedings no. 865/2012. In November 2013, the Investigating Judge charged the applicant with money laundering under Article 199 bis of the Criminal Code and ordered preventive seizure of a life insurance policy worth roughly EUR 6.8 million, a bank account and other assets. In April 2015, the applicant was indicted on two charges: first, transferring and concealing money derived from crimes through apparent commercial operations with company A.G., including deposits, investments, transfers and the opening of a life insurance policy, with conduct continuing until the policy was seized on 5 December 2013; second, together with L.C., transferring EUR 310,000 through company O. The applicant was represented by counsel throughout.

At trial, the applicant argued that there was no proof of the illicit origin of the funds and that self-laundering had only been introduced by Law no. 100/2013, after the alleged conduct. In January 2019, the first-instance court convicted him of money laundering, but only for acts after 29 July 2013, when Law no. 100/2013 entered into force. He was sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment, and the seized property was confiscated under Article 147 of the Criminal Code.

On appeal, in November 2020, the Judge of Appeal upheld the first charge but changed its legal basis. It found that the applicant had committed self-laundering, which was prosecutable because Law no. 99/2010 already excluded the exception for false-invoice predicate offences. The offence was found to run from 10 March 2011 to 27 December 2011. The applicant was acquitted of the second charge, his sentence reduced to four years and three months, and the confiscation confirmed. In December 2020, the Enforcement Judge ordered confiscation of the previously seized assets, including the life insurance policy, to the San Marino State treasury. The Article 6 complaints therefore appear to concern the fairness of proceedings and the applicant’s ability to know and respond to the case against him, particularly after the appellate court recharacterized the offence and applied a different legal basis. The Protocol No. 1 complaint concerns the mandatory confiscation of his property.

**Summary of *Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir v. Türkiye* (Application no. 18980/20)**

The case of *Kasım Özdemir and Mehmet Özdemir v. Türkiye* concerns a father and son who were shot and injured by a gendarmerie officer during a confrontation in their village. The applicants alleged violations of Articles 2 (right to life) and 3 (prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment) of the European Convention on Human Rights, primarily focusing on the use of force against them and the subsequent ineffectiveness of the domestic investigation.

The incident occurred on the morning of 10 November 2014 in Deliosman village. Three gendarmerie officers were pursuing a suspect vehicle that had ignored their order to stop. The vehicle entered the applicants' village, and a confrontation ensued. According to the applicants, upon arriving in the village, one of the officers, C.Ç., began firing shots into the air. The first applicant (the son) warned him not to shoot, as it would frighten the children. In response, Officer C.Ç. shot him in the leg. When the second applicant (the father) arrived at the scene and saw his injured son, the officer shot and wounded him as well. Both sustained serious fractures to their tibia and fibula.

The official gendarmerie account starkly differs. The officers claimed they were ambushed by a hostile crowd of villagers who threw stones, damaged their vehicle, and attempted to seize their rifles. Officer C.Ç. stated that after firing multiple warning shots that were ignored by a violent mob intent on lynching them, he was forced to shoot two individuals who were actively attacking him and attempting to take his weapon. He maintained he fired in self-defence, aiming only at their legs to neutralize the threat.

The domestic investigation heavily favoured the officers' version of events. The Kilis public prosecutor decided not to prosecute Officer C.Ç., concluding that his actions were justified under self-defence and the legal framework for police use of force. Conversely, the prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicants and other villagers for resisting public officers. The Kilis Criminal Court convicted the applicants, finding that the first applicant had grabbed the officer's rifle and the second had attempted to draw a weapon, leading the officer to shoot them. Their sentence was suspended.

The applicants' appeals to the Constitutional Court were unsuccessful. The Constitutional Court found no violation, accepting that the use of force was necessary and proportionate given the crowd's attack on the officers. It also determined the investigation was adequate.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicants complained about the disproportionate use of force and the failure of the national authorities to conduct an effective and impartial investigation. The key factual disputes at the heart of the case were the nature of the confrontation and whether the applicants posed a direct threat to Officer C.Ç. when they were shot. The applicants contended they were unarmed victims, while the official records, supported by the testimony of the officers and others, portrayed them as active participants in a violent riot aimed at preventing law enforcement from performing their duties. The Court was therefore tasked with assessing the evidence to determine if the force used was absolutely necessary and if the investigation was sufficiently thorough to establish the true facts.

**Case:** *M v. the Netherlands* (Application no. 2156/10), European Court of Human Rights, Third Section, judgment of 25 July 2017.

The applicant, a Netherlands national born in 1970, worked for the AIVD, the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service, as an audio editor and interpreter. He had access to classified information and was bound by a duty of secrecy. He was suspected of forwarding classified AIVD documents to unauthorized persons, including individuals under covert AIVD investigation for possible terrorist activity. On 30 September 2004 he was arrested and charged with divulging State secret information. His complaint before the ECtHR alleged violations of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b), (c) and (d) of the Convention: that the AIVD exercised decisive control over the evidence, restricted his and the domestic courts’ access to documents, controlled how information could be used, made it impossible for him to instruct his defence counsel effectively, and prevented him from offering witness evidence effectively.

After his arrest, the AIVD informed the applicant that he remained bound by secrecy and that discussing covered matters with anyone, including his lawyers, could constitute a further criminal offence. His counsel were similarly warned they could be prosecuted if they disclosed State secrets. At trial before the Rotterdam Regional Court, the defence protested these communication restrictions and requested the internal AIVD report that formed the basis of the prosecution, the allegedly leaked documents in unredacted form, and an unconditional release from the duty of secrecy. The prosecutor added some documents but refused unconditional release.

The AIVD head granted only conditional release: the applicant could discuss secret matters solely with his named counsel; could not reveal AIVD staff or human-source identities; could discuss only what was already in the case file; and only information strictly necessary for the defence. Counsel’s use of such information required consultation with the investigating judge, who would assess relevance, after which the AIVD would decide whether State secrets were at stake. The AIVD further proposed screening defence questions and allowing closed hearings or official reports instead of direct answers.

The Regional Court refused an unconditional exemption, finding the applicant’s interests sufficiently protected. It ordered some witnesses to be heard but refused many others. The investigating judge later declined to hear sixteen defence witnesses for scheduling reasons. Unnamed AIVD witnesses were heard at a secret location, heavily disguised and with voice distortion; an AIVD official was present and could prevent answers. The defence objected and refused to cooperate in such hearings. The applicant was convicted on 14 December 2005 and sentenced to four years and six months’ imprisonment.

On appeal, the defence repeated objections about restricted communication, disguised anonymous witnesses, withheld evidence, and redacted documents. The Court of Appeal, in an interlocutory judgment of 12 October 2006, held that the secrecy duty permitted only statutory exceptions, that the conditional release was not unreasonable, and that if the defence believed a breach was justified under Article 6, it could plead justification; the Advocate General promised no prosecution if such a breach was justified. The Court of Appeal refused the uncensored AIVD internal materials, finding no equality-of-arms violation because they were not in the prosecution’s possession.

During the February 2007 appeal hearing, when the applicant began naming AIVD staff, the Advocate General objected and threatened prosecution; the public was excluded, and the applicant then complied with secrecy. Counsel submitted questions identifying AIVD members and sources, but the Advocate General warned that answering them would trigger prosecution. The Court of Appeal convicted the applicant on 1 March 2007 and sentenced him to four years. The Supreme Court later reduced the sentence for excessive length but upheld the conviction, noting that if secret information were necessary for a fair trial and the defence handicap could not be compensated, the prosecution might have to be declared inadmissible. The ECtHR ultimately found a violation of Article 6 § 1 read in conjunction with § 3(b) and (d).
