text:
**Summary of Jóhannesson and Others v. Iceland (Application no. 22007/11)**

The case of *Jóhannesson and Others v. Iceland* concerns an alleged violation of Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 to the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibits double jeopardy (the right not to be tried or punished twice for the same offence). The application was lodged with the European Court of Human Rights by two Icelandic nationals, Mr. Jón Ásgeir Jóhannesson and Mr. Tryggvi Jónsson, and an Icelandic private limited liability company, Fjárfestingafélagið Gaumur. The core of the applicants’ complaint was that they were subjected to two separate sets of proceedings—one administrative and one criminal—based on identical facts, resulting in two distinct punishments.

The factual background begins with an audit initiated by the Directorate of Tax Investigations in November 2003 into the applicants' tax affairs, focusing on the years 1998 to 2002. The investigation revealed significant financial irregularities. For the first applicant, these included the failure to declare substantial payments received, car allowances, life insurance payments, and profits from the sale of shares in the Baugur Group. Similar findings were made against the second applicant regarding undeclared payments and paid life insurance premiums. The third applicant, a company, was found to have failed to properly account for and declare employee allowances (like cars and housing), failed to withhold public levies on these amounts, and incorrectly declared profits, losses, and expenses related to the Baugur Group.

Based on these findings, the Directorate of Internal Revenue issued rulings in late 2004 and 2005, re-assessing the applicants’ taxes for the relevant years and imposing a 25% tax surcharge on the undeclared amounts. The third applicant also faced an additional 10% surcharge for failing to withhold and remit public levies. These decisions were largely upheld by the Internal Revenue Board in 2007. Critically, the applicants did not seek judicial review of these tax surcharge decisions, which subsequently became final and legally binding in early 2008.

Separately, the tax investigation reports were forwarded to the National Police Commissioner in November 2004. After a lengthy investigation, the applicants were indicted in December 2008 for aggravated tax offences under the General Penal Code. The charges were based on the same underlying facts that had already formed the basis for the tax surcharges—namely, the underdeclaration of income and failure to remit public levies.

In a significant development, the Reykjavik District Court ruled on 1 June 2010 that the criminal charges were based on the same facts as the tax surcharge decisions. Relying on Article 4 of Protocol No. 7 and the European Court’s judgment in *Sergey Zolotukhin v. Russia*, the District Court dismissed the indictment, finding that the applicants had already been tried and punished for the same offences through the administrative tax proceedings. However, this ruling was overturned by the Supreme Court of Iceland on 22 September 2010. The Supreme Court held that under the principle of dualism, domestic courts could not invalidate the established system of imposing tax surcharges followed by criminal proceedings, even if based on the same facts.

Consequently, the criminal case proceeded. In December 2011, the District Court convicted the applicants, though it suspended the determination of the penalty for one year. On appeal, the Supreme Court in February 2013 upheld the convictions for the most part, convicting the first applicant on additional charges. The final sentences included suspended prison terms and substantial fines for the first two applicants. In determining the sentences, the Supreme Court took into account the excessive length of the proceedings and the fact that the tax authorities had already imposed a 25% tax surcharge. The applicants then brought their case to the European Court of Human Rights, alleging that the combination of the final tax surcharges and the subsequent criminal convictions for the same conduct constituted a violation of their right not to be punished twice.

Ahmed v. the United Kingdom (Application no. 59727/13) concerned a Somali national, Mr Liban Mohamud Ahmed, who alleged that his prolonged detention pending deportation breached Article 5 § 1(f) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applicant, born in 1977, left Somalia in 1992 for the Netherlands and later entered the United Kingdom in December 1999, where he claimed asylum using a false name and false immigration history to avoid return to the Netherlands. Although asylum was refused, he received exceptional leave to remain until 2004. Between November 2001 and August 2005 he received ten criminal convictions; in December 2007 he was convicted of public order and failing to surrender and sentenced to four and a half months’ imprisonment.

In January 2008 the Secretary of State notified him of an intention to deport and refused indefinite leave to remain. His appeal against deportation was dismissed in June 2008. In February 2008, after serving half his sentence, he was detained under Schedule 3 to the Immigration Act 1971 pending deportation. A deportation order was signed in October 2008. In June 2009 removal directions were set, but they were cancelled after the European Court of Human Rights granted an interim measure under Rule 39, preventing removal. He remained in immigration detention until July 2011—about three years and five months.

The alleged violations arose primarily from the lawfulness of that detention. Detention reviews were conducted monthly. Some review forms suggested he could reduce his detention by withdrawing his Rule 39 application or by returning voluntarily to Somalia under the Facilitated Return Scheme. Bail applications were refused in 2009 and 2010 because immigration judges found him a significant abscond risk. In June 2010 he made representations against removal, treated as an application to revoke the deportation order; this was refused in November 2010, though the refusal was later withdrawn in July 2011. In November 2010 he began judicial review proceedings claiming unlawful detention. Permission was granted in June 2011, and he was granted bail in July 2011, shortly after the Court’s judgment in Sufi and Elmi v. the United Kingdom concerning removals to Somalia.

The domestic courts applied the Hardial Singh principles: detention pending deportation must be for deportation, must be reasonable in all circumstances, must end if removal cannot occur within a reasonable period, and authorities must act with due diligence. The Administrative Court dismissed his claim in November 2011, finding a substantial risk of absconding and reoffending, that alternatives to detention were insufficient, and that there remained a realistic prospect of removal within a reasonable time despite the Rule 39 measure. The Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in October 2012. It rejected his arguments that detention was vitiated by public law errors—namely, failing to ascertain when the Rule 39 measure might be lifted and maintaining detention on the basis that he could withdraw his Strasbourg application and return voluntarily. It found the Rule 39 measure was fact-insensitive and did not reflect a specific risk assessment, and that voluntary return did not materially affect the detention reviews. Elias LJ dissented only on whether the two-week delay after Sufi and Elmi before release was reasonable. The Supreme Court refused leave to appeal in March 2013. The case therefore centred on whether prolonged immigration detention pending deportation became arbitrary or unlawful under Article 5 § 1(f), particularly in light of the Rule 39 interim measure, the risk of absconding, and the alleged public law errors in the detention decision-making.

**Asatryan v. Armenia (Application no. 3571/09), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 27 April 2017.**

The applicant, Ms Silva Asatryan, an Armenian national born in 1960, was convicted of instigating the attempted murder of M.G., a businessman and former parliamentarian. Her principal complaint was that she had been denied a fair trial because the Criminal Court of Appeal relied on pre-trial witness statements that were neither read out in court nor subject to examination, and she had no opportunity to question those witnesses.

The facts arose from a bomb placed under M.G.’s car on 29 December 2001. M.G. survived without major injuries. During the investigation, M.G. pointed to the applicant’s ex-husband, A.G., as the likely offender because of business disputes. A.G. denied involvement, and his son V.G. was briefly arrested but later released. Several people were interviewed in early 2002. A.At., a family friend, said the applicant had opposed A.G.’s business dealings with M.G. and considered M.G. a “scammer.” A.A., a neighbour, mentioned that the applicant had complained that M.G. owed money. L.G., the applicant’s daughter, stated that although her parents had divorced, they maintained good relations and the applicant often stayed at A.G.’s apartment. Another neighbour, A.B., described knowing the family.

In September 2005, Y.W., a family friend, was arrested after firearms and explosives were found at his home. He confessed to M.G.’s attempted murder and claimed he had acted on the applicant’s orders. The applicant was arrested on 23 September 2005 and charged with instigation of attempted murder and property damage.

At trial, Y.W. retracted his pre-trial statements, alleging duress. The applicant denied any involvement, stating that she had divorced A.G. in 1999, lived separately with her daughter L.G., and had no connection with A.G.’s business. The indictment’s witness list included L.G., but not A.At., A.A., or A.B. L.G. was later excluded after invoking her right not to testify against a close relative. The District Court convicted the applicant and sentenced her to nine years’ imprisonment, relying mainly on trial statements by Y.W.’s spouse and former colleague, and on the applicant’s court disputes with M.G.

On appeal, Y.W. changed his account again, saying he had organised the explosion at the applicant’s request but had only intended to frighten M.G. The applicant maintained her innocence. The Criminal Court of Appeal dismissed her appeal and upheld the conviction. In doing so, it found that although the applicant had divorced A.G., she had maintained a family-like relationship with him and had expressed annoyance at M.G. before various people. To support this, the Court of Appeal relied on the pre-trial statements of L.G., A.At., A.A., and A.B. These statements had not been read out or examined in either the District Court or the Court of Appeal, and the applicant had no opportunity to question the witnesses.

The applicant appealed on points of law, arguing that reliance on these untested pre-trial statements violated her fair-trial rights. The Court of Cassation declared her appeal inadmissible. After the Constitutional Court found provisions allowing the Court of Cassation to give no reasons unconstitutional, the proceedings were reopened, but the Court of Cassation again declared the appeal inadmissible, noting that the guilt finding was based partly on the statements of L.G. and A.A.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 15 June 2009. The case was communicated to the Armenian Government on 24 May 2012. The key alleged violation concerned the appellate court’s use of pre-trial witness statements from witnesses who were not examined in court, thereby preventing the applicant from challenging the evidence central to her conviction.

The case originated in application no. 53600/20 against Switzerland, brought by Verein KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz, a Swiss non-profit association, and four of its members. The association promotes effective climate protection on behalf of its members, mainly women over 70. It has over 2,000 members with an average age of 73; nearly 650 are aged 75 or older. The four individual applicants were older women who described serious health effects from heatwaves. Ms Schaub (born 1931) collapsed during hot weather, had a pacemaker, suffered severe gout and was once hospitalised; she died during the proceedings. Ms Volkoff Peschon (born 1937) had cardiovascular problems, had to stay indoors, adjust medication and measure blood pressure, and suffered breathing difficulties. Ms Molinari (born 1941) had asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease worsened by heat. Ms Budry (born 1942) had asthma and said heatwaves drained her energy and restricted her activities.

The applicants alleged that Swiss authorities’ omissions in climate-change mitigation violated their rights under Articles 2, 6, 8 and 13 of the European Convention on Human Rights. They claimed that climate change, especially more frequent and intense heatwaves, disproportionately threatened older women’s life, health and physical integrity. They argued that Switzerland had a positive obligation to protect them by adopting and implementing sufficient measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

In November 2016, relying on section 25a of the Federal Administrative Procedure Act and Articles 6 and 13 of the Convention, the applicants requested the Federal Council, the Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications, the Federal Office for the Environment and the Federal Office for Energy to issue a formal decision on alleged omissions in climate protection. They sought measures to reduce Swiss greenhouse gas emissions in line with the Paris Agreement target of holding global warming well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, or at least not exceeding 2°C. Their requests included at least a 25% domestic reduction below 1990 levels by 2020, a 50% reduction by 2030, initiation of preliminary legislative proceedings, information to Parliament and the public, a higher CO2 tax, and building and transport measures. Alternatively, they sought a declaration that the omissions were unlawful. They contended that current targets and measures were insufficient, unconstitutional and incompatible with the Convention and international law.

The DETEC rejected the request for lack of standing. It found that no individual rights or obligations were affected because the request concerned general, abstract regulation and political choices, not a “real act” affecting individual legal positions, and amounted to an actio popularis. The Federal Administrative Court dismissed the appeal, finding no close proximity or interest worthy of protection. It considered climate-change impacts to be general, held that older women were not sufficiently differentiated from the public, and found no genuine, serious dispute directly decisive for civil rights under Article 6, with Article 13 absorbed by Article 6. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the final appeal. It held that the alleged omissions did not affect the applicants’ rights with sufficient intensity at present; their rights under Articles 2 and 8 were not threatened enough; they had no subjective right or arguable claim; and the action was an inadmissible actio popularis better pursued through political means.

These facts formed the basis of the applicants’ alleged violations before the Grand Chamber: that Switzerland’s inadequate climate mitigation breached positive obligations to protect life and private/family life, and that domestic authorities denied them access to court and an effective remedy.

**Vlahović v. Montenegro** (Application no. 62444/10), European Court of Human Rights, First Section, judgment of 22 February 2024, final on 24 June 2024. The applicant, Zoran Vlahović, a Croatian national born in 1964 and living in Split, complained under Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 about the non-enforcement of domestic judgments and decisions delivered in his favour in 2010.

The applicant was co-owner of two plots of land, nos. 1084/4 and 1084/10, in Herceg Novi. He owned one third and one half of the plots respectively; a certain M.D. owned smaller fractions. The land was registered as an uncategorised road. In June 2005, M.D. constructed a sewage collection system and paved the road in concrete without the approval of the other co-owners or authorisation from the Municipality of Herceg Novi. The applicant and another co-owner sued M.D.

Expert evidence showed that the concrete paving altered rainwater drainage, accelerating water flow and likely causing flooding, soil deposits and erosion to adjacent land. The sewage system had been built without prior administrative authorisation and might not have complied with construction standards.

On 26 February 2010, the Herceg Novi Court of First Instance found that M.D. had violated the applicant’s rights by unlawfully paving the entirety of the plots and constructing a sewage system on plot no. 1084/10. It ordered M.D. to remove the objects within fifteen days. On 8 February 2011, the Podgorica High Court upheld that judgment, making it final. Separately, on 29 and 30 March 2010, the municipal police ordered M.D. to remove the sewage system and concrete paving; those decisions were upheld in April 2010.

Enforcement became complicated after M.D. transferred his ownership rights to the municipality free of charge on 18 May 2010, and the municipality sought to expropriate the plots in December 2010. Between December 2010 and May 2019, the municipal police repeatedly postponed enforcement; all postponements were quashed. On 15 April 2011, an enforcement order was issued, but it was quashed in October 2011 because M.D. was no longer a co-owner and expropriation proceedings were pending. In 2012, the courts dismissed the applicant’s request to enforce against the municipality because the judgment had been against M.D., not the municipality, and advised him to bring separate civil proceedings.

In April 2015, the Court of First Instance imposed an interim measure prohibiting removal of the concrete and sewage system until the expropriation proceedings ended. It found that enforcement would cause nearly irreparable damage to occupants, as the road was the only access to their homes and was needed for water and sewage infrastructure. In 2017, the Supreme Court held that expropriation proceedings could not obstruct enforcement of decisions ordering removal. Nevertheless, in April 2021, enforcement was terminated because circumstances entirely prevented it, notably that the respondent was no longer a co-owner. The applicant was again advised to pursue separate civil proceedings against the municipality.

The applicant repeatedly sought enforcement against M.D. and the municipality, relying on section 28 of the Enforcement Act. In June 2023, the Constitutional Court quashed a 2019 decision rejecting that reliance and found a violation of Article 6 due to insufficient reasoning. By 12 December 2023, the expropriation proceedings were still pending, the 2015 interim measure remained in force, and the 2010 judgment and two administrative decisions in the applicant’s favour remained unenforced. The key alleged violations therefore concern the prolonged failure to enforce final domestic decisions in the applicant’s favour, engaging Article 6 and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

**Case: Moreira Ferreira v. Portugal (No. 2)**  
**Application no. 19867/12 – Grand Chamber, 11 July 2017**

The applicant, Francelina Moreira Ferreira, a Portuguese national, complained under Articles 6 and 46 of the European Convention on Human Rights that the Portuguese Supreme Court had dismissed her application for review of a criminal conviction. The key facts concerned her original criminal case, the first Strasbourg judgment finding a fair-trial violation, and her subsequent unsuccessful attempt to have the conviction reopened.

In 2007, following an altercation, the applicant was prosecuted for threatening and insulting conduct. A psychiatric expert report stated that she had limited intellectual and cognitive capacities but should still be held criminally responsible. On 23 March 2007, the Matosinhos District Court rejected her defence of diminished criminal responsibility and sentenced her to 320 day-fines, totalling EUR 640, and ordered her to pay damages to the victims.

The applicant appealed to the Oporto Court of Appeal on 13 April 2007. She maintained that she had been unaware of the unlawfulness of her acts and lacked criminal responsibility due to psychiatric disorders. She requested a fresh assessment of the facts and the opportunity to present her case at a hearing. On 12 December 2007, the Court of Appeal held a hearing attended by the public prosecutor and her counsel, but the applicant herself was not examined. In its final judgment of 19 December 2007, the Court of Appeal upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to 265 day-fines, amounting to EUR 530. It found no need for a fresh factual assessment because the applicant had not successfully challenged the first-instance court’s findings. She later paid the fine in instalments.

In her first application to the European Court of Human Rights (no. 19808/08), the applicant complained that she had not been heard in person by the Court of Appeal. In a judgment of 5 July 2011, the Court found a violation of Article 6 § 1. It held that the Court of Appeal should have conducted a full rehearing, especially because the diminished-responsibility issue required direct assessment of her personal testimony. The Court awarded EUR 2,400 in non-pecuniary damages. It rejected the pecuniary claim, noting that it could not speculate on what the appeal court would have decided had she been heard. It also observed that retrial or reopening of proceedings was in principle an appropriate way of remedying the violation and that Article 449 of the Portuguese Code of Criminal Procedure allowed reopening where the Court found a fundamental-rights violation.

During execution of that judgment, the Portuguese Government paid the award but its proposed amendment to the Code of Criminal Procedure—to require hearings in appeal courts determining guilt or sentence—was not adopted. Supervision by the Committee of Ministers remained pending.

On 18 October 2011, the applicant applied to the Supreme Court for review under Article 449 § 1 (g) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, arguing that the Court of Appeal’s judgment was incompatible with the Court’s 2011 judgment. The prosecution supported the application, citing serious doubts about the conviction, particularly sentencing. However, on 21 March 2012, the Supreme Court refused review. It held that the conviction itself was not incompatible with the Strasbourg judgment; the lack of a hearing was a procedural irregularity not amenable to review; and the judgment did not cast serious doubt on the validity of the conviction. The Supreme Court emphasised that the Court had compensated a procedural defect rather than established that the conviction was unfair.

The applicant then complained to the Grand Chamber that the dismissal of her review application violated Articles 6 and 46 of the Convention. The central facts were therefore the absence of a personal hearing before the appellate court, the prior finding of a violation, and Portugal’s refusal to reopen the conviction as a remedy.

The case *Ković and Others v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 39611/08, 50121/13 and 2490/14) concerned three Serbian nationals—Nikola Ković, Zoran Ranković, and Ivan Bojanić—who lodged applications against Serbia with the European Court of Human Rights under Article 34 of the Convention. The applications were introduced on 21 July 2008, 5 June 2013, and 16 December 2013 respectively. All applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the excessive length of different administrative and civil proceedings. On 18 December 2014, the Court communicated to the Government the complaints concerning the length of administrative and civil proceedings; the remainders of the applications were declared inadmissible under Rule 54 § 3. The Government objected to examination by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

Nikola Ković (application no. 39611/08), born 21 July 1941, had domestic proceedings that began in October 2001 and on 9 November 2001. Both remained pending at the relevant time. Since 3 March 2004, when the Convention entered into force in respect of Serbia, the proceedings had lasted 10 years and 8 months at one level of jurisdiction. Ković obtained a decision of the Constitutional Court of Serbia finding a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time. Under the regulations applicable at the time, the Constitutional Court established his right to seek compensation for non-pecuniary damage before the Commission for Damage Compensation. He submitted a request for damages to the Commission on 26 December 2010, but had received no response to date. This unresolved compensation request was a key fact relevant to the alleged violation and the effectiveness of the domestic remedy.

Zoran Ranković (application no. 50121/13), born 3 September 1954, had proceedings that started on 25 July 2002 and ended on 18 May 2012. Since 3 March 2004, the proceedings had lasted 8 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. He was represented by Mile Petković. The Constitutional Court found a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time and awarded him a certain sum in respect of non-pecuniary damage.

Ivan Bojanić (application no. 2490/14), born 22 April 1978, had proceedings that started on 11 March 2004 and ended on 25 May 2011. Since 3 March 2004, the proceedings had lasted 7 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. He was represented by Dragan Radin. The Constitutional Court also found a violation of his right to a hearing within a reasonable time and awarded him a certain sum for non-pecuniary damage.

The alleged violations therefore concerned Serbia’s failure to ensure that the applicants’ administrative and civil proceedings were determined within a reasonable time, contrary to Article 6 § 1. Although the Constitutional Court had acknowledged delays and granted redress—by awarding compensation to Ranković and Bojanić and by directing Ković to seek compensation before the Commission—Ković’s compensation request remained unanswered. The case accordingly raised issues about the length of domestic proceedings and the adequacy of the domestic remedies provided in response to established delays.

**Summary of the Case**

The case of *Cosovan v. the Republic of Moldova (No. 2)* concerns the confiscation of money from an individual whose criminal proceedings were discontinued due to the expiration of the statute of limitations. The applicant, Mr. Serghei Cosovan, was the director of a company, V.G., which operated a public car park in Chișinău. On 15 January 2007, a criminal investigation was initiated against him for illegal commercial activity, based on complaints from the Chișinău municipality. The prosecution alleged that between April and November 2006, the applicant operated the car park without proper state authorization and failed to pay taxes, calculating the illegal income at 116,428 Moldovan lei (approximately 7,080 euros).

On 27 June 2011, following a request by the applicant, the prosecutor discontinued the investigation because the limitation period had expired. However, in the same decision, the prosecutor ordered the special confiscation of the sum of 116,428 lei from the applicant, stating it represented income obtained from a criminal offence under Article 241 of the Criminal Code. The prosecutor reasoned that special confiscation was a precautionary measure permissible under the law even without a conviction. The applicant challenged the confiscation order, arguing that he had never admitted guilt, that his guilt had not been determined by a court, and that the confiscation was therefore unlawful.

On 6 April 2012, a superior prosecutor dismissed the applicant’s appeal, reiterating that the discontinuance of proceedings on the grounds of the expired limitation period did not entail rehabilitation and implied a waiver of the right to have guilt proved in criminal proceedings. The applicant then complained to an investigating judge, asserting that the prosecutor’s decision breached his right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. He emphasized that he had never been formally charged or acknowledged as a suspect during the proceedings.

On 15 January 2013, the Buiucani District Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint. The court found that sufficient evidence had been gathered during the investigation to confirm the suspicion against the applicant, including witness statements and records showing the car park’s takings. It concluded that even though criminal liability was barred by the limitation period, the prosecutor was authorized to order special confiscation as a precautionary measure under Article 106 of the Criminal Code. The court noted that the applicant had not contested the factual findings and that the confiscation was justified as the income derived from an act prohibited by criminal law.

The applicant complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention, alleging a violation of his right to a fair trial and the presumption of innocence. He argued that the confiscation order effectively deemed him guilty without a formal conviction, and that the proceedings lacked procedural safeguards. The applicant died in 2021, and his wife pursued the application. The case centers on whether the confiscation of assets following a time-barred discontinuance of criminal proceedings violates the presumption of innocence and the right to a fair trial.

Tretyakov and Others v. Russia (Applications nos. 33610/18 and 21 others) is a European Court of Human Rights case decided by the Fifth Section Committee on 4 April 2024. The applicants were 22 individuals who lodged applications against Russia under Article 34 of the Convention on various dates between 2018 and 2021. The Russian Government was given notice of the applications. The central complaint was the excessive length of their pre-trial detention; some applicants also raised other Convention complaints, but the appended table focused on detention facts.

According to the table, each applicant was detained in Russia under orders issued or reviewed by district, town, city, regional, or supreme courts. The detention periods varied widely. Dmitriy Tretyakov was detained from 14 March 2018 to 28 March 2019, lasting 1 year and 15 days, with orders from the Frunzenskiy District Court of Vladivostok and the Primorskiy Regional Court. Igor Dontsov was detained from 6 September 2017, still pending when he applied and possibly as of 16 September 2022, totalling 5 years and 11 days; Moscow City Court handled his orders. Dmitriy Martynov was detained from 1 February 2017 to 6 February 2019, lasting 2 years and 6 days, under Moscow courts.

Reyal Rasulov had one of the longest periods: from 15 August 2015, pending at application and possibly as of 16 September 2022, amounting to 7 years, 1 month and 2 days; Karelia courts issued the orders. Oleg Krasnov was detained from 28 February 2017, pending as of 16 September 2022, for 5 years, 6 months and 20 days. Dmitriy Gusakov was held from 18 July 2017 to 29 August 2022, for 5 years, 1 month and 12 days. Ilya Vyguzov was detained from 27 July 2018, pending, for more than 4 years, 7 months and 19 days. Sergey Zakharov was detained from 25 May 2018, pending, for 4 years, 3 months and 23 days, while Mikhail Fomin was held from 20 June 2018, pending, for 4 years, 2 months and 28 days.

Other examples include Vyacheslav Kruglov, detained from 5 March to 19 July 2019 (4 months and 15 days); Nikita Kolesnikov, from 17 May 2018 to 12 August 2019 (1 year, 2 months and 27 days); Vasiliy Sukhorukov, from 30 January 2019 to 27 January 2020 (11 months and 29 days); and Aleksandr Petrov, from 25 September 2019 to 16 January 2020 (3 months and 23 days), the shortest listed period. Aleksandr Pisarev had two detention periods: 21 April 2018 to 18 June 2019 and 20 June to 16 September 2019, together about 1 year, 4 months and 27 days.

Several applicants remained in detention pending the application and possibly until 16 September 2022, including Safonov, Tran, Mezin, Belov, Podrezova and Kachayev. The courts involved included district and regional courts across Moscow, St Petersburg, Vladivostok, Karelia, Samara, Perm, Tula, Chita, Astrakhan, Tver, Novosibirsk, Izhevsk, Krasnoyarsk and other regions.

The key factual issue was whether these pre-trial detention periods, many lasting years and several still pending, were excessively long. The applicants complained that Russia violated their Convention rights, principally the right to liberty and security requiring trial within a reasonable time or release pending trial. The Court deliberated on 14 March 2024 and adopted its judgment on 4 April 2024.

**A.D. and Others v. Sweden** (ECtHR, First Section, Application no. 22283/21, judgment 7 May 2024) concerned five Albanian nationals—a father, mother, and their three children—who sought asylum in Sweden on 6 December 2018. Their claim centred on alleged risks in Albania linked to the first applicant’s work as a police officer from 1998, particularly against cannabis production and trafficking.

The key triggering incident was the attempted kidnapping of the third applicant, the eldest daughter, on 3 October 2017 by three masked men. She was traumatised and later developed depression. The family also cited two further incidents in 2017–2018: shots fired at their front door and a hand grenade exploding near their home. They believed these acts were connected to the first applicant’s anti-drug police work, although they did not know who was responsible. They claimed they did not trust Albanian law enforcement because of widespread corruption and feared that reporting would worsen their situation. However, the first applicant had direct contact with a senior police officer and submitted documents including a prosecutor’s report about threats in August 2017 and a police document about the October 2017 attempted kidnapping. They said return to Albania would put them at risk of being killed, noting that a former police officer and his wife had been killed in their home town.

On 18 January 2019, the Swedish Migration Agency rejected the asylum request and ordered deportation. It did not doubt that the incidents had occurred but found that the perpetrators were unknown, their intent and possible connection unclear, and the acts primarily ordinary crimes for Albanian authorities to prosecute. Citing country information, it concluded that Albania had a general ability and willingness to protect citizens despite corruption problems. It held that the applicants had not exhausted available State protection, especially by failing to report the attempted kidnapping. The first applicant’s prior report was insufficient because the perpetrators were unknown and he had resigned from the police. The Migration Court upheld the decision on 28 April 2020, finding that protection was not generally effective enough for criminal-gang threats, so an individual assessment was needed. But because the father had long police service and contacts within the Albanian judicial system, it was not shown that the authorities lacked the will or ability to act. The Migration Court of Appeal denied leave to appeal on 22 June 2020.

In July 2020, the applicants sought re-examination or residence permits based on new circumstances. They alleged that their house in Albania had been damaged by an explosion on 7 January 2020, causing the first applicant’s mother to seek medical care. A police document stated that an anonymous caller had threatened the first applicant before the explosion, saying he “has nowhere to hide” and must pay debts, and linked the explosion to the 2017 incidents. A second explosion allegedly occurred on 12 July 2020. They submitted photographs, news articles, medical certificates, and police documents.

On 20 July 2020, the Migration Agency refused re-examination, treating the new incidents as additions to previously assessed circumstances. It found State protection still available and not exhausted, as the police reports did not show what had resulted from them or that the applicants had completed the legal process. The Migration Court upheld this on 10 August 2020, and the Migration Court of Appeal denied leave on 21 September 2020.

The applicants applied to the European Court of Human Rights on 23 April 2021. Their complaint under Article 3 alleged that removal to Albania would expose them to ill-treatment by non-State actors and that Albanian authorities could not provide appropriate protection. The Court granted anonymity, priority, and an interim measure under Rule 39 preventing removal, which Sweden complied with. The Albanian Government did not intervene. Country information described Albanian reforms and anti-corruption efforts, but also persistent corruption, political influence, capacity problems, and low public confidence in the judiciary and police.

The case concerns Adrianus van Wesenbeeck, a Dutch national convicted in Belgium of drug trafficking, participation in an international criminal organisation and money laundering. He complained to the European Court of Human Rights under Article 6 § 1 and Article 6 § 3 (d) that his defence rights had been breached and that he had been unable to question the undercover agents whose evidence helped convict him.

In May 2006 the Hasselt public prosecutor authorised a proactive investigation against the applicant and others, including infiltration and later observation. A separate confidential case file was created for the special investigative methods. The proactive phase ended in September 2008, and police reports summarising the evidence were added to the criminal file. A judicial investigation then began. The Federal Prosecutor took over in October 2008. Observation and infiltration ended in June 2009, when the applicant and others were arrested.

Because evidence came from special investigative methods, the Indictments Division of the Antwerp Court of Appeal reviewed the confidential file under Articles 235ter and 235bis of the Code of Criminal Procedure. It heard the Federal Prosecutor separately, without the parties, and had access to the confidential file. The defendants, including the applicant, were later invited to present arguments. In May 2010 the Division found that some evidence concerning the special methods had not yet been added to the criminal file and ordered the Federal Prosecutor to complete it. After additional authorisations and a report were added, the Division declared the file complete in June 2010, finding no nullity or irregularity. It held that the proactive investigation, including observation and infiltration, met statutory conditions, including reasonable suspicion, proportionality and subsidiarity.

The applicant appealed unsuccessfully to the Court of Cassation and was committed for trial. In March 2011 the Hasselt Court of First Instance convicted him and sentenced him to ten years’ imprisonment and a fine. The conviction relied partly on evidence from the special investigative methods. He requested a face-to-face meeting with the undercover agents

**Case: Wa Baile v. Switzerland (ECtHR, Third Section, judgment of 20 February 2024, final 20 May 2024)**  

The case concerns an alleged racial profiling identity check and the subsequent failure of Swiss authorities to determine whether the applicant had been discriminated against because of his skin colour.

The applicant, a Swiss national born in 1974 living in Bern, was stopped for an identity check on the morning of 5 February 2015 at Zürich railway station while on his way to work. Three municipal police officers approached him at about 7 a.m. The officer in charge later reported that his attention had been drawn by a “dark-skinned” male who seemed suspicious because he allegedly averted his gaze upon seeing the police and tried to avoid them. The officer suspected a breach of the Federal Aliens Act and decided to check his identity. The applicant refused to comply. The officers then took him aside, asked him to raise his hands and spread his legs, and searched his pockets and backpack until they found a document confirming his identity. He was then allowed to leave.

The applicant claimed that he was the only person checked in a crowd of people going to work, whom he described as almost all white, and that he received no explanation for why he had been stopped. He alleged that the check amounted to racial profiling and discrimination based on his skin colour.

In the criminal proceedings, the applicant was fined CHF 100 for refusing to comply with police orders, plus CHF 150 in procedural costs. The District Court found both the applicant’s and the officer’s accounts credible, but concluded that there was nothing to show that the applicant’s skin colour had been a decisive factor. It also held that even if the identity check had been unlawful, the police order had not been null and void, so the applicant was still obliged to comply; any unlawfulness could be established later by administrative courts. The Cantonal Court upheld the conviction, finding no indication of manifestly discriminatory grounds and emphasising the busy railway station context and the officer’s credible explanation. The Federal Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, holding that his discrimination complaint relied on a different version of the facts from that established below and was therefore inadmissible.

In parallel administrative proceedings, the applicant sought a declaration that the identity check had been unlawful. After several lower bodies dismissed his request, the Administrative Court of the Canton of Zürich held on 1 October 2020 that the check had been unlawful: even accepting the officer’s account that it was prompted by the applicant looking away, that was not a sufficient justification. However, the Administrative Court expressly left open whether the check had also been discriminatory on the ground of skin colour. The applicant appealed to the Federal Supreme Court, seeking a ruling on discrimination under Article 14 read with Article 8 of the Convention. In December 2020, the Federal Supreme Court declared his appeal inadmissible, finding that he had already obtained full satisfaction and merely sought additional reasoning, which did not give him a legitimate interest.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant complained under Article 14 of the Convention read in conjunction with Articles 6 and 8, and under Article 13. The central alleged violations were that the identity check had been based on racial profiling, that the domestic authorities had failed to decide whether he had been subjected to such discrimination, and that he lacked an effective remedy in that respect.

**Case: H.T. v. Germany and Greece (Application no. 13337/19, judgment 15 October 2024)**

The case concerns H.T., a Syrian national, who alleged that Germany violated Article 3 of the Convention by removing him to Greece on the same day he expressed an intention to seek asylum there, and that Greece violated Articles 3 and 5 §§ 1 and 4 in respect of his subsequent detention and its judicial review.

H.T. first arrived in Greece on 30 June 2018, on Megisti island, where he was detained. On 4 July 2018 Greece ordered his removal to Türkiye under the EU-Türkiye Statement. On 18 July 2018 he applied for asylum in Leros, but a geographical limitation confined him to Leros. He alleged that conditions in the Leros Reception and Identification Centre were overcrowded and inadequate, and he left the island. His asylum application was discontinued on 13 August 2018 after he failed to attend an interview. He then left Greece.

On 4 September 2018, H.T. was stopped entering Germany from Austria by bus. He used a stolen Bulgarian identity card but also possessed a Syrian identity card and a Greek arrival certificate. He told German police that he wished to apply for asylum in Germany and to join his brother in Dortmund. He was provisionally arrested, informed of his rights in Arabic, and questioned with an interpreter. Germany refused him entry and returned him to Athens by plane the same day under the 2018 administrative arrangement between Germany and Greece concerning refusal of entry to protection seekers at the German-Austrian border. The arrangement applied where a Eurodac hit showed that the person had already requested protection in Greece after 1 July 2017. A Eurodac hit confirmed his earlier Leros asylum application. Germany notified Greece of the refusal.

H.T. alleged that he never agreed to return to Greece, that his asylum application was not registered in Germany, that he had no lawyer or reliable legal information, and that he received contradictory information: an initial written refusal said he would be returned to Austria, while the later refusal-of-entry decision for asylum-seekers, issued shortly before departure, was allegedly explained only orally in English, without an Arabic interpreter.

On arrival in Athens, Greek authorities arrested and detained him with a view to executing the earlier removal decision. He was initially held in the Attica Directorate for Foreigners for up to six months, then transferred to Leros police station and the Leros Reception and Identification Centre. The detention grounds included risk of absconding, lack of documents, danger to public order, and the pending removal to Türkiye. H.T. sought continuation of his asylum proceedings and challenged his detention before the Rhodes Administrative Tribunal. He alleged that his detention was unlawful because he was an asylum-seeker and that conditions violated Article 3: he claimed he was held 24 hours a day in a cell, had no outdoor exercise, endured dampness, poor ventilation, lack of hygiene items, delayed medication, and no recreation or outside contact. EASO later identified him as vulnerable, suffering from an anxiety-depressive disorder, and exempt from the border procedure. He was released on 27 November 2018. Greece recognised him as a refugee on 7 April 2020.

The key alleged violations therefore arose from Germany’s immediate removal of an asylum-seeking individual to Greece despite claimed risks of inhuman or degrading treatment and without individual assurances or a Dublin III procedure, and from Greece’s detention of him allegedly in unlawful and inadequate conditions, with ineffective judicial review.
