**M v. the Netherlands** (Application no. 2156/10), a 2017 European Court of Human Rights case, concerned a Netherlands national employed by the AIVD, the Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service, as an audio editor and interpreter. Because of his role, the applicant had access to classified information and was bound by a duty of secrecy. He was suspected of forwarding copies of classified documents to unauthorized persons, including individuals then under covert AIVD investigation for possible terrorist activity. On 30 September 2004 he was arrested, charged with divulging State secret information, and detained on remand.

The alleged Article 6 violations arose from the way national-security secrecy shaped the criminal proceedings. The AIVD informed the applicant that he remained bound by secrecy and that discussing covered matters with anyone, including his defence counsel, could constitute a further offence. His lawyers were also warned they could be prosecuted if they disclosed State secrets to third parties. At trial before the Rotterdam Regional Court, defence counsel protested that these restrictions undermined effective communication and defence preparation. They requested the internal AIVD report forming the basis of the prosecution, which was absent from the case file, and unredacted copies of the allegedly leaked documents, which were included only in redacted form. They also sought an unconditional release from the secrecy duty. The prosecutor added some documents but refused unconditional release.

The AIVD head granted only a conditional exemption: the applicant could discuss covered matters solely with two named counsel; he could not reveal AIVD staff or source identities; he could discuss only material contained in the case file; the information had to be strictly necessary for the defence; and counsel’s use of such information required consultation with the investigating judge. The AIVD would then determine whether State secrets were at stake. Witnesses were also affected. Some AIVD witnesses refused to answer based on secrecy. Unnamed AIVD staff were heard at a secret location, heavily disguised, with voice distortion, and an AIVD official present could prevent answers. Requests to hear numerous other witnesses were refused, partly for lack of time.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal accepted that the secrecy duty restricted confidential lawyer-client consultation and could, if unmitigated, prevent a fair trial. It nonetheless found the conditional release not unreasonable and said that if the defence believed it necessary to breach secrecy to secure a fair trial, it could invoke Article 6 as a justification; the Advocate General initially assured no prosecution would follow. Yet during the appeal hearing, when the applicant began naming AIVD staff, the Advocate General objected and threatened prosecution. The court excluded the public. Defence counsel later submitted questions naming AIVD members and sources and addressing working methods, but the Advocate General again threatened prosecution if those questions were answered. The Court of Appeal convicted the applicant and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment.

The Supreme Court later reduced the sentence by two months for excessive length but upheld the conviction. It stated that if disclosure were necessary for a fair trial and the defence handicap was not sufficiently compensated, the prosecution should be declared inadmissible. The applicant alleged that the AIVD had exercised decisive control over the evidence, restricting his and the courts’ access to information, controlling its use, making it impossible to instruct counsel effectively, and preventing him from offering witness evidence, in violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(b), (c), and (d) of the Convention.

**Summary of *Winther v. Denmark* (Application no. 9588/21)**

In *Winther v. Denmark*, the applicant, Mr Martin Treesh Winther, a Syrian national born in 1994, entered Denmark in September 2014 at the age of 20 and applied for asylum. In February 2015, he was granted a time-limited refugee residence permit under section 7(1) of the Danish Aliens Act, valid until February 2020. The application to the European Court of Human Rights was lodged on 28 January 2021, complaining under Article 8 of the Convention about an expulsion order made in criminal proceedings.

By a District Court judgment of 1 March 2019, the applicant was convicted of several offences. The most serious was aggravated assault under Article 245 § 1 of the Danish Penal Code. Together with three co-accused, he had beaten and kicked a man in the head and body with a bat or similar weapon and a bottle, including while the victim was lying prostrate. He was also convicted of blackmail and attempted duress. These three offences were committed on different days in November 2018 and related to debt collection for a third person. He was further convicted of possessing 2.44 grams of cannabis for personal use and 5.94 grams for distribution, and of importing ninety-one forged 100-euro banknotes. He was sentenced to seven months’ imprisonment and ordered expelled with a six-year re-entry ban.

The District Court found that expulsion would not “for certain” be contrary to Denmark’s international obligations. It weighed the serious nature of the offences against the applicant’s residence in Denmark, his Danish girlfriend—who was expecting twins—his attendance at an educational programme, some Danish language ability, and two aunts in Denmark. It also noted that he was born and raised in Syria, had attended school there, spoke and wrote Arabic, and still had ties to Syria.

On appeal, the High Court of Western Denmark upheld the expulsion order on 29 January 2020. The applicant presented new information: his twins had been born in March 2019, one with health problems; he had lived with his family since release and participated in childcare; he had completed ninth grade and found work. His girlfriend and children were Danish nationals, and his girlfriend did not wish to move to Syria. The High Court nonetheless found no reason to alter the outcome.

The Supreme Court, on 14 August 2020, increased the prison sentence to eight months but upheld expulsion and the six-year re-entry ban. It found that expulsion interfered with the applicant’s Article 8 § 1 right to respect for private and family life. Applying the *Maslov v. Austria* criteria, it concluded that his ties to Syria remained strong, while his ties to Denmark were relatively limited apart from his partner and children. Although separation from his Danish partner and young children would be serious, their family life had been relatively short, the children were young, and they could visit or communicate with him. The six-year re-entry ban was limited in time. The Supreme Court held that the societal interest in preventing disorder or crime outweighed the applicant’s private and family life considerations, so expulsion was not disproportionate under Article 8.

After serving his sentence, the applicant was placed in a deportation centre away from his family. In April 2022, the Aliens Appeal Board refused asylum but found that forcible expulsion to Syria could not currently be implemented, leaving him on “tolerated stay.” Later, authorities reported that he failed to comply with obligations and had absconded from the deportation centre in June 2022. In January 2023 he applied for asylum in the Netherlands; Denmark accepted his readmission, but Dutch authorities reported him disappeared in July 2023. He was arrested in Denmark in May 2024.

The alleged violation is that the expulsion order and six-year re-entry ban disproportionately interfered with his right to respect for private and family life under Article 8, particularly his relationship with his Danish partner and young children.

In *Votta Ronza v. Italy* (Application no. 38083/10), the European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Committee, examined an application brought by Anna Votta Ronza, born in 1957, against Italy. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Romano, a lawyer practising in Rome. The Italian Government were given notice of the application. The application was lodged under Article 34 of the Convention on 7 July 2010.

The central alleged violation concerned the non-enforcement of a domestic decision. According to the appended table, the relevant domestic decision was given by the Campania Regional Administrative Court (R.G. 5620/2012) on 28 December 2013. That decision concerned Consorzio AS.CO.S.A. – Associazione Costruttori S. Antimo, and it ordered payment of compensation to the applicant for the unlawful occupation of her land in view of its expropriation. In substance, a domestic administrative court had recognised the applicant’s right to compensation for the occupation of her property in connection with expropriation, but that compensation order allegedly remained unenforced.

The non-enforcement period began on 28 December 2013, the date of the domestic decision. By the time the Court dealt with the case, enforcement was still pending. The length of the enforcement proceedings was recorded as more than ten years, seven months and sixteen days. This prolonged failure to execute the domestic decision formed the factual core of the applicant’s complaint. She complained of the non-enforcement of a domestic decision and also raised other complaints under the Convention. The excerpt does not set out the full merits reasoning, but the principal alleged violation is clearly the continued failure to secure compliance with the administrative court’s compensation order.

The underlying facts therefore involve a land dispute: the applicant’s land was allegedly occupied unlawfully with a view to expropriation, and a domestic court ordered compensation. The subsequent non-enforcement meant that the applicant did not receive the compensation awarded to her for more than a decade. The delay and continuing failure to enforce the decision were the key facts relevant to her application before the European Court. Such non-enforcement complaints ordinarily engage fair-trial and property-protection concerns under the Convention, although the provided extract does not detail the Court’s final findings on those points.

Procedurally, the First Section Committee comprised Krzysztof Wojtyczek (President), Lətif Hüseynov and Erik Wennerström, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The Committee deliberated in private on 17 October 2024 and delivered its judgment on 14 November 2024. The judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision. The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus the existence of the domestic administrative decision ordering compensation for unlawful occupation/expropriation of the applicant’s land; the identity of the debtor, Consorzio AS.CO.S.A.; the start of non-enforcement on 28 December 2013; the fact that enforcement remained pending; and the resulting period of non-enforcement exceeding ten years, seven months and sixteen days.

The case of *Ković and Others v. Serbia* (Applications nos. 39611/08, 50121/13, and 2490/14) concerned complaints under Article 6 § 1 of the European Convention on Human Rights that administrative and civil proceedings in Serbia had exceeded a reasonable time. The applicants were three Serbian nationals: Nikola Ković, Zoran Ranković, and Ivan Bojanić. They lodged their applications with the European Court of Human Rights on 21 July 2008, 5 June 2013, and 16 December 2013, respectively. On 18 December 2014, the Court communicated to the Serbian Government only the complaints concerning the length of administrative and civil proceedings; the remaining complaints were declared inadmissible. The Government initially objected to the case being examined by a Committee, but the Court rejected that objection.

The key facts relating to each applicant’s alleged violation are set out in the appended table. Nikola Ković, born 21 July 1941, had proceedings that began in October and November 2001 and were still pending at the time of the application. Since the Convention entered into force with respect to Serbia on 3 March 2004, the proceedings had lasted 10 years and 8 months at one level of jurisdiction. Zoran Ranković, born 3 September 1954, had proceedings that started on 25 July 2002 and ended on 18 May 2012. Measured from 3 March 2004, they lasted 8 years and 2 months across two levels of jurisdiction. Ivan Bojanić, born 22 April 1978, had proceedings that began on 11 March 2004 and ended on 25 May 2011. Since 3 March 2004, they lasted 7 years and 2 months at two levels of jurisdiction.

All three applicants had previously obtained decisions from the Constitutional Court of Serbia finding a violation of their right to a hearing within a reasonable time. However, the subsequent domestic remedial steps differed. In Ković’s case, under the regulations applicable at the time, the Constitutional Court established his right to seek compensation for non-pecuniary damage before the Commission for Damage Compensation. Ković submitted his compensation request to that Commission on 26 December 2010, but he had not received any response by the time the case was examined. This unresolved compensation request was therefore relevant to whether Serbia had provided effective redress for the excessive length of his proceedings. In contrast, Ranković and Bojanić were awarded certain sums by the Constitutional Court in respect of non-pecuniary damage suffered as a result of the length violations, as recorded in the appendix to the judgment.

The central alleged violation was thus the excessive duration of administrative and civil proceedings, contrary to the right to a fair trial within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1. The facts relevant to that complaint were the dates, duration, and number of judicial levels of each applicant’s domestic proceedings; the fact that the domestic Constitutional Court had already recognized a length violation; and the different forms of compensation or redress subsequently afforded. For Ković, the key additional fact was that his compensation claim before the Commission remained unanswered, while Ranković and Bojanić had received domestic awards for non-pecuniary damage. The Court’s judgment of 4 April 2017 therefore assessed these circumstances against Serbia’s obligations under the Convention.

The case of *Rybářství Třeboň a.s. and Rybářství Třeboň Hld. a.s. v. the Czech Republic* concerns two applications lodged in 2019 and 2022. The applicant companies complain under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that two privatisations of fishponds and land were annulled without compensation after about 26 and 25 years.

The land, situated in Novosedly nad Nežárkou and Lutová (232,312 m²), originally belonged to the Roman Catholic Parishes of Novosedly and Lutová. In 1949, those parishes were deprived of the land without compensation by the Třeboň District National Committee. It was later managed by the State-owned enterprise *Státní rybářství Třeboň*. In 1992, under the Privatisation Act, the State enterprise was privatised. However, the Act contained a blocking provision: property transferred to the State after 25 February 1948 from churches, religious orders or communities could not be privatised. Despite this, the land was included in the privatisation project approved by the Ministry for Administration and Privatisation of National Property and transferred to the newly created second applicant company as part of its registered capital. The transfer record was signed by J.H., then director of the State enterprise, who also signed for the National Property Fund and for the second applicant company, preventing independent verification. In 2007, the second applicant was split and the Novosedly land passed to the first applicant.

A 1994 Supreme Audit Office audit found that the privatisation had unlawfully included property the State enterprise did not have the right to manage or that should have been subject to restitution. It estimated at least CZK 349,715,895 (about EUR 13.9 million) of State property was unlawfully transferred. The audit noted that J.H. knew some property had been church property before 1950.

In 2013, the Church Property Settlement Act entered into force. It allowed churches to seek restitution and to bring declaratory actions claiming State ownership where property had been transferred to private persons in breach of the blocking provision. In 2015, the Novosedly and Lutová Parishes sued the State and the applicant companies. The domestic courts declared the privatisations void *ab initio* for breach of the blocking provision. They rejected the applicants’ good-faith defence: the privatisation project identified the land as former church property; management knew this; and the 1994 audit should have raised grave doubts. The Supreme Court and Constitutional Court upheld those rulings, stressing that restitution claims were overriding and that no truly exceptional circumstances justified protecting the applicants. The Constitutional Court acknowledged State inertia but held it could not be remedied at the expense of the restitution claimants. The State was later ordered to surrender the land to the parishes or their successor.

The applicants allege that the annulment of their ownership without compensation violated their property rights and their right to a fair trial. They also argue that they had no effective remedy against the State due to limitation periods and that the domestic courts failed to properly balance their interests against the parishes’ restitution claims.

The case, *J. Paul Getty Trust and Others v. Italy* (Application no. 35271/19), concerns an Italian confiscation order over the “Victorious Youth,” an ancient Greek bronze statue in the possession of the J. Paul Getty Trust. The applicants—the Getty Trust and fourteen American trustees—allege that the confiscation violates their right to peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the European Convention on Human Rights, particularly because Italy is seeking recognition and enforcement of the order in the United States, where the statue remains displayed at the Getty Villa in Malibu.

The key facts are as follows. In 1964 Italian fishermen discovered the bronze in the Adriatic Sea off Pedaso and brought it to Fano. It was later sold and disappeared until 1973, when it reappeared in Munich in the hands of a German art dealer acting for a Liechtenstein company. Italian criminal proceedings in the 1960s over receiving stolen goods ended in acquittal in 1970 because it could not be proved that the statue had been found in Italian territorial waters or that the defendants knew of any unlawful origin. Italian investigations into unlawful export were later discontinued, partly due to lack of evidence and statute-barring.

Between 1972 and 1977, the Getty Trust negotiated to purchase the statue. Getty representatives knew of “possible legal complications” and Italian claims but relied on legal opinions and assurances from the vendor’s Italian lawyers that title was clear and Italy had no valid claim. The Trust bought the statue in July 1977 for USD 3,950,000. It was exported without an Italian export licence or payment of customs duties and entered the United States in 1977. Italian authorities made various diplomatic and administrative attempts to recover it, but the Trust refused to return it.

In 2007, Italian prosecutors charged several individuals with unlawful export. The proceedings were discontinued as time-barred, but the prosecutor sought confiscation of the statue. Initially, the preliminary investigations judge refused confiscation because the Trust was not involved in the offence and good faith could not be excluded. However, in subsequent enforcement proceedings, the judge ordered confiscation “wherever located” in 2010, finding the Trust at least negligent in purchasing the statue. After procedural challenges, the order was upheld by the Pesaro judge in 2018 and finally by the Court of Cassation in January 2019.

The Court of Cassation held that confiscation under Italian cultural heritage law is not a penalty but primarily serves a recovery purpose and can be imposed on persons not criminally involved if they negligently or knowingly benefited from the unlawful export. It found the Trust negligent because Getty Senior had doubts, the Trust relied only on the vendor’s lawyers, and it failed to verify compliance with Italian export law with Italian authorities. It also held that Italy had ownership or a sufficient cultural link to the statue, including because it was found by an Italian-flagged vessel and exported without licence or customs duties.

The applicants complain that this confiscation order unlawfully deprives them of their property and creates a real risk of loss of the statue if enforced in the US. The Italian authorities sent a mutual legal assistance request to the US in July 2019 seeking recognition and enforcement; that proceeding remains pending.

The case of Szustak and Others v. Poland concerns four applications lodged against Poland under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The applications were considered by the First Section of the European Court of Human Rights, sitting as a Committee composed of Péter Paczolay, Gilberto Felici, and Raffaele Sabato, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar. The judgment was adopted on 18 January 2024 and delivered on 8 February 2024. The Polish Government were given notice of the applications.

The applicants complained of the excessive length of civil proceedings and of the lack of any effective remedy in domestic law. The appended table sets out the key facts relevant to these alleged violations. Each applicant had been involved in civil proceedings in Poland that remained pending at the time of the application, and each had attempted to use the domestic complaint mechanism under the 2004 Act concerning unreasonable delays in judicial proceedings.

In application no. 52773/22, Łukasz Tomasz Szustak, born in 1982, lodged his application on 24 October 2022. His civil proceedings began on 27 February 2018 and were still pending. They had lasted more than 5 years, 9 months and 8 days at one level of jurisdiction. He filed a domestic complaint under the 2004 Act, and on 1 July 2022 the Warsaw Regional Court, in case no. V S 209/22, awarded him PLN 3,500.

In application no. 56294/22, Jarosław Świątek, born in 1965, introduced his application on 16 November 2022. His civil proceedings started on 3 August 2017 and were still pending. They had lasted more than 6 years, 4 months and 2 days at one level of jurisdiction. He also made a complaint under the 2004 Act, which was decided by the Warsaw Court of Appeal on 4 June 2020 in case no. III S 86/20. No monetary award is indicated in the appended table.

In application no. 1349/23, Paweł Zakrzewski, born in 2005, and Piotr Zakrzewski, born in 2004, lodged their application on 9 December 2022. They were represented by Tomasz Andrzej Muszyński. Their civil proceedings began on 14 November 2005 and were still pending. They had lasted more than 18 years and 21 days across two levels of jurisdiction. Their domestic complaint under the 2004 Act was decided by the Warsaw Court of Appeal on 31 August 2022 in case no. I S 238/22, which awarded PLN 8,500 to each applicant.

In application no. 4304/23, Małgorzata Kolasa, born in 1967, introduced her application on 13 January 2023. She was represented by Karol Konsek. Her civil proceedings started on 28 January 2011 and were still pending. They had lasted more than 12 years, 10 months and 7 days across three levels of jurisdiction. She filed several domestic complaints under the 2004 Act. The Katowice Court of Appeal decided them on 22 August 2016 in case no. V S 26/16, on 10 September 2019 in case no. V S 36/19 awarding PLN 2,000, and on 28 October 2022 in case no. V S 53/22.

These facts form the basis of the applicants’ complaints. Despite the availability of the 2004 Act remedy and, in some instances, domestic awards, the civil proceedings remained pending for lengthy periods. The applicants therefore alleged that the duration of the proceedings exceeded the reasonable-time requirement and that the domestic remedy was not effective. The Court was required to assess whether the proceedings were excessively long and whether Polish law provided an effective remedy for such delays.

**Case: Tsyoge Fon Manteyfel v. Ukraine (Application no. 29804/16), ECtHR Fifth Section, Judgment of 11 January 2024**

The applicant, Ms Karina Volodymyrivna Tsyoge fon Manteyfel, is a Russian national born in 1978 and living in Elektrostal. She lodged her application against Ukraine on 19 May 2016 under Article 34 of the Convention, represented by Ukrainian lawyers. The Ukrainian Government was represented by its acting Agent. The Russian Government declined to intervene.

The case concerns the applicant’s compulsory psychiatric treatment following a court order made in criminal proceedings in which she was charged with murder. The applicant suffers from paranoid schizophrenia. She was detained in various psychiatric hospitals under different supervision regimes from 23 August 2010 to 14 November 2017. During that period, courts periodically reviewed her detention on the basis of submissions from the hospitals and extended her compulsory inpatient treatment.

The most relevant order for the alleged violations was issued by the Samarskyy District Court of Dnipropetrovsk on 19 August 2016. According to the applicant, that order expired on 19 February 2017, because the Psychiatric Assistance Act required reviews of such orders at least every six months. After that date, she remained in compulsory inpatient treatment without any further court decision extending her detention. The Dnipro Psychiatric Hospital lodged requests on 13 January and 19 May 2017 for her continued compulsory inpatient treatment, but the courts dismissed those requests on 13 May and 2 November 2017 respectively. The courts instead ordered that she be treated as an outpatient, and she was discharged from hospital on 14 November 2017.

A central issue was the applicant’s inability to challenge her continued detention. The courts did not examine her subsequent appeals against the detention orders or her requests for release because, under the relevant domestic law, she lacked locus standi to lodge an appeal or initiate a review of the lawfulness of her continued detention. Requests for her immediate release lodged by her mother and her lawyer after 19 February 2017 were dismissed by the hospital on the ground that no court decision had ordered her release.

In August 2017, the applicant brought a civil claim against the hospital. By a final judgment of 19 June 2019, the Supreme Court partly allowed the claim. It declared that her continued detention after 19 February 2017—after the expiry of the six-month period from the 19 August 2016 court decision and in the absence of any further decision extending her detention—had no basis in law. The Supreme Court specifically noted that the Psychiatric Assistance Act’s requirement that compulsory medical measures be extended each time for a period not exceeding six months was a guarantee against unlawful detention. It remitted the case to the Dnipropetrovsk Court of Appeal to determine compensation.

In January 2021, the Court of Appeal awarded the applicant 30,000 Ukrainian hryvnias for non-pecuniary damage. That judgment was not appealed and became final. However, the award remains unpaid to the applicant.

The applicant’s complaints under Article 5 of the Convention concerned the lawfulness of her compulsory psychiatric detention, particularly after 19 February 2017, and the lack of effective judicial review or ability to challenge her continued confinement. The application also invoked Articles 34 and 38. The domestic courts’ findings—especially the Supreme Court’s recognition that her post-19 February 2017 detention had no legal basis—are key facts supporting the alleged Article 5 violations concerning unlawful detention and inadequate review.

In A.P. v. Armenia, the applicant, A.P., is an Armenian national born in 1997 who has a mild intellectual disability. At the time of the events she was a 14-year-old ninth-grade pupil at her local State school. A.G., a married 49-year-old man, was both the administrative head of her village and her sports teacher. The case concerns her alleged sexual abuse by A.G., the publication of her identity in an online judicial database, and the absence of any effective possibility to obtain compensation from the State for the ill-treatment she suffered.

The alleged abuse occurred between late November 2011 and February 2012. According to the investigation, A.G. used his authority as village head and teacher to isolate A.P. and sexually abuse her. The first incident allegedly took place in the village administrative office building, where he threatened to kill her if she made noise and raped her. Further incidents allegedly occurred in January and early February 2012 in an empty classroom during sports lessons. On 22 February 2012, he called A.P. into a classroom, touched her intimate body parts, and stopped only when he noticed someone watching through a hole in the door. A.P. was a vulnerable child with limited intellectual capabilities; a forensic psychiatric and psychological examination later found that she understood only the superficial side of what had happened, not the nature and meaning of the acts.

On 23 February 2012, A.P.’s mother reported the abuse to the police. A key witness, N.M., a twelfth-grade pupil, testified that A.G. had a reputation as a “skirt-chaser.” On 22 February, N.M. saw through the door hole that A.G. was pulling A.P. towards himself and touching her bottom while A.P. resisted. N.M. urgently sought help from several teachers, including A.S., N.G. and H.B., and from the headmistress, but they refused or failed to intervene. A.P. was later seen in a distressed and weak condition. This failure by school staff is central to the Article 3 complaint that the State did not protect a disabled minor from sexual abuse by a public official and teacher.

A.G. was charged with aggravated rape and indecent acts. In February 2013, the Regional Court convicted him of rape of a minor and indecent acts, sentencing him to eight years’ imprisonment. That judgment was upheld on appeal and by the Court of Cassation.

The applicant’s Article 13 complaint concerns her inability to obtain compensation from the State. In February 2014, she lodged a civil claim against the State for non-pecuniary damage, arguing that Armenia had failed to create effective protective mechanisms for children, especially disabled children, in State schools. The District Court rejected the claim for procedural deficiencies. The Civil Court of Appeal held that Armenian law did not provide for compensation for non-pecuniary damage and that the claim should not have been admitted. The Court of Cassation declared her appeal inadmissible.

The Article 8 complaint concerns publication. In her civil claim, A.P. requested closed proceedings and that her name not be published in Datalex, the official online judicial database, because she was a minor victim of a sexual crime. Nevertheless, after the Court of Appeal’s decision, her full name, address and the decisions concerning her damages claim were published on Datalex. Details of the criminal case were not published. She complained that this disclosure violated her right to respect for private life.

The applicant lodged her application with the European Court of Human Rights on 19 August 2014. The Court gave notice to the Armenian Government of complaints under Articles 3, 8 and 13 of the Convention.

**Case: Lypovchenko and Halabudenco v. the Republic of Moldova and Russia**  
**Applications nos. 40926/16 and 73942/17 – ECtHR judgment of 20 February 2024**

The case concerns alleged human-rights violations in the self-proclaimed “Moldovan Republic of Transnistria” (“MRT”), a separatist administration on Moldova’s territory. The applicants were Oleksandr Lypovchenko, a Ukrainian national, and Oleg Halabudenco, a Moldovan national. Both complained against Moldova and Russia.

**Mr Lypovchenko’s case (no. 40926/16)**  
On 7 July 2015, the de facto “MRT authorities” arrested Lypovchenko and charged him with extremism for allegedly critical social-media posts and an old diary note stating that “Transnistria can be ruled only if the UN forces are introduced”. He was detained from 9 July 2015 to 28 March 2016. During proceedings, the “MRT court” refused to let him choose his own lawyer or represent himself, relying on an alleged schizophrenia diagnosis. In January 2016 he was removed from the courtroom until sentencing. On 28 March 2016 he was convicted and sentenced to three years and six months’ imprisonment in a semi-open prison; the sentence was upheld on 10 May 2016.

He alleged overcrowded detention, passive smoking, limited outdoor access, unfit food and water, and only weekly showers. In August 2016 he was transferred to a closed-regime prison for alleged disciplinary breaches. He went on hunger strike several times and was forcibly hospitalised and subjected to psychiatric assessment and psychotropic medication without consent in 2015 and 2016. He alleged inadequate medical care for hepatitis C, thrombophlebitis, dermatitis, varicose veins and other conditions, and was refused external consultations. He also alleged ill-treatment in April 2016 after hunger strikes and refusal to hand over a copy of his sentence to his mother. The “MRT militia” refused to investigate and confirmed that prisoners could not give documents to visitors. Requests for his medical file were refused. Moldova opened a criminal investigation into his kidnapping and the usurpation of official powers by “MRT officials”; the Moldovan Supreme Court later quashed the “MRT” judgments. He relied on Articles 3, 5, 6, 13 and 34 of the Convention.

**Mr Halabudenco’s case (no. 73942/17)**  
From 2014 to 2016, Halabudenco was a part-time lecturer at a university in Tiraspol. On 2 April 2016, the “MRT authorities” apprehended and remanded him on bribery charges. On 5 April 2016, the “Tiraspol City Court” set bail at 18,400 Transnistrian roubles (about EUR 1,400), which he posted, and he was released. He then left Transnistria and lived in Chișinău. In December 2016 the case was sent to the “MRT court”. On 1 February 2017, he asked to be tried in absentia. On 17 March 2017, the “MRT court” rescinded his bail, ordered his preventive arrest, issued a search-and-arrest order, and suspended proceedings. On 4 April 2017, the “MRT Supreme Court” confirmed that decision and ordered the bail forfeited to the “MRT treasury”. He complained that this interfered with his professional activities, deprived him of his bail money, restricted his freedom of movement, and left him without effective remedies. He relied on Articles 8 and 13, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4.

Both applicants complained to Moldovan and Russian authorities. Moldova initiated investigations but they were suspended; Russia generally denied jurisdiction or breach. The case therefore concerns alleged unlawful arrest and conviction, unfair proceedings, ill-treatment and detention conditions, forced psychiatric treatment, inadequate medical care, obstruction of communication with the Court, bail forfeiture, movement restrictions, and lack of effective remedies.

In *Kotsev and Ermenkova v. Bulgaria*, App. No. 33864/03, judgment of 10 May 2012, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints about the excessive length of two sets of judicial-review proceedings in Bulgaria and the lack of an effective remedy. The applicants, Mr Valentin Kotsev and Ms Yarmila Ermenkova, were co-owners, together with B.I. and his parents, of a building and plot in Sofia. In 1992 B.I. acquired one quarter of the property, and in 1993 he began constructing an adjoining building. The authorities repeatedly ordered the construction halted or demolished, but B.I. challenged those orders, producing lengthy litigation.

In the 1996 proceedings, the mayor ordered demolition on 21 March 1996 because the building could not be legalised. B.I. sought judicial review. In March 1999 the applicants joined as interested parties. At least fifteen hearings were held between June 1999 and October 2007, at intervals of four to eight months. Five hearings failed because parties were not duly summoned. At least six hearings between January 2005 and October 2007 were adjourned to summon a newly added party in Toronto by letter rogatory. The Sofia City Court gave judgment in 2010, and by October 2010 the case was pending on appeal. Thus, for the applicants, the proceedings had lasted over eleven years.

In the 1999 proceedings, on 16 June 1999 building control ordered B.I. to demolish the building after the applicants alerted the authorities. B.I. and his wife sought judicial review. At the first hearing on 26 November 1999, the applicants intervened. About twenty hearings were held until February 2006, at intervals of two to nine months. At least four hearings were adjourned because parties, including B.I.’s brother in Canada, were not properly summoned. After the brother died in 2002, at least six hearings were adjourned because his widow in Canada could not be summoned by letter rogatory. By October 2010 the proceedings were still pending before the Sofia City Court, nearly eleven years after the applicants joined.

The applicants complained about delays on 23 November 2000, 18 December 2002, and again in 2007, to the Sofia City Court and the Supreme Judicial Council. In 2007 the Ministry of Justice replied that no delays were attributable to the authorities. In 2002, however, the Ministry had informed local authorities that an inspection by the Supreme Judicial Council Inspectorate established that delay had occurred, caused by B.I.’s abuse of process and the Sofia City Court’s high caseload; the Inspectorate wrote to the court chairman.

The key alleged violations were under Article 6 §1 of the Convention—the right to a hearing within a reasonable time—and Article 13—the lack of an effective domestic remedy for the delay. The relevant facts were the very long intervals between hearings, repeated failures to summon parties, protracted efforts to serve parties in Canada by letters rogatory, admitted delay and caseload problems, and the applicants’ unsuccessful complaints. The Court found Bulgaria responsible for excessive length and an ineffective remedy.

**Case Name:** CASE OF TAGANOVA AND OTHERS v. GEORGIA AND RUSSIA

**Summary:**

The case of *Taganova and Others v. Georgia and Russia* (Applications nos. 18102/04 and 4 others) was brought before the European Court of Human Rights by six applicants, all of whom were forced to leave their homes in Abkhazia, Georgia, following the 1992-1993 armed conflict. The applicants, comprising both Russian and Georgian nationals, alleged violations of Articles 3, 8, 13, and 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights, as well as Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, primarily concerning their inability to peacefully enjoy their homes and movable property and their lack of access to a court to remedy this situation.

The applicants fell into two groups: the Taganovas, a mixed-ethnicity couple who remained in Abkhazia, and the other applicants, ethnic Georgians who fled to Tbilisi and were granted Internally Displaced Person (IDP) status. All applicants owned property in Abkhazia—houses in Gagra, Sukhumi, and Gulripshi—which they lost during or after the conflict. The Taganovas’ homes were seized by Abkhaz fighters, and their attempts to reclaim them through the de facto Abkhaz authorities were repeatedly frustrated; one court order in their favor was quashed, and subsequent proceedings were dismissed on procedural grounds, including a demand for unaffordable state taxes and legal fees. While their house was briefly returned in 2006, it was uninhabitable, and its ownership was again challenged.

The other applicants, whose homes were occupied by ethnic Abkhaz and other families, faced similar barriers. Their efforts to secure their property rights through the de facto Abkhaz judicial system were futile. When they turned to the Georgian authorities, their applications for property registration were rejected. The National Public Registry Agency (NPRA) stated it could not register properties in Abkhazia because the region was outside Georgia’s control. Similarly, the Sukhumi District and City Court exiled in Tbilisi declared their claims inadmissible, citing its inability to exercise jurisdiction in Abkhazia or to identify the current occupants of the properties. The High Court of the Autonomous Republic of Abkhazia upheld this decision, confirming that the situation did not invalidate their property rights but that it could not confirm them in non-contentious proceedings.

The applicants also appealed to the Russian authorities, given Russia’s significant influence in the region. The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs acknowledged the complexity of their situation, citing Abkhaz laws that confiscated "abandoned" property. A joint Russian-Abkhaz Property Commission was established in 2010, but its efficacy was disputed. The Georgian Government alleged it discriminated against ethnic Georgians. For most applicants, these efforts yielded no practical result.

In summary, the key facts revolve around the applicants’ permanent loss of their homes and possessions in Abkhazia due to the conflict and subsequent appropriation, followed by a persistent and systemic denial of any effective legal remedy. The de facto Abkhaz courts erected procedural and financial barriers, while the Georgian courts refused to act due to a lack of territorial jurisdiction. This combination of circumstances formed the basis for the applicants’ complaints that their rights to property, private life, and an effective remedy were violated by both respondent States.

Zdjelar and Others v. Croatia (Application no. 80960/12) concerned nine Croatian nationals, all children of Milan Zdjelar, who died on 8 August 1995 in Crni Potok, shortly after Croatia’s Operation Storm. The applicants alleged that Croatia failed its procedural obligations under Articles 2 and 14 of the Convention and that they had no effective remedy under Article 13.

During 1991–92, Serbian paramilitary forces controlled part of Croatia, including the so-called Krajina. Operation Storm, from 4 to 7 August 1995, aimed to regain that territory; between 100,000 and 150,000 people fled. Milan Zdjelar, a Serbian civilian, remained in Crni Potok with his daughter Dragica, the third applicant. According to Dragica, on 8 August 1995 they were in front of their house when a military transport vehicle stopped. Three soldiers in camouflage approached. Milan ran; Dragica heard three gunshots and saw him shot in the chest and leg. He died soon afterwards. She hid in the woods for two days. Croatian soldiers later buried her father.

In 2001, a person named S.K. submitted a list to the State Attorney’s Office stating that Milan Zdjelar had been shot in the head and leg by members of the Croatian Army’s “Tigers” brigade. Police photographed the grave and interviewed Dragica. In 2002, the body was exhumed; a post-mortem failed to establish the cause of death and noted only a broken collarbone. In 2004, police reported to the Sisak County State Attorney that Dragica alleged Croatian soldiers from the “Tigers” brigade had killed her father. In 2005, the family lodged a criminal complaint, classifying the killing as a war crime against a civilian and alleging that Milan was Serbian, unarmed, and not involved in military activity.

The investigation then stalled. Between 2005 and 2011, the State Attorney’s Office repeatedly asked police for progress; each time police reported none. The Military Police had no relevant information. In 2009, Dragica gave evidence before an investigating judge. Neighbours were interviewed; one confirmed Croatian Army soldiers had come to the village. The Ministry of Defence provided information about members of the 153rd Brigade and about soldiers who had buried Milan. Several former Croatian soldiers, including members of the “Tigers,” were interviewed and denied knowledge of civilian killings.

In 2012, Ž.L., a former member of the “Tigers” brigade, alleged that he had seen an elderly man shot in Crni Potok and that the killing had been tolerated by the Third Battalion command. He described a logistics officer bringing in a civilian called a “četnik,” commanders taking him away, and later finding an elderly man with gunshot wounds to the back and head; one soldier allegedly said he had shot him in the head to “shorten his pain.” However, in 2014 Ž.L. refused to testify, denied witnessing any crimes, and stated that his earlier allegations had been unfounded. In 2015, the investigation was reassigned to the Osijek County State Attorney’s Office. Further requests and interviews followed in 2016–17, but some witnesses had died and former soldiers continued to deny involvement. No prosecution appears to have resulted.

Separately, in 2004 the applicants sought civil compensation from the State. The claim was dismissed in 2005 as time-barred; appeals were rejected in 2009 and 2011, and a constitutional complaint was dismissed in 2012.

These facts were central to the alleged violations: whether Croatia conducted an effective investigation into the killing of a Serbian civilian by alleged state agents, whether ethnic bias affected the investigation under Article 14, and whether the time-barred civil proceedings and ineffective criminal investigation left the applicants without an effective remedy under Article 13.

text:
In *Spahiu and Others v. Albania* (Application nos. 79452/17, 39155/18 and 2248/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Third Section, sitting as a Committee) delivered a judgment on 18 July 2024. The applications were lodged against Albania under Article 34 of the Convention on 10 November 2017, 9 August 2018, and 3 January 2019 respectively. The Albanian Government was notified. The applicants complained of non-enforcement or delayed enforcement of domestic decisions. The applicants in applications nos. 79452/17 and 39155/18 also raised other complaints under the Convention.

The relevant facts, set out in the appended table, concern three administrative proceedings.

The first applicant, Sadik Spahiu (born 1979), represented by Sheta Xhevdet, Tirana, introduced application no. 79452/17 on 10 November 2017. The relevant domestic decision was given by the Tirana Administrative Court of Appeal on 25 March 2014 (decision no. 1200). It ordered the nullification of the General Directorate of Taxation’s decision transferring him to another position and city. The non-enforcement period began on 29 July 2014 and ended on 9 February 2018, lasting 3 years, 6 months and 12 days.

The second applicant, Marjeta Armiri (born 1957), introduced application no. 39155/18 on 9 August 2018. The relevant domestic decision was issued by the Tirana Administrative Court of First Instance on 30 March 2015 (decision no. 1696). It ordered the Central Technical Inspectorate to reinstate her to her previous post and to pay salary arrears from the moment of dismissal until her reinstatement. The decision was not enforced from 12 April 2017 to 18 December 2018, a delay of 1 year, 8 months and 7 days.

The third applicant, Valbona Shegani-Vocaj (born 1977), represented by Mujo-Bodo Vjosa, Tirana, introduced application no. 2248/19 on 3 January 2019. The relevant domestic decision was given by the Tirana Administrative Court of First Instance on 28 April 2014 and amended by the Administrative Court of Appeal on 21 September 2015. It ordered the Public Administration Department to reinstate her to her previous post and to pay salary arrears from the dismissal date until reinstatement. Following the amendment, reinstatement to a similar position was permitted if the previous post was unavailable. Enforcement was delayed from 11 July 2017 to 2 June 2022, a period of 4 years, 10 months and 23 days.

The factual core of the alleged violations is that each applicant obtained a final, binding domestic administrative decision in their favour—principally requiring reinstatement and payment of salary arrears—but the Albanian authorities failed to enforce it promptly, or enforced it only after substantial delay. The delays ranged from just over one year and eight months to almost five years. The applicants alleged that this non-enforcement or delayed enforcement breached their Convention rights, particularly the right to a fair trial and/or the right to the peaceful enjoyment of possessions. The Court considered the applications together. Although the applicants in the first two cases also raised other complaints, the key facts relevant to the alleged violations concern the prolonged failure to execute the domestic decisions in their favour.

The case of Solomakhin v. Ukraine (Application no. 24429/03) concerned a Ukrainian national, Mr Sergey Dmitriyevich Solomakhin, who alleged violations under Articles 6 and 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Specifically, he complained that domestic court proceedings were excessively lengthy and that his health had suffered as a result of medical malpractice, particularly an allegedly unlawful diphtheria vaccination. The application was lodged on 22 July 2003. After the applicant died in September 2010, his mother, Mrs Vera Petrovna Solomakhina, expressed her wish to continue the case.

The key facts arose in late 1998. On 23 November 1998, the applicant sought medical assistance at Donetsk City Hospital No. 16 and was diagnosed with an acute respiratory disease. He received out-patient treatment. On 27 November 1998, he was tested for his reaction to a diphtheria vaccination. On 28 November 1998, he was vaccinated against diphtheria. The applicant claimed the vaccination was contraindicated for him and that he had consistently objected to it. On 30 November 1998, a doctor noted improvement and diagnosed tracheobronchitis, which was confirmed during visits on 3, 4 and 7 December 1998. From 28 December 1998, the applicant spent more than six months in various medical institutions receiving treatment for chronic conditions including pancreatitis, cholecystitis, hepatitis and colitis.

A significant fact supporting the applicant’s allegations was that on 4 February 1999, the Hospital’s Chief Doctor reprimanded doctor Ya. and nurse Sh. for vaccinating the applicant although he had objected and was being treated for an acute respiratory infection. The Chief Doctor found that they had violated vaccination rules and ordered them to take a test on those rules.

On 26 April 1999, the applicant sued the local public health department and the Hospital in the Budyonnovskiy District Court, seeking compensation for damage to his health. He alleged that the vaccination, administered while he was ill, had caused chronic diseases; that the vaccine was uncertified, expired and improperly stored; and that doctors had tried to falsify medical records and conceal negative effects. Between 2000 and 2003, several medical expert examinations were conducted.

On 2 June 2003, the District Court dismissed the claim. Relying on expert conclusions, it found no causal link between the vaccination and the applicant’s diseases. The only condition possibly associated was urticaria, which appeared more than eight months later and was not linked. It found no acute symptoms at vaccination and no violation of medical rules. It noted the regional diphtheria epidemic required vaccination, that no physical force was used, and that as a sound-minded adult he could have refused, as he had before. The court accepted the vaccination occurred in a doctor’s office rather than the vaccination room, but found it was performed by a qualified nurse in a doctor’s presence after prior testing, with no negative side-effects. It rejected vaccine-quality and falsification allegations as unsubstantiated. The Donetsk Regional Court of Appeal upheld the judgment on 19 March 2008, and the Supreme Court did so on 22 August 2008.

In *Oghlishvili v. Georgia*, the European Court of Human Rights examined complaints by Nana Oghlishvili under Articles 2, 3 and 13 that Georgia failed to protect her daughter E.N. from domestic violence and to investigate her death effectively. E.N. had lived since 2013 with her husband R.G., their daughter and mother-in-law T.G. in Shilda. The marriage became strained after T.G. accused E.N. of infidelity because she worked late. On 12 October 2017 the applicant called police, reporting physical assault by T.G. and R.G. Officers interviewed the family. E.N. said T.G. punched her during an argument and asked police to take restraining measures against T.G. She stated R.G. had never abused her and had been named only because she was in emotional distress. T.G. and R.G. denied abuse, claiming E.N. had stayed out overnight and had hit T.G. A medical exam found a minor bruise on E.N.’s shoulder; T.G. had no visible injuries. No protective measures appear to have been taken.

On 18 October 2017 E.N. was found hanged in the family wine cellar by G.G., R.G.’s brother. Police opened an investigation into incitement to suicide under Article 115. Investigators examined the scene, conducted forensic and autopsy exams, questioned over 25 witnesses, and retrieved phone data. The autopsy found extensive bruises and skin lesions on E.N.’s face, throat, knees, thighs, abdomen, hips, buttocks, vulva and legs. Some injuries were six to seven days old; most were inflicted shortly before death. The cause of death was asphyxia from strangulation. No semen was found on the body, but semen-stained trousers found in the cellar belonged to an unidentified man not matching G.G. or two neighbours. E.N.’s black bra had been cut with a sharp object. Blue cotton fibres under E.N.’s fingernails, on her wrists and on her clothes matched G.G.’s denim trousers worn around 11–12 October. G.G. attempted suicide at E.N.’s funeral, and R.G. publicly accused G.G. of raping and murdering E.N. Witnesses described frequent altercations between E.N. and T.G.; some said G.G. visited E.N. late in the evening when R.G. was away, and a neighbour saw G.G. near the house early on 18 October. Family members claimed E.N. had previously attempted suicide in August 2017 and was emotionally unstable.

The applicant was granted victim status in December 2017 and later obtained access to case materials. By April 2022, the investigation remained ongoing under the less serious offence of incitement to suicide, but no significant investigative measures had been taken since February 2019. The key alleged violations were that the State knew of domestic violence but failed to protect E.N., and that the investigation into her death was ineffective, delayed and failed to address evidence of possible domestic violence or third-party involvement.

In *Shylina v. Ukraine* (Application no. 2412/19), the European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section) delivered judgment on 15 February 2024. The applicant, Ms Elvira Shylina, a Ukrainian national living in Rivne, complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, alone and together with Article 14, that the suspension of her social allowance was discriminatory and interfered with her right to peaceful enjoyment of her possessions.

The case arose after Russia occupied Crimea and armed hostilities occurred in parts of Donetsk and Luhansk. Many residents moved to Government-controlled territory and acquired internally displaced person (“IDP”) status. Ukrainian law entitled IDPs to the same social benefits as other citizens and to certain special benefits, including a monthly targeted allowance under Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 505 to cover living expenses, housing and municipal services. However, from 1 July 2016, amendments to Resolution No. 637 required social benefits for IDPs to be paid solely through accounts at Oshchadbank, the State Savings Bank, with periodic physical identification at the bank. Failure to comply allowed the bank to suspend transactions and inform social security authorities.

The applicant left Crimea in November 2014 and registered as an IDP in Rivne. As her family’s representative, she had received the monthly allowance into an account with a private bank, bank R. In April 2016, payment was suspended because the authorities had no information that she had opened an Oshchadbank account. The Department of Labour and Social Protection told her it would not pay the allowance into any other bank. She challenged that suspension and the domestic courts granted her claim for April to June 2016, finding no legal basis for suspension; she received 2,400 Ukrainian hryvnas per month.

From July 2016, however, the allowance was again suspended under Resolution No. 637, as amended, because she refused to open an Oshchadbank account. In July 2016 she challenged the relevant provisions before the administrative courts. She alleged that the requirement was discriminatory and incompatible with higher-ranking legislation, relying on the Law on Ensuring the Rights and Freedoms of Internally Displaced Persons, the Anti-Discrimination Law, and the Court’s discrimination case-law. She argued that non-IDP benefit recipients did not have to open an Oshchadbank account, while IDPs did, and that IDPs who already had such accounts were treated differently from those who did not.

The domestic courts dismissed her claims. The Kyiv Circuit Administrative Court found that the Cabinet of Ministers acted within its competence and that the measure merely established practical payment arrangements. The Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal upheld that judgment, stating that the measure safeguarded payments to socially vulnerable IDPs, prevented fraud and unlawful actions, and prevented terrorist financing. It noted that IDPs could withdraw or deposit money elsewhere, and that a September 2017 amendment allowed transactions through any bank, although payments still had to be made via Oshchadbank. The Supreme Court upheld the lower courts in September 2018, finding no discrimination and describing the measures as special protection for IDPs.

Meanwhile, in November 2017, the applicant closed her allowance file because she was unemployed and no longer entitled. She had still not received payments for July 2016 to November 2017 because she refused to open an Oshchadbank account. Payments later resumed when her husband opened such an account.

The key alleged violation was that the by-law requiring IDPs to receive benefits through a designated State bank, and the resulting suspension of her allowance, interfered with her possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. She also alleged that this requirement amounted to discrimination under Article 14 taken with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, both compared with other benefit recipients and among IDPs. The Article 6 complaint was declared inadmissible.

Case of Mirzoyan v. the Czech Republic concerns a Russian national, Artur Mirzoyan, who had lived in the Czech Republic since 2006 and held a long-term residence permit for business purposes. He lived there with his Armenian wife and four Russian-national children. His wife and three younger children had permanent residence in the Czech Republic from 2013; one daughter acquired Czech citizenship in 2020.

In June 2011 the applicant applied to extend his long-term business residence permit. The Ministry of Interior repeatedly rejected his application on the ground that his residence was not in the interests of the Czech Republic, relying on classified information from police and organised-crime units alleging that he posed a threat to national security and public order. The decisions were annulled several times by the Regional Court and the Supreme Administrative Court because the classified information was not sufficiently specific, credible or verifiable, and did not show concrete criminal or subversive activity by the applicant. A fifth decision in 2018 again rejected the application, relying on several classified reports; some were made accessible to the applicant’s lawyer, but others were withheld because they described operational police activities. The Ministry asserted that the applicant’s long-term contacts with a criminal community created a serious security risk, and that it was irrelevant that he had no criminal record or prosecution.

In 2020 the administrative courts ultimately upheld the refusal. The Supreme Administrative Court found the classified material sufficient and credible, describing it as a long-term mosaic of contacts with criminal circles. The Regional Court rejected the applicant’s family-life arguments, holding that his children’s long residence was not exceptional, that his family could remain in the Czech Republic and was financially independent, and that no exceptional circumstances required hearing his wife. The Supreme Administrative Court placed the burden on the applicant to raise and prove proportionality factors; the Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint, finding that the children’s interests had been considered and that procedural limits on the applicant were counterbalanced by judicial review.

Separately, in 2014 the applicant applied for a long-term residence permit for family purposes based on his wife’s permanent residence. This was rejected in 2018 under the Aliens Act on the ground that there was a reasonable risk he could seriously disrupt public order, relying on the same classified information. The Ministry found the public interest outweighed family life, noting that the family could live in Russia and that his wife could support them. The administrative courts upheld the refusal, emphasising the applicant’s failure to provide specific evidence about his role in the family or the children’s best interests; the Supreme Administrative Court treated the case as one affecting the child only factually, so authorities were not required to investigate further. The Constitutional Court dismissed his complaint in 2021.

Relevant to the alleged violations, the applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that the refusals disproportionately interfered with his private and family life and failed to sufficiently consider the best interests of his children. He also complained under Article 1 of Protocol No. 7 that the proceedings were procedurally unfair because the decisions rested on classified information not disclosed to him, preventing him from effectively challenging the core grounds against him. The domestic courts considered the classified material sufficient and judicial review adequate, but the applicant argued that this did not cure his inability to contest the decisive secret evidence or ensure proper weighing of his family and children’s interests.

In *Independent Newspapers (Ireland) Limited v. Ireland* (ECtHR, 15 June 2017), the applicant company published the Irish daily newspaper the *Evening Herald*. Between 30 November and 17 December 2004, it ran eleven articles over nine editions about Ms L., a public relations consultant engaged by Government departments. The articles concerned Government contracts awarded to her, particularly while Mr C. held ministerial office. They questioned the tendering process, her qualifications, her remuneration, the work actually done, and her participation in eight foreign trips, including a New York United Nations conference. They also implied an intimate or adulterous relationship between Ms L. and Mr C., referred to her appearance and lifestyle, and used altered or cropped photographs. One front-page photomontage placed her close to the Minister against a New York skyline and suggested, through manipulation, that her skirt had a high slit. The Supreme Court later described the series as a serious and sustained attack on her business and personal integrity.

Ms L. sued the applicant company for defamation. In June 2009, a High Court jury found that the articles meant she had had an extra-marital affair with Mr C. It found the second alleged meaning—that she travelled to New York at public expense but did not attend the conference—was not defamatory. The jury awarded €1,872,000 in damages. Under Irish law at the time, the trial judge was constrained by the *Barrett* rules and *De Rossa* jurisprudence. He could explain the functions of defamation damages—consolation, repairing reputation, and vindication—but could not suggest a figure or range, nor inform the jury of comparable awards. The jury therefore assessed damages with little concrete guidance.

The applicant accepted the finding of defamation, published an apology, and appealed only the quantum. It argued that the award was grossly disproportionate and violated its freedom of expression. In December 2014, the Supreme Court found the award excessive and set it aside. The majority substituted €1.25 million; one judge would have ordered a retrial and indicated €1 million would have been appropriate. The applicant paid an additional €500,000 plus approximately €240,000 in appellate costs.

Before the European Court of Human Rights, the applicant alleged a violation of Article 10 of the Convention. Its core complaint was not the defamation finding itself, but the disproportionately high damages award and the inadequacy and ineffectiveness of domestic safeguards designed to prevent such awards. The key facts were that the jury had broad discretion, the trial judge could not give meaningful guidance on quantum, and appellate review was highly deferential: an award would be disturbed only if so disproportionate that no reasonable jury would have made it. Even after the Supreme Court reduced the sum, it remained very high, and earlier Irish cases showed that retrials could produce equally or more generous awards. The Defamation Act 2009, which introduced clearer factors and allowed the Supreme Court to substitute damages, did not apply to this case.

The ECtHR found a violation of Article 10, holding that the award was disproportionate to the harm suffered and that Irish law and practice at the relevant time did not provide effective safeguards against excessive defamation damages. The case thus concerned the chilling effect of large, unpredictable jury awards on media freedom of expression.

In *Carreto Ribeiro v. Portugal* (Application no. 20075/21), the European Court of Human Rights (Fourth Section), sitting as a Committee, considered an application lodged against Portugal by Vitor Manuel Carreto Ribeiro, born in 1956. The application was introduced on 5 April 2021 under Article 34 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The Portuguese Government were given notice of the application. The judgment was delivered on 25 April 2024, after private deliberations on 4 April 2024. The Committee consisted of Branko Lubarda (President), Anne Louise Bormann, and Sebastian Răduleţu, with Viktoriya Maradudina as Acting Deputy Section Registrar.

The factual background concerns disciplinary proceedings instituted against the applicant by the Portuguese Bar Association. According to the appended table, those proceedings began on 30 July 2008 and ended on 11 March 2014. Their total length was therefore five years, seven months, and twelve days. The proceedings took place at only one level of jurisdiction, before the *Conselho Distrital de Lisboa da Ordem dos Advogados* (Lisbon District Council of the Portuguese Bar Association), under domestic file number 516/2008-L/D.

The applicant relied primarily on Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, complaining of the excessive length of the disciplinary proceedings. Article 6 § 1 guarantees the right to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law in the determination of civil rights and obligations or of any criminal charge. Here, the alleged violation was not directed at the substantive outcome of the disciplinary case, nor at any specific procedural irregularity such as bias or improper evidence-taking. Instead, the core complaint was temporal: that proceedings at a single level of professional disciplinary adjudication lasted more than five and a half years.

The applicant also raised a complaint under Article 13 of the Convention, which guarantees an effective remedy before a national authority for violations of Convention rights. In the context of an excessive-length complaint, Article 13 requires the availability at domestic level of an effective remedy capable of addressing the alleged delay, whether by expediting proceedings or by providing adequate compensation. The applicant therefore argued not only that the disciplinary proceedings were unreasonably long, but also that Portuguese law failed to provide him with an effective domestic remedy for that length.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations are thus narrowly defined: the applicant was subject to disciplinary proceedings by the Portuguese Bar Association; those proceedings commenced on 30 July 2008 and concluded on 11 March 2014; they lasted 5 years, 7 months, and 12 days; and they occurred before one disciplinary body, the Lisbon District Council of the Portuguese Bar Association. On those facts, the applicant alleged violations of Article 6 § 1 and Article 13 of the Convention. The judgment was final but subject to editorial revision.

In *Bernotas v. Lithuania*, the applicant, a Lithuanian national born in 1957, accidentally shot Ž.K. in January 2010 while cleaning a rifle after a hunt. The victim suffered serious abdominal, hip and leg injuries, was hospitalised for months, underwent several surgeries, had a hip replacement, and his working capacity was eventually assessed as diminished by 45% until retirement. The applicant admitted guilt and in February 2011 was convicted of negligently causing serious damage to health; he received a suspended two-year prison sentence. In the criminal proceedings, Ž.K. claimed pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages. The applicant paid part of the sums due, and the courts awarded additional non-pecuniary damages, reduced on appeal to about EUR 10,725. The applicant paid that award.

Separately, the State Social Insurance Fund (SSIF) paid Ž.K. a lost working capacity pension from August 2010. The pension varied over time, depending on assessments of diminished working capacity, length of service, previous salary and economic factors. Payments included approximately EUR 2,687 for 2010–2011, EUR 2,291 for 2011–2013, EUR 3,146 for 2013–2015, EUR 1,021 for 2015–2016, EUR 1,799 for 2016–2017, EUR 5,597 for 2017–2019, and EUR 6,790 for 2019–2022. Relying on Civil Code Article 6.290 §3 and the Law on State Social Insurance, the SSIF required the applicant to reimburse the pension. It argued that social allowances paid because of another person’s unlawful act constitute damage for which the tortfeasor must compensate.

Between 2011 and 2022 the SSIF brought repeated reimbursement claims against the applicant. At first, he agreed to repay some amounts in instalments. Later, he sometimes failed to respond, leading to default judgments which he did not seek to review. From 2017 onward he actively contested the claims. He argued that the victim was employed and earned more than before the accident; that the pension did not necessarily correspond to actual pecuniary damage; and that the working-capacity assessments were inconsistent. In the 2017 proceedings, a forensic examination confirmed that Ž.K.’s 45% diminution in working capacity was directly caused by the hunting accident.

The domestic courts consistently allowed the SSIF’s claims. They held that the lost working capacity pension compensated post-accident loss of income and additional expenses, distinct from the damages already paid in the criminal case. They found that the applicant had caused the damage, that the pension corresponded to the damage sustained, and that increases due to economic factors did not make reimbursement unfair. They rejected his reliance on Constitutional Court and Supreme Court case-law.

The applicant complained that the repeated proceedings and reimbursement obligation violated his fair-trial rights and the principles of fairness, proportionality and legal certainty. He argued that requiring him to reimburse amounts higher than the 2010 pension, based on unforeseeable future factors, was contrary to *lex retro non agit*. He also submitted that the SSIF’s successive claims forced him into repeated litigation, contrary to Article 6 §1, and that he had already fully compensated the victim. In 2022, a further SSIF claim was adjourned pending the European Court’s examination of his application. The core alleged violation therefore concerned the fairness and reasonableness of imposing on him a continuing, unpredictable reimbursement obligation through repeated civil proceedings.
