text:
In *Zavridou v. Cyprus* (Application no. 14680/22), the European Court of Human Rights considered a Cypriot mother’s complaint under Article 8 that the domestic authorities failed to secure her custodial rights and to enforce domestic custody and contact decisions concerning her two children, C.K. (born 2010) and A.K. (born 2012).

The applicant separated from the children’s father in 2018. A July 2018 temporary Family Court order gave both parents contact rights. In November 2018 the order was amended to require the father to return the children to the applicant after contact and to establish their residence with her. The father did not comply. The children remained with him, and the applicant’s contact became infrequent and then stopped in March 2019. In June 2019, Mental Health Services reports found that the father had alienated the children from their mother and recommended that contact be immediately re-established without the father present. In September 2019, the Social Welfare Services recommended that custody and care be granted to the mother, that the father’s contact be gradually reduced, and that the family receive psychological support. On 25 October 2019, the Nicosia Family Court granted the applicant custody and made a residence order in her favour.

Between October 2019 and March 2020, the SWS, police, and multidisciplinary meetings attempted to enforce the orders, but without success. The children were hostile towards the applicant, and the father was obstructive and not genuinely willing to comply. The applicant lodged enforcement proceedings in December 2019. In February 2020, the Supreme Court refused a habeas corpus petition. In June 2020, the Family Court ordered the father to surrender the children within four days, warning of possible imprisonment. An enforcement attempt on 12 June 2020 failed because of the children’s opposition. A police report noted that the father had not prepared the children psychologically or practically, leaving them barefoot and in pyjamas, and suggested investigating contempt and psychological violence and considering temporary SWS custody. A further enforcement application followed in July 2020.

The Ombudsman’s August 2020 report was critical. It found that the police had failed to immediately investigate the father’s disobedience under section 137 of the Criminal Code, treating the initial order as merely regulatory rather than mandatory. It stated that police inaction from July 2018 had caused lost time and growing alienation, despite 2019 police guidelines requiring proactive investigation and possible arrest for non-compliance with mandatory family court contact orders. The Ombudsman also faulted the SWS for doing too little beyond preparing reports to restore the mother-child relationship. It recommended reassessment of the children, possible partial removal of parental responsibility, individualised measures, and police investigation of disobedience and child abduction offences.

In February 2021, the Family Court found the father guilty of non-compliance, noting methodical, systematic and deliberate alienation of the children from the applicant. He was sentenced to 45 days’ imprisonment in March 2021. During his imprisonment, SWS attempts to enforce custody failed; relatives were present, the father continued to influence the children negatively from prison, and the children stopped attending school. In April 2021, the Supreme Court dismissed a mandamus petition seeking forceful police removal of the children, finding no such police duty. Contact remained brief, often at the father’s home, with him present and later cameras installed.

In January 2023, the father was convicted on over 60 charges of disobedience and sentenced to one year. The Family Court temporarily assigned custody to the Director of the SWS in January/March 2023. A.K. later moved in with the applicant, while C.K. refused. After the father’s release, the children again became hostile, including physically violent, and returned to the father. SWS custody became absolute in April 2024; the second custody application remains pending. The alleged Article 8 violation concerns the authorities’ failure to effectively enforce custody and contact orders and protect the applicant’s family life.

**Albertina Carvalho e Filhos Lda v. Portugal** (Application no. 23603/14) concerned a Portuguese company’s complaint to the European Court of Human Rights that civil enforcement proceedings had lasted unreasonably long and that Portugal lacked an effective domestic remedy for such delay. The applicant company, based in Valongo, lodged its application on 14 March 2014. On 18 November 2015, the Court communicated to the Portuguese Government the complaints concerning the length of the civil proceedings and the absence of an effective remedy; the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible.

The underlying facts began on 18 July 2005, when the applicant company brought enforcement proceedings before the Valongo Court against M.C. It sought payment of an alleged debt of EUR 32,992.99 plus EUR 18,413.35 in interest, amounting to EUR 51,406, and further interest until full repayment. A judicial enforcement officer was appointed in October 2005. M.C. was summoned on 20 November 2005 and, on 14 December 2005, lodged an opposition to enforcement, which was joined to the enforcement proceedings the following day.

The proceedings then experienced repeated delays and procedural difficulties. Information was exchanged between the Valongo Court and the judicial enforcement officer about the date of M.C.’s summons. On 30 May 2006, the applicant replied to the opposition. Between February 2007 and August 2008, several steps were taken concerning the possible freezing of M.C.’s bank accounts. In February 2008, a preparatory decision was issued in the opposition proceedings, identifying established and outstanding facts.

In November 2010, the applicant company’s lawyer withdrew. In December 2010, the court requested a report from the judicial enforcement officer on steps taken. In January 2011, the court was unable to contact the applicant at the address provided. In December 2011, a hearing in the opposition proceedings was scheduled for May 2012, but it was postponed to November 2012 because of the health of M.C.’s lawyer, and then postponed again to 6 March 2013, when it finally took place.

Meanwhile, in December 2011, the Chamber of Judicial Officers informed the Valongo Court that a new judicial enforcement officer was to be appointed; a new officer was appointed in January 2012. Another lawyer began representing the applicant company. Between September and December 2012, discussions took place between the new enforcement officer, the court and the previous officer about transmitting the case documents. Between April and October 2013, correspondence continued about whether and by whom the applicant company was represented.

On 29 April 2013, the Valongo Court ruled against the applicant company in the opposition proceedings. The applicant appealed to the Oporto Court of Appeal, which upheld the first-instance decision on 20 May 2014. The applicant then appealed to the Supreme Court of Justice, but on 11 September 2014 the Oporto Court of Appeal rejected the appeal because no grounds of appeal had been submitted. The enforcement proceedings were then terminated. In total, the proceedings had lasted approximately nine years and two months.

The key facts relevant to the alleged violations were therefore the prolonged duration of the enforcement and opposition proceedings, repeated procedural delays, changes of judicial enforcement officers, difficulties in transferring case files, uncertainty over the applicant’s legal representation, the court’s inability to contact the applicant, and repeated postponements of the hearing. The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention concerning the length of proceedings and Article 13 concerning the lack of an effective domestic remedy.

Pasquinelli and Others v. San Marino (App. no. 24622/22) is an ECtHR First Section judgment delivered on 29 August 2024 and final on 29 November 2024. The applicants were nineteen San Marino nationals, six Italian nationals and one Moldovan national, all healthcare and social-health workers employed by San Marino’s Social Security Institute (SSI). The case arose from their refusal to be vaccinated against COVID-19 and the resulting employment measures.

In May 2021 the SSI urged the applicants to be vaccinated under section 14 of Law no. 85/2021. They declined. The legal regime was then amended by Law no. 97/2021, ratified by Law no. 107/2021, which entered into force on 16 June 2021. Section 8 provided that, for unvaccinated SSI healthcare and social-health personnel, the SSI first had to consider reorganising the service to minimise contact with users. If reorganisation was possible, the workers could remain on duty but had to take an antigen test every 48 hours at their own expense (€7 per swab). If reorganisation was not possible, options included reassignment to other SSI services or vacant public-administration posts with the corresponding salary, or using accrued ordinary/other leave or 2020 overtime. If none of these options was viable or accepted, the worker could be temporarily suspended with a gross monthly allowance of €600, plus family allowances. Suspension involved performing socially useful activities, and refusal to do so meant losing the allowance. Workers who could not be vaccinated because of documented certified health conditions were entitled to full-salary leave. Law no. 72/2022 ended the health emergency on 1 April 2022, but maintained measures for this sector until section 17 was repealed on 29 September 2022 by Law no. 137/2022.

A domestic constitutional challenge by popular initiative alleged that sections 2 and 6 of Law no. 107/2021 breached equality and non-discrimination, and that section 8 unlawfully interfered with healthcare workers’ private sphere, right to work, self-determination and health. It argued that the vaccines were experimental or conditionally authorised and that vaccinated persons could still spread the virus. Only San Marino citizens eligible to vote could participate, so the Italian and Moldovan applicants could not. By judgment no. 11 of 2 November 2021, the Constitutional Court declared the application admissible but upheld the law. It found there was no compulsory vaccination, only a recommendation and limited differential treatment. The pandemic created extraordinary necessity; protecting public health and vulnerable health-service users justified the measures under positive obligations to protect life. Referring to Vavřička and Others v. the Czech Republic, it held that even mandatory vaccination could be justified for serious disease, so lesser measures were proportionate. The vaccinated/unvaccinated distinction was objectively justified because vaccinated persons suffered less severe consequences and spread infection less. The measures were not disciplinary but aimed to balance the right to work against users’ right to health, with temporary restrictions and social solidarity prevailing.

Separately, four suspended applicants sought administrative annulment. Three applications were inadmissible on procedural grounds concerning the authority form on 7 October 2021; one applicant withdrew on 23 December 2021.

The key facts relevant to the alleged Convention violations are that the applicants suffered employment consequences solely because they refused COVID-19 vaccination, including testing costs, reassignment, leave use, suspension, reduced pay and socially useful work, while vaccinated staff were exempt from comparable burdens. The central issues concern private life, freedom of conscience/religion, work/property rights and non-discrimination.

text:
In *Bakradze v. Georgia* (Application no. 20592/21), the applicant, Maia Bakradze, is a former Georgian judge and founding member and President of the NGO “The Unity of Judges of Georgia” (“Unity of Judges”). She complained before the European Court of Human Rights that she was discriminated against in two judicial competitions because of her role in that organisation and her critical stance towards the High Council of Justice (“HCJ”) and its judiciary policies. She relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention read with Article 14, and on Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

The applicant had served as a judge without any disciplinary proceedings and was dismissed in September 2015 after her ten-year term expired. Unity of Judges, founded in 2013 by judges, aimed to support judicial independence and transparency and became vocal in criticising the HCJ, particularly regarding recruitment, promotion, secondment, reserve lists, bonus rules, and the lack of reasoned appointment decisions. Its executive director made public statements critical of the HCJ, including a letter challenging bonus payments to judges in managerial positions, which some HCJ members found insulting.

In October 2015 and May 2016, the applicant applied for vacancies at the Tbilisi Court of Appeal. In both competitions she was interviewed and then rejected. She alleged that the interviews were not focused on her judicial qualifications. During the December 2015 interview, after brief questions about education and experience, HCJ members asked extensively about Unity of Judges—its aims, membership, relations with the Association of Judges, and critical Facebook posts by its executive director. She was asked whether she agreed with allegedly insulting posts. One HCJ judge said he had been personally offended and suggested she, as a representative of Unity of Judges, should be held responsible. The applicant objected that these questions were unrelated to her competences. She was rejected without reasons.

In the June 2016 interview, questions again focused on public criticism of judges, NGO media campaigns allegedly aimed at discrediting the judiciary, and whether such criticism was healthy or permitted. She was also asked about her salary as President of Unity of Judges. She was again rejected without reasons. Under the domestic system, interviews were closed, voting was secret, and refusals contained no reasons and were not appealable at the relevant time.

The applicant brought discrimination proceedings before the Tbilisi City Court. She argued that the real reasons for her rejection were her role in Unity of Judges and her critical views. She requested recordings and files of other candidates’ interviews to compare how interviews were conducted, but the courts refused. The Public Defender of Georgia submitted that the prima facie threshold for discrimination was lower than the final standard and warned of risks of bias, lack of transparency, secret voting, and unreasoned decisions. A document by HCJ member V.M. alleged that the appointment system had been abused to undermine judges with opposing views and that “cancelled ballots” were used against Unity of Judges members.

The domestic courts dismissed her claim, finding she had not established a prima facie case; therefore, the burden of proof did not shift to the HCJ. They relied on statistics showing that many Unity members participated in competitions and some were appointed. The applicant countered that 41% of Unity members were refused reappointment compared with 18% of non-members, and that successful members had not been vocal critics and later left the organisation. The Court of Appeal and Supreme Court upheld the refusal, finding no bias, accepting that the HCJ had wide discretion in questioning, and treating V.M.’s document as subjective. The ECtHR gave notice of the complaints under Articles 10 and 11 in conjunction with Article 14, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 12.

**Case: Domenjoud v. France (Applications nos. 34749/16 and 79607/17), ECtHR, 16 May 2024**

The case concerned two compulsory residence orders imposed under French state-of-emergency legislation during the 2015 UN climate change conference (COP21). The applicants, brothers Cédric and Joël Domenjoud, were left-wing/environmental activists. They complained before the European Court of Human Rights of violations of Articles 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention and, alternatively, Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, arguing that the measures were not covered by France’s Article 15 derogation.

The background was the November 2015 Islamist terrorist attacks in Paris and Saint-Denis, after which France declared a state of emergency under the Law of 3 April 1955, extended it several times, and notified a derogation under Article 15 ECHR on 24 November 2015. Despite the terrorist threat, France hosted COP21 in Paris and Le Bourget from 30 November to 12 December 2015. Security measures included compulsory residence orders, demonstration bans and security perimeters.

On 25 November 2015, the Minister of the Interior placed each applicant under a residence restriction in his municipality until 12 December 2015. They had to report to a police station three times daily and remain at home between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. The orders relied on general concerns about violent “black bloc” protests disrupting COP21 and on specific intelligence. The Minister described both brothers as leaders of the radical protest movement in greater Paris. Cédric was alleged to have organised meetings in a squat, planned blockades and violent actions, and to have participated in the August 2015 Bure anti-authoritarian camp, including an attack on the ANDRA radioactive waste site involving severed fibre-optic cables, torn fencing and Molotov cocktails; he was also seen at a banned migrant rally in Paris. Joël was alleged to have been active in anti-state and anti-capitalist actions, helped organise the Bure camp and preparations to disrupt COP21.

The applicants challenged the orders before administrative courts. They argued that the measures seriously interfered with individual liberty, freedom of movement and family life, and were disproportionate. They also complained that the Minister relied on secret, unsigned “notes blanches” from intelligence services, which they could not effectively rebut. Domestic courts upheld the measures. The Conseil d’État held that compulsory residence orders did not amount to deprivation of liberty under Article 5 and were not manifestly incompatible with Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. It accepted that, during the emergency, such orders could be based on substantial grounds that a person’s conduct threatened public safety and order, in view of the emergency’s triggering danger. The Constitutional Council upheld section 6 of the 1955 Law, subject to proportionality review. Administrative courts found the notes blanches admissible if precise, detailed and not seriously contested, and concluded the measures were necessary and proportionate.

Before the ECtHR, the applicants alleged breaches of Articles 5, 6 and 13 and, alternatively, Article 2 of Protocol No. 4. They contended that the residence orders were not truly covered by Article 15 and that the emergency regime allowed public-order measures against activists during COP21. The Court gave notice of the complaints under Articles 5 and 6 § 1 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, declaring the remainder inadmissible. The key alleged violations therefore concerned the deprivation of liberty/freedom of movement, the fairness of proceedings relying on secret intelligence notes, and the compatibility of the emergency measures with France’s derogation.

In *T.V. v. Croatia* (ECHR, Second Section, 11 June 2024), the applicant, a Slovenian national, complained under Articles 2, 3 and 13 about the death of her partner, V.D., during a Croatian police intervention and the alleged ineffectiveness of the ensuing criminal investigation.

V.D. suffered from schizophrenia. On 16 November 2017 he left a Slovenian psychiatric institution and entered Croatia. Croatian border police were informed by Slovenian police that he had travelled to Opuzen and posed a danger to himself and others. The same day, after a fight at a hotel, hotel staff called the Metković police. The responding officers allegedly knew V.D. might be a mentally disabled person in distress.

At the hotel car park, four officers found V.D. sitting on his car, visibly mentally distressed and mumbling. He emptied his pockets but refused orders to turn around and spread his legs. He took out his phone, shouted that he would press a button and “blow up” everyone, then sat on the ground. After repeated warnings, Officer G. used pepper spray. V.D. lay on his side, bleeding from biting his lips and tongue. Three officers then forced him onto his stomach and put his hands behind his back. He resisted, banged his head on the pavement, and bit off part of his little finger. Police called an ambulance at about 2:35 p.m.; officers, joined by a fifth, continued holding him face down until the ambulance arrived around 2:47 p.m. A doctor gave him a sedative and noted he was bleeding, blue in the face, and had swallowed part of his finger. He was transported face down, restrained with three straps, on a roughly 1.5-hour journey to Dubrovnik General Hospital. After a second sedative, he was found dead. The coroner recorded natural death from cardiac arrest.

The scene was washed before inspection. The official autopsy found no violent death, only scratches, a finger fragment in the oesophagus, and five broken ribs likely from a fall; it deemed the injuries grave but not causally linked to death. A police report found the force lawful and proportionate. The applicant arranged a second autopsy in Ljubljana, which found additional inflammation, lung and brain swelling, myocardial fibrosis, acute cardiac arrest, and two front teeth recently knocked out.

In November 2018 the applicant filed criminal complaints against the police for serious bodily injury resulting in death and against the ambulance doctor and nurse for medical negligence. The complaints were rejected in February 2019 based on natural causes. After higher-level review, interviews took place in 2020 and a formal investigation opened in October 2020. A May 2021 forensic report concluded V.D. suffered a violent death from mental trauma: grave injury resulted from his resisting police while prone, self-harming, and officers pressing hard on his back. Those factors, combined with police and medical actions, aggravated his agitated mental state and led to shock and cardiac arrest as the mechanism of dying. It found no medical negligence but stated medical staff should have sat next to him during transport.

In August 2021 the complaint was again rejected: force was proportionate, no fatal injuries were caused, and medical staff were not negligent. This was upheld. In July 2023 the Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint, finding the investigation independent and thorough despite delays, and that V.D. died from serious mental trauma caused by extreme agitation and resistance, with police measures lawful and proportionate. Civil damages proceedings remained pending.

The alleged violations concern whether the police use of force and prone restraint against a mentally ill person, delayed medical assistance, and conflicting medical evidence breached substantive Articles 2 and 3, and whether the investigation was effective and adequate under Articles 2, 3 and 13.

**Case: Mukhtarli v. Azerbaijan and Georgia (App. no. 39503/17), ECtHR, 5 September 2024**

The applicant, Afgan Mukhtarli, is an Azerbaijani investigative journalist known for critical reporting on the Azerbaijani Government. After alleged harassment and persecution, he moved with his family to Georgia in January 2015 and applied for asylum, continuing to report on high-level corruption in Azerbaijan.

The case concerns his alleged abduction in Georgia, ill-treatment, and forcible transfer to Azerbaijan on 29 May 2017, and the subsequent responses of the Georgian and Azerbaijani authorities.

According to the applicant, at about 7:30 p.m. on 29 May 2017, while walking home in Tbilisi, he was stopped by four unknown men speaking Georgian; three wore uniforms allegedly belonging to the Georgian criminal police. They forced him into a silver Opel car, handcuffed him, and beat him. He was driven toward Tbilisi International Airport and then in the direction of Sagarejo, blindfolded, and transferred between vehicles twice. In the final car, Azerbaijani music was playing, and he realized he had been handed over to Azerbaijanis across the State border. The men reportedly made frequent telephone reports to a person they called “Mr General.”

At about 10:40 p.m., he arrived at an unknown location and saw Azerbaijani State Border Service insignia. He realized he was detained in a military unit in Balakan District, Azerbaijan. Servicemen told him he had illegally crossed the border and allegedly found EUR 10,000 in cash in his pocket, which he said was not his. His mobile telephone, Georgian bank and transport cards, and coins were seized. He did not have his international passport.

The Azerbaijani Government gave a different account: border guards spotted the applicant moving from Georgia into Azerbaijan, ordered him to stop, and after he tried to flee and allegedly punched an officer, he was apprehended and subjected to administrative arrest for breaching border regulations. He was transferred to Baku, where criminal proceedings were instituted on various charges, including illegal border crossing, resisting an official, and smuggling.

The Georgian Government submitted that the applicant’s allegations were unsubstantiated and unsupported by evidence. Georgian officials publicly called for a thorough investigation and denied involvement by Georgian State institutions. An Azerbaijani parliamentarian claimed the arrest resulted from cooperation between Georgian and Azerbaijani intelligence services, but Azerbaijan’s Prosecutor General’s Office denied this.

Georgian authorities opened an investigation into the applicant’s disappearance under Article 143 § 1 of the Criminal Code, later transferred to the Chief Prosecutor’s Office. Investigators questioned many witnesses, reviewed CCTV footage, interviewed border guards and customs officers, and sought mutual legal assistance from Azerbaijan. However, key CCTV footage was missing, deleted, or unreadable; border-crossing footage was initially unavailable; and several requests to Azerbaijani authorities went unanswered. The applicant alleged that Georgia failed to protect him and to conduct an effective investigation into his abduction, ill-treatment, and forcible transfer.

Against Azerbaijan, he alleged that his arrest and detention were unlawful and unjustified, and that his abduction and prosecution were intended to silence and punish him for his journalistic activities. He relied on Articles 3, 5 §§ 1(c), 3 and 4, 8, 10, 13, and 18 of the Convention, Article 2 of Protocol No. 4, and Article 1 of Protocol No. 7.
